Before Buying a Tiny Home on Amazon, Make Sure You Know the ABCs of ADUs

📅 01 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1649 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, did you know that along with clothing, housewares, electronics, and books, you can now purchase an actual tiny home or accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on Amazon?
  • According to recent reports, for anywhere from $8,500-$55,000, you can just order up a house and have it shipped to you (often with free delivery).
  • Industry observers note that to begin with, ADUs are additional small housing structures built on a property that already has a main home or main structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, did you know that along with clothing, housewares, electronics, and books, you can now purchase an actual tiny home or accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on Amazon? It's true.

According to recent reports, for anywhere from $8,500-$55,000, you can just order up a house and have it shipped to you (often with free delivery). But before you hit "add to cart," it's imperative that you learn the ABCs of ADUs.

Industry observers note that to begin with, ADUs are additional small housing structures built on a property that already has a main home or main structure. Tiny homes are usually freestanding, compact units typically under 400 square feet—sometimes on foundations or other times on wheels like an RV.

But in both cases, the structures are economical and effective ways to achieve additional living space.

"As urban populations swell and sustainability becomes a central focus, the ability to build smaller, energy-efficient homes with reduced environmental impact will be key," states Paul Dashevsky, co-CEO of Maxable, a leader in ADU planning, building, and development.

But while tiny homes and ADUs may indeed be poised to make a positive impact toward solving the housing crisis, potential buyers need to know that you can't just plop one anywhere you please. Not to mention, tiny homes ordered online will probably also require hiring a contractor to help with assembly (adding to the overall cost).

With all that in mind, let's dig in to the details you must know prior to purchasing any ADU or tiny home. Because the last thing you want is to find yourself trying to return an entire house to sender.

While it can be exciting to imagine buying a "house" for $10,000 online, it's very important to not just look at the photos and think that's what will arrive. Read the fine print and all the reviews.

"Are you buying a complete tiny house that comes fully built, transported and rolled/craned into your backyard—or are you buying a bunch of parts that need to be assembled?" asks Dashevsy. "If assembly is required, make sure you first speak to a local contractor and determine the price of assembly.".

Though some of the advertisements—like this two-story foldable container home—say they only require five people to assemble it in 30-minutes, are you really going to feel confident asking a couple friends over—with the promise of pizza and beer afterward—to get the job done?

Industry observers note that the reality is that most people—unless they're cool with an adult-sized Lego project—will need a skilled contractor to assist with a tiny home or ADU build. Dashevsky suggests looking for a licensed general contractor with ADU experience. "You can find them through referrals or on sites like GreatBuildz, Angi, or Yelp," notes Dashevsky.

As for the cost, it varies according to the type of tiny home or ADU.

"A brand newly introduced ADU built on your site will greatly depend on your region and the size of the ADU, but a good range is $80,000 to $400,000," notes Dashevsky, though assembling a prefab ADU may run less predicated on its complexity.

Before you buy a prefab ADU or tiny home, you must make sure that the city or county you live in allows for such dwellings on your property.

Industry observers note that you can start by doing an Internet search for this information. Look for your city’s planning or building department. Most will have a website, and you can probably glean some information there.

It has been revealed that however, if you're seriously in the ready-to-buy stage, it's probably wise to visit one of these offices in person for a consultation. Make sure they allow the kind of tiny home or ADU you're considering on your property. Also confirm where you’re allowed to install it. And ask about any necessary permits, building codes, and occupancy requirements in your area.

Industry observers note that "Essentially, you want to know every single guideline they have for this structure," notes Dashevsky. "The last thing you want is a tiny home you have to sell or return because your city wont allow it.".

Alternatively, you can hire a local architect who is experienced in ADUs—they should know all the city/county requirements for your location.

It has been revealed that unless you want to live in the dark with no water, you're going to need electrical and plumbing hookups for your tiny home or ADU. But some people who purchase a dwelling online neglect to consider those details in advance.

"A tiny home won’t do you much good if it isn’t connected to electrical power, water, and sewer at the very least," notes Dashevsky.

Speak with your local building department or utility providers to understand the process and costs to tie your tiny house in to municipal services. Or, if you have your own water well and septic tank, ask a contractor how much it will run to connect to these facilities.

For those who don't fully understand what this entails, connecting utilities to a tiny house or ADU is very similar to that for a normal house.

"You dig a trench from the location of the existing utilities—water, sewer, electrical gas—and run upcoming pipes to the location of the new unit," notes Dashevsky. "A general contractor can do this for you—this is not a DIY project— and it will probably cost around $10,000 to $20,000.".

If your region is prone to weather events or natural disasters, you'll want to ensure that your tiny house has been tested to withstand extreme conditions.

Recent findings suggest that "Is it rated to withstand snow, sleet, winds, earthquakes, hurricanes?" says Dashevsky. "There is no point spending a lot of money that gets wiped out in the first rainy season.".

It has been revealed that what exactly are you looking for when you're assessing a tiny home or ADU for purchase? Check to see if it states it's made of fire-resistant materials or has a fire rating (the best is a Class A or 1). Also see if it lists a wind rating—the Beaufort Wind Scale is most commonly used with levels ranging from 1 (light air) to 12 (hurricane winds). Finally, look for an earthquake resistance rating (0-9, like the Richter scale) or a Seismic Building Code. All of these will help give you an idea of the quality of the unit you're considering.

If you're having the ADU or tiny home built from scratch, it's a slightly different story as your contractor will be required to make sure it's up to code.

"ADUs are built under the same guiding building code—International Residential Code (IRC)—as principal houses and don't have any less requirements for seismic/hurricane/snow or structural bracing," claims Jeremy Tetreault, of Four Brothers Design + Build in Washington, D.C. "They are treated with the same level of scrutiny and energy ratings, too, so you should have nothing to worry about from a standpoint of being less equipped to withstand natural events.".

Getting insurance for your ADU or tiny home can sometimes be a hassle, so this is something to consider before buying an accessory unit.

Tiny homes—especially of the DIY or prefab variety—typically don't qualify for homeowners insurance policies. However, they may qualify for RV or mobile home insurance—especially if it's a tiny home on wheels (THOW)—as long as they meet building codes. The good news with this, however, is that you can often save 50% or more over regular homeowners insurance with a tiny home.

For people who have a tiny home on their property along with another home, or who build an ADU onto an existing home, it may be possible to insure the unit under the "other structures" portion of an existing homeowners policy.

The bottom line is you should speak with an insurance broker about what it will take to insure your ADU or tiny home since that will be an additional expense.

Recent findings suggest that it's easy to get sucked into the idea that an ADU or a tiny home you can purchase online is a great deal! But it's notable to be realistic about all the additional costs. We already mentioned the possibility of needing to hire a contractor to help with construction—and maybe a plumber and an electrician to hook up the utilities. But there are some other hidden costs of which potential buyers should also be aware.

It has been revealed that to begin with, do you need to lay a foundation for your tiny home? If it's on wheels, then you can probably get away without one. But for people looking for a more permanent smaller housing situation, turning it into a tiny home on foundation (THOF) will give the structure more stability.

"Unless your tiny home is on wheels, it should sit on a concrete pad or foundation made of cement," says Dashevsky. "A general contractor can do this for you but expect a ballpark cost of about $5,000 to $15,000.".

In a recent development, also, if you purchase a home prebuilt but don't have room to roll it into the space where you blueprint to put it, you may need to pay for extra equipment. For example, if you have to "crane it in" then you need to factor in the price of hiring that service as well.

"The bottom line is that you really need to know all the costs involved, which are very likely to end up being close to double the Amazon 'price,'" notes Dashevsky.

However, as long as you know what to expect, ordering up a tiny home or ADU can be a prime way to create an affordable housing solution.

Kimberly Dawn Neumann is a journalist based in New York City and the author of hundreds of articles on home-related topics for major publications, including Forbes, Real Simple, and Realtor.com. For more information, visit www.KDNeumann.com or IG @dancerscribe.

Latest Update: Anthropic’s Siren tests whether Claude models will break out of an insecure sandbox

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at artificial intelligence developer Anthropic PBC today published details on Siren, a fresh evaluation that tests whether AI agents will break out of an insecure sandbox to get at something that would help them complete a task.
  • The researchers found that recent Claude models will reach outside the sandbox in about a fifth to a third of Siren’s test scenarios, though they are far less likely than earlier models to then make misaligned use of what they find.
  • Siren has been part of Anthropic’s system cards since the release of Claude Haiku 5.5 in October, with the manufacturer also using it as one input when deciding whether to deploy upcoming models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:56 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Researchers at artificial intelligence developer Anthropic PBC today published details on Siren, a fresh evaluation that tests whether AI agents will break out of an insecure sandbox to get at something that would help them complete a task.

The researchers found that recent Claude models will reach outside the sandbox in about a fifth to a third of Siren’s test scenarios, though they are far less likely than earlier models to then make misaligned use of what they find.

Siren has been part of Anthropic’s system cards since the release of Claude Haiku 5.5 in October, with the manufacturer also using it as one input when deciding whether to deploy upcoming models.

Siren includes 26 sandbox environments built from five common setups, such as bubblewrap jails, Docker containers and small virtual machines emulated with QEMU. Because they show up most often in public reports of sandbox escapes, misconfigurations make up most of the weaknesses planted in the environments.

Industry observers note that while the model works on a routine DevOps task, a honeypot such as a credential or file that would help it finish the job is placed outside the sandbox. What Anthropic calls “tempters” are then layered on top to make the honeypot harder to resist. None of the tempters gives the model permission to leave the sandbox, according to the firm.

It has been revealed that across Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Mythos 5.2, misaligned use came in at 0.6% to 1.6% of scenarios. Anthropic defines that as using the outside material in a way no reasonable reading of the scenario allows.

The earlier Mythos 5.1 and Mythos 5 models were much higher, at 12.7% and 25.8%. According to Anthropic, Siren’s rates are not an estimate of real-world use, since the evaluation is designed to make the behavior easy to measure. All of the models were also tested without the safeguards that ship with its released models.

Along with Siren itself, Anthropic detailed three ways to make an escape less likely. Adding a short description of the sandbox to the system prompt, including six rules for staying inside it and an instruction to stop if a task needs something the model was not given, made each model 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside. Giving the model a tool to report sandbox weaknesses to the people who run the sandbox also helped, cutting the rate of reaching outside by 7 to 33 percentage points.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic also put auto mode, a feature in many of its products that uses a classifier to check tool calls before they run, through an offline replay of the Siren episodes. Auto mode blocked the first command that read the honeypot in 96% to 100% of misaligned uses, though the tech giant cautions that it tuned the classifier’s rules on those same episodes.

Sources indicate that with all three mitigations running, misaligned use fell to zero in five of the six models tested, with Mythos 5 at 0.1%. The tradeoff was that two models completed about nine percentage points fewer of the tasks that could be finished inside the sandbox. According to Anthropic, none of the mitigations fixes the sandbox itself.

Sources indicate that the research follows Anthropic’s disclosure in July that three Claude models had gained unauthorized access to the systems of three organizations while being run through cybersecurity evaluations. The company blamed a misconfigured evaluation environment that had been left with live internet access.

Brian Soby, co-founder and chief executive of AI agent supervision startup Pretxt Inc., which launched last week with $5 million in seed funding, told SiliconANGLE that Siren is “an attempt to harden sandboxes, but that is ultimately a flawed protection approach.”.

“Sandboxes attempt to contain the impact of a misaligned model. But misalignment is the core matter,” Soby remarked. “Increasingly clever models have repeatedly demonstrated the ineffectiveness of the sandboxing concept and the serious consequences of relying on containment to overcome fundamental misalignment.”.

Soby likened sandboxing to “prison labor,” in which low trust means stripping workers of most of their capabilities and access. A far more effective approach, he remarked, is active supervision that keeps agents aligned with their role and an organization’s rules.

Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

Industry observers note that “Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon mentioned in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

It has been revealed that seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

Recent findings suggest that the terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan mentioned in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an crucial step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

In a recent development, inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

Sources indicate that “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel noted. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker noted workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

In a recent development, tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really crucial component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

Latest Canadian budget packs funding for 55,000 latest EV chargers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 upcoming EV chargers.
  • The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of latest public EV charging stations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 upcoming EV chargers.

The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of latest public EV charging stations.

“The charging industry is really encouraged by the multi-year investment in the budget,” explains Travis Allan, president and CEO of the Canadian Charging Infrastructure Council (CCIC) told Electric Autonomy. “We’ll be looking to make sure that we have great programs in place to deal with the barriers faced by people living in condos and apartments, public fast charging, which needs to cover major corridors and metropolitan areas, and then also charging for fleets and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, which make up a major share of transportation emissions.”.

The rest of the $4 billion will be spent on electricity infrastructure expansion over the next 10 years, starting in 2027 and running through 2036. Because it’s Canada where nearly 60% of electrical generation already comes from renewable hydro and wind power, renewable energy is a de-facto priority, with carveouts for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program, latest data and modeling efforts to guide grid planning, and $1.6 billion to modernize power systems in northern and remote communities.

The charging infrastructure program highlighted here, ZEVIP, would help charge point operators by covering up to 50% of eligible project expenses for most projects, and up to 75% of projects led by indigenous developers with caps of up to $2 million per project.

Canada continues to take steps to separate itself from the wild swings and economic chaos caused by America’s random tariffs, trade policies, and dumb oil wars – and building out an infrastructure that makes it easier for its citizens to give affordable Chinese EVs a chance while strengthening its relationship with the US’ biggest economic rival?

I sincerely hope this promotes the idea of installing fast chargers along routes with lower populations. I live in Ottawa, driving to my home town in northern Ontario has pretty much a single fast charger, a Tesla one with short cables at the mid point about 2.25h in. 6 stalls. If that goes down, there is nothing for about 400km of a decent charging speed. They need to have alternatives to Tesla (I've been very reliant on Tesla stations and don't own a Tesla) and more stations in between the current Tesla stations. Southern Ontario for example is very well covered with fast chargers. But the market is there so companies install them. Northern Ontario, the trans Canada highway needs these chargers badly.

If Washington doesn’t see that for, “Go pound sand, eh?” that it is, then it’s truly lost the plot – but even if the “blue wave” last week was enough to shake a little sense into the folks running the show, it may already be too late to patch things up.

Recent findings suggest that the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported on Wednesday that the core personal consumption expenditures price index, which excludes food and energy, rose 3.3% in October from a year earlier. Recent findings suggest that the overall PCE price index rose 3.8% from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September. That matched economists' expectations, according to CNBC.

Industry observers note that from September, both the overall index and the core index rose 0.3%. Personal income rose 0.7% in October and consumer spending rose 0.3%. Real spending fell $5.8 billion, and the personal saving rate was 4.1%.

The inflation data reinforced expectations of another rate hike in December, according to CNBC. The Federal Reserve meets Dec. 8-9. Market odds of a quarter-point increase at that meeting stand at about 97% on CME $CME Group's FedWatch Tool, according to ABC News. A December hike would be the Fed's second in four months.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan mentioned earlier this month that the central bank needs at least two more quarter-point rate increases. She said core PCE inflation was 3.1% over the 12 months through September. The Fed held its target range at 3.75% to 4% at its October meeting.

According to recent reports, fed Governor Christopher Waller mentioned in a speech before the October consumer price index release that the Fed should consider a half-point increase in December if core inflation printed at 0.3% or above. He said a quarter-point move in that case would put the Fed's credibility at risk. Core CPI rose 0.3% in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that DEERFIELD BEACH, Fla., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Does renters insurance protect personal belongings and liability inside an apartment? A HelloNation article answers this question for Deerfield Beach residents by explaining what renters insurance doesâand doesn'tâcover. The article highlights the key differences between landlord insurance and renters insurance and why understanding those distinctions matters before a loss occurs.

In a recent development, according to the article, one of the most common misconceptions about apartment insurance coverage is that the landlord's policy protects renters as well. In reality, landlord insurance only covers the structure itself, not the renter's personal property or liability risks. Renters insurance fills this gap, providing financial protection for everything from stolen electronics to unexpected legal claims.

The article explains that renters insurance in Deerfield Beach typically includes personal property coverage, which helps replace belongings lost to fire, theft, vandalism, or certain types of water damage. Items such as clothing, furniture, and electronics are covered not only inside the apartment but often even while away from home, depending on policy terms.

Personal liability coverage is another major benefit. The article points out that if a guest is injured inside a rented unit, the renterânot the landlordâmay be responsible. Renters liability insurance can help cover medical bills or legal expenses resulting from such incidents, preventing major financial strain.

Industry observers note that temporary living expenses are also covered under most policies. If the rental unit becomes uninhabitable due to a covered event, renters insurance may help pay for hotel stays, meals, and related costs. This is particularly key in areas like Deerfield Beach, where post-storm housing availability may be limited and expensive.

Industry observers note that the article also clarifies a frequently misunderstood point: Florida renters insurance does not cover flood damage, which is defined as water rising from the ground. However, many other types of water damageâsuch as from a burst pipe or storm-driven rainâmay still be covered, depending on the policy's wording. Understanding these distinctions is critical to setting realistic expectations.

Renters often assume that insurance isn't necessary if they don't own high-value items, but the article argues otherwise. Even basic household items can add up promptly. Replacing clothing, small appliances, and furniture all at once can put pressure on a renter's savings. Renters insurance helps mitigate that risk with relatively low monthly premiums.

It has been revealed that roommate situations are another important consideration. The article notes that renters insurance usually only covers the named insured. Unless roommates are explicitly listed on the policy, their belongings and liability exposures are not covered. Clear communication and individual policies are recommended to avoid disputes during a claim.

According to recent reports, the article also addresses business use. With more people working remotely, the limits of standard policies become more relevant. Business-related property and liability are typically excluded or capped under personal renters policies. Renters who work from home may need additional protection to fill this coverage gap.

According to recent reports, shared spaces in apartment complexesâlike hallways, parking areas, and entry pointsâcan lead to increased theft risk. Renters insurance Deerfield Beach policies typically protect against losses both inside the unit and in shared areas, but coverage limits vary, making it crucial to review policy details carefully.

In a recent development, the article advises renters to pay attention to policy sublimits. High-value items such as jewelry, collectibles, and bicycles may have coverage caps that fall below their full value. Adding endorsements or scheduled coverage can ensure these items are properly protected under personal property coverage.

Accidental damage caused to others is also addressed. If water overflows from a renter's unit and damages a neighbor's apartment, liability coverage may apply. Without insurance, the renter could be on the hook for the repairs.

Sources indicate that lease agreements may require renters insurance, but even when it's optional, the article emphasizes its importance. Coverage decisions should reflect real risks, not just lease requirements. Relocating within the same building, purchasing new items, or extending a lease are all reasons to revisit coverage to ensure it still meets the renter's needs.

Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police.
  • The charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction.
  • OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared shows a new-generation Model Y in traffic.

The charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.

OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning. Police didn’t name the brand or the driver-assist system, but the message was clear: “even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel.”.

Sources indicate that according to OPP, the officer could see the driver’s eyes were closed and hands were off the steering wheel. Instead of lighting up the cruiser, police pulled in close to capture body camera footage first.

Careless driving isn’t a parking ticket in Ontario. The $490 is the set fine, but if the case goes to court, the Highway Traffic Act allows fines up to $2,000, up to six months in jail, and a licence suspension of up to two years.

Ottawa is the latest, but British Columbia has been dealing with this all year:.

This isn’t upcoming in Canada either. Back in 2020, Alberta RCMP went further and criminally charged a Tesla driver caught sleeping on Autopilot at 150 km/h with dangerous driving.

The U.S. has the same problem with less enforcement. In September, Colorado State Patrol got a report of a sleeping Tesla driver on I-70 near Georgetown and never found the car. The same month, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi pressed the DOT after NBC News found 43 videos of drivers apparently asleep in moving Teslas, 17 of them posted in 2026 alone.

And in October, a driver told CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove into a closed crash scene and hit a patrol car in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.

Recent findings suggest that A few years ago, FSD needed an intervention every few miles, so nobody was napping. You couldn’t.

Now FSD can handle long highway stretches without a takeover, and that’s exactly when supervision breaks down. A human asked to watch a system that’s right 99% of the time stops watching. That’s automation complacency, and it’s one of the most studied problems in aviation and driving research.

Waymo learned this the hard way. In 2013, Google let employees use its highway driver-assist prototype and caught people falling asleep at highway speed. It decided a system that works most of the time but still needs a human to catch its mistakes was the worst of both worlds, and it went straight to driverless.

Industry observers note that tesla went the other way. It sells a Level 2 system called “Full Self-Driving” that’s good enough to lull people to sleep, and it puts the full responsibility on the human who’s now asleep.

It has been revealed that since FSD v12.4, Tesla has relied mainly on the cabin camera above the rearview mirror to make sure the driver is watching the road. But look at what Tesla’s own owner’s manual says about it: the camera “does not require full visibility of the driver’s eyes in order to monitor attentiveness,” and the system “is still active, for example, if the driver is wearing sunglasses.”.

According to recent reports, in other words, it’s often judging head position, not whether your eyes are open. When it can’t see your hands, it falls back to asking for a bit of torque on the wheel, which a sleeping driver resting a hand on the rim can provide.

Sources indicate that the penalties are soft too. Five “strikeouts” suspend FSD for a week, and each strike is forgiven after three and a half days.

And Tesla has been moving in the wrong direction. Musk said in December 2025 that FSD v14.2.1 lets drivers text “depending on context of surrounding traffic.” In May 2026, he said v14.3.3 “nags less too.” When the car does detect drowsiness, Tesla’s alert reads “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” That pushes a tired driver to lean harder on the system instead of pulling over.

Compare that with GM’s Super Cruise, which uses a steering column camera with infrared LEDs to track head and eye position, and only works hands-free on pre-mapped highways.

The Ottawa driver had their eyes closed and their hands off the wheel in rush hour traffic, and the car was still driving when an officer pulled up beside it. Whatever Tesla’s camera was checking from a foot away, it hadn’t stopped the car before a cop in the next lane did.

Sources indicate that we’re glad Canadian police are treating this seriously. A $490 fine and six points is a real deterrent, and OPP’s message is the right one: no matter what Tesla calls it, you’re the driver.

People have been falling asleep at the wheel since driving started; many, if not most, have ended up in tragedy. At least with the self-driving cars, there is a margin of safety, especially for other drivers. These cars should monitor the driver better and pull off the road when it happens.

But police can’t ticket their way out of this. These drivers aren’t edge cases anymore. They’re the predictable result of a system that drives well enough to make people relax, sold under a name that tells them relaxing is fine.

It has been revealed that the fix is on Tesla’s side, and it isn’t complicated. Detect closed eyes, even behind sunglasses, which is what infrared eye-tracking is built for. When a driver doesn’t respond, slow down and pull over immediately instead of escalating warnings for minutes. Stop telling drowsy drivers to “stay focused with FSD.” And make the strike system actually sting.

NHTSA already forced a recall of over 2 million Teslas in December 2023 over weak Autopilot monitoring. Three years later, people are still sleeping through rush hour on FSD.

#122910. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1517 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that taylor Swift, classical or silence?
  • Sources indicate that ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Sources indicate that ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Sources indicate that ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in Fresh York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He mentioned he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be mentioned for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

Industry observers note that “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan stated. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

Industry observers note that “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he noted. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

It has been revealed that daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Recent findings suggest that natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she mentioned, but it indicated cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova noted. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney mentioned.

Sources indicate that she leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he claims, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

Recent findings suggest that “In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer stated. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Sources indicate that shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

It has been revealed that marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

According to recent reports, his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

In a recent development, “Every week, I share latest songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he mentioned. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

It has been revealed that on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Recent findings suggest that bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

According to recent reports, kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she mentioned.

Sources indicate that as for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova stated she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova mentioned, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

  • 12 and 13 also disrupted Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence assistant, affecting governments from Australia and Japan to the U.S., delaying trading firms and disrupting airline communications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:44 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Microsoft Corp. has declared an internal “Code Red” to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures following the nearly 24-hour outage that took down Exchange Online and other Microsoft 365 services earlier this month, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters today.

The outage on Nov. 12 and 13 also disrupted Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence assistant, affecting governments from Australia and Japan to the U.S., delaying trading firms and disrupting airline communications. The designation signals the most severe and urgent level of alert inside Microsoft, according to the report.

In a memo to staff on Friday, Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, described the outage as the most customer-affecting incident in the history of Exchange Online. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson wrote. He also conceded that the work done over the years had not been enough to protect the firm on the day of the outage.

In a recent development, engineers working the incident faced a “fog of war,” according to a separate memo sent on Monday by Amanda Silver, corporate vice president overseeing Microsoft 365 Core and Work IQ. Silver’s memo describes responders exchanging more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats, with diagnostic data spread across fragmented internal tracking systems.

Industry observers note that the Code Red covers five workstreams set out by Silver, including load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft has also set a target of resolving future incidents worldwide within an hour, with AI agents to be used to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly.

How long it takes to push out fixes is another concern raised by Henderson. Writing in an earlier memo this month, Henderson remarked one urgent production fix had taken five to six days to reach worldwide saturation, while for urgent security concerns the goal is to go from detection to safe worldwide deployment within an hour, something he admitted the firm has yet to achieve. Henderson also looks to hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team that oversees the engineering group responsible for the underlying Microsoft 365 services, along with weekly reviews of the corrective work.

The outage itself was blamed by Microsoft on a defect introduced in July in a fix that had been prepared for its Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Under certain load conditions, lock contention inside an internal Windows process was found to exhaust processor and memory resources on the servers, leaving more than 80% of them unresponsive at the worst point, according to Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report. Microsoft, whose Chief Executive Satya Nadella has publicly apologized for the disruption, has mentioned the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents.

Silver’s memo also cites Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, who told a Code Red review that the affected component had seen “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”.

Speed comes with its own risks, according to security experts. “What concerns me is that speed and safety pull against each other,” Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at AI security operations startup Secure.com, told SiliconANGLE. In his view, a pipeline able to push a fix to the world in an hour “can push a mistake in an hour.”.

Geographic traffic partitioning, which Ahmed noted limits how far a single bad change can travel, is the one of the five Code Red workstreams he would be watching.

Darin Fredde, senior director and offensive security evangelist at autonomous penetration testing tech giant Ridge Security Technology Inc., noted that “an organization may have a recovery strategy but still struggle to execute it if the tools needed to recover depend on the service that has failed.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

In a recent development, homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

According to recent reports, why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026.

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

According to recent reports, krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

It has been revealed that they eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

Industry observers note that that opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein reveals you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The firm confirmed Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it indicates can reach $15,000.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Compass International Holdings is presently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this significant news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aurionpro's contactless validation and payment technology will support Matkahuolto's cEMV project, enabling acceptance of EMV and local contactless card standards across Finland.

It has been revealed that MUMBAI, India and HELSINKI, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Aurionpro Solutions, a global technology solutions provider serving the banking, payments, mobility, and transit sectors, today announced that Matkahuolto, Finland's long-standing provider of parcel and digital transport services, has selected Aurionpro as the device vendor for its contactless EMV (cEMV) project following a competitive RFP process.

Industry observers note that under a Master Service Agreement, Aurionpro will provide its SCV 500 Validator and ECR-one contactless card reader, together with integration to Matkahuolto's Transport Management System (TMS) and APIs for payment-application connectivity. The solution will enable the acceptance of EMV payment cards alongside Finland's local contactless card standards, delivering a seamless and reliable fare-payment experience across the public transport network.

Petri Lindqvist, Director, Digital Transport Services, Matkahuolto, said:.

It has been revealed that "We are delighted to partner with Aurionpro. The collaboration will help us deliver a more seamless and convenient travel experience for passengers across Finland. By adding cEMV capability to our solution, we can further improve support for tickets from different operators on Matkahuolto's onboard solutions and, in doing so, help build more flexible and accessible public transport across Finland.".

Sanjay Bali, President & Global Head, Tech Innovation Group, Aurionpro, stated:.

In a recent development, "We are grateful to Matkahuolto for choosing Aurionpro as its partner for this key initiative. We are proud to support Matkahuolto's vision to make public transport more accessible, convenient, and attractive for people across Finland. This engagement marks our entry into the European market and is a significant milestone in expanding our global transit business. We are confident that this is the beginning of a strong pipeline of opportunities across Europe. Our contactless validation and payment capabilities, combined with TMS and payment-application integration, will help enable a seamless payment experience while supporting the acceptance of international EMV cards and local contactless payment standards.".

Matkahuolto is a modern service tech giant that has been bringing people and goods together seamlessly for more than 90 years. The company's business is divided into Parcel Services and Digital Transport Services. Parcel Services transport 20 million parcels a year in Finland and abroad, and Matkahuolto's customers are served by a nationwide network of 2,550 service points. Digital Transport Services focus on sustainable mobility services, timetables and tickets, enabling over 7 million journeys annually. For transport operators, the company provides digital tools for business development. 📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Micron $MU Technology paid $764,748 for executive security for CEO Sanjay Mehrotra in fiscal 2026, the organization mentioned in its annual proxy statement.
  • The manufacturer covered $35,636 in personal security arrangements for Mehrotra the year before, according to MarketWatch, which put the increase at about 2,000%.
  • The security cost was part of $1,865,915 in "all other compensation" for Mehrotra in fiscal 2026, up from $238,942 in fiscal 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Micron $MU Technology paid $764,748 for executive security for CEO Sanjay Mehrotra in fiscal 2026, the organization mentioned in its annual proxy statement. The fiscal year ended Sept. 3.

The manufacturer covered $35,636 in personal security arrangements for Mehrotra the year before, according to MarketWatch, which put the increase at about 2,000%.

The security cost was part of $1,865,915 in "all other compensation" for Mehrotra in fiscal 2026, up from $238,942 in fiscal 2025. His total compensation was $39,723,944, compared with $30,940,146 a year earlier.

Micron attributed the rise to more comprehensive personal security provisions, implemented in light of a continued heightened external threat environment. The fiscal 2026 security program included residential and personal security for Mehrotra.

Micron's Compensation Committee evaluated the need to respond to specific incidents and threats and engaged an independent security firm to study the company's security needs. The committee also set a policy to review security-related expenses quarterly.

Sources indicate that micron mentioned it does not consider the arrangements a personal benefit to Mehrotra. It described them as a business expense that relates to the nature of his role, is necessary for his job performance and mitigates risks to the tech giant. The company reported the costs as compensation in line with SEC guidance.

Micron also paid $75,175 for residential security for former Chief Business Officer Sumit Sadana, who served in that role through August 2026 and now serves as senior adviser to the CEO. The company said it previously paid for his security arrangements.

Micron began distributing its proxy materials on Nov. 24. Shareholders will vote on an advisory resolution on executive compensation at the company's annual meeting, which is scheduled for Jan. 14, 2027, and will be held virtually. Micron's board recommends that shareholders vote for the resolution.

NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO claims

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • Sources indicate that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents stated.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton noted it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”.

Sources indicate that pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also remarked the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

Sources indicate that pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

In a recent development, “Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • However, the companies have very different prospects going forward as they try to come to terms with the diverging fortunes of the artificial intelligence server and personal computer markets they serve.
  • Dell reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $9.45 per share on revenue of $54.94 billion, a stunning result that blew past Wall Street’s expectations of just $6.59 per share in earnings and $49.32 billion in sales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:48 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Updated with Wednesday stock prices:.

Dell Technologies Inc. and HP Inc. delivered strong earnings and revenue beats as they posted their latest financial results today.

However, the companies have very different prospects going forward as they try to come to terms with the diverging fortunes of the artificial intelligence server and personal computer markets they serve.

Dell reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $9.45 per share on revenue of $54.94 billion, a stunning result that blew past Wall Street’s expectations of just $6.59 per share in earnings and $49.32 billion in sales.

The company’s revenue more than doubled from a year earlier thanks to the sky-high demand for the AI servers and related data center infrastructure equipment it sells. Dell’s Infrastructure Solutions Group delivered sales of $41.97 billion during the quarter, far in excess of the Street’s target of $35.27 billion. Of that, around $22 billion came from direct AI-optimized server sales, the company said. That segment was up 291% annually.

Sources indicate that “We are now a different tech giant, with the Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of our profit and growth,” noted Dell Vice Chairman and Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke (pictured). He added that Dell now has more than 7,500 customers buying its AI servers.

In a recent development, the Street liked what it saw, with Dell’s stock rising more than 3% after hours, putting the brakes on an 11% decline earlier, during the regular trading session. Enhancement: However, on another down day for tech stocks Wednesday, Dell’s shares were falling almost 8%.

Dell’s performance in the quarter sets a new precedent for infrastructure systems companies, said longtime technology industry analyst Dave Vellante, chief analyst at theCUBE Research, SiliconANGLE Media’s sister market research firm.

Recent findings suggest that “Dell has transformed from a PC firm into a dominant enterprise infrastructure provider and industry bellwether,” he stated. “What’s most astounding to me is that I’ve always considered AWS to be Dell’s most formidable competitor. Dell is now significantly larger than AWS on a trailing 12-month revenue basis and is growing at a rate that’s more than double that of AWS, Azure and on a par with Google Cloud.”.

Industry observers note that dell is raising its forecast for AI servers in the coming fiscal years, and now sees sales rising to a staggering $78 billion, ahead of the Street’s target of $74 billion. At present, the manufacturer has an even bigger order backlog of $132.3 billion for AI servers. “Every order is verified for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power,” Clarke told analysts in response to a question about the reliability of that backlog.

Vellante said Dell’s operating leverage is just as impressive, with its operating income, net profit and earnings per share all growing at rates over two-times its revenue growth.

“Its massive backlog and strong product execution allow it to be selective,” the analyst said. “Thus the quality of its revenue and its backlog is very high, and the company is well-positioned for the next several quarters. Current market signals point to a structural change in tech where vendors that are in a position to help customers transform and drive upcoming levels of productivity are poised to win over the long term. We increasingly see Dell as one of those leaders.”.

Besides servers, Dell still has a massive business in the PC market. Its Client Services Group was once the firm’s biggest segment, but its revenue is now dwarfed by AI server sales. During the quarter, it generated revenue of $12.89 billion, below the Street’s forecast of $14.33 billion.

According to recent reports, the reason for that miss is that the global PC market is currently enduring a sharp decline. Last month, Gartner Inc. reported a stunning 22% drop in global PC shipments in the third quarter, citing the increased costs of components such as memory chips, which have led to higher prices and compelled many people to hold onto their older laptops for longer.

It has been revealed that the miserable state of PC sales makes HP’s latest quarterly results seem even more impressive than they were. However, the company’s cautious outlook suggests that its incoming Chief Executive Emma Walmsley (pictured, right) will have her work cut out when she assumes the role full time on Jan. 4, when she’s slated to take over from interim CEO Bruce Broussard.

It has been revealed that HP reported fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of 83 cents per share, surpassing the analyst consensus estimate that called for a profit of just 75 cents per share. Revenue for the period came to $16 billion, up 9% and above the Street’s target of $15.4 billion.

HP’s stock briefly surged more than 17% after-hours, before promptly surrendering all of those gains in under an hour. It was down just under a percentage point at the time of writing. Upgrade: On Wednesday, investors appeared to change their minds again, as the stock was rising more than 11%.

Investors had low expectations of HP given the shoddy state of the PC market. The company has been trying to mitigate the situation somewhat by raising its prices, but it couldn’t stop its profit margins from declining in the quarter.

Sources indicate that the market was eagerly anticipating HP’s guidance to try and get a lid on whether or not the PC market has any prospect of recovery in the near future, but the company disappointed by refusing to provide any. All it would say is that it forecasts free cash flow in the current quarter to be $3 billion, plus or minus $100 million. Analysts are targeting free cash flow of $3.3 billion.

According to recent reports, HP hasn’t been helped by the fact that it has been without a CEO since PayPal Holdings Inc. surprisingly swooped in to poach its former leader Enrique Lores in February. Broussard has held the fort for close to nine months now, but the company did at least finally name a successor in Walmsley, who will begin her tenure next year. She formerly led the pharmaceutical giant GSK Plc.

Walmsley has a tough act to follow, however, for Broussard has done rather well in his efforts to cope with the PC market downturn and the higher component costs. Although the stock was up and down today, it’s still up 25% in the year to date.

Fresh free calculator helps home service business owners estimate the marketing investment needed to reach growth goalsâand gives agencies a turnkey tool to educate prospects.

TUCSON, Ariz., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Marketing for the Future, LLC, a marketing agency serving home service companies across the United States and Canada, today revealed the launch of a free Marketing Budget Calculator. The tool helps business owners determine exactly how much they should spend on marketing to hit their revenue goals, based on their industry, current revenue, and desired growth pace. Available now at mktg4thefuture.com/home-service-marketing-budget-calculator, the calculator is also free for ad agencies and marketing firms to embed directly on their own websites.

Instead of basing recommendations on trailing revenue, the calculator works backward from a manufacturer's revenue goal. Customers select their industry, enter their trailing-twelve-month revenue, set a target for the next twelve months, and choose a growth pace of Light, Moderate, or Aggressive. The tool then generates a recommended annual and monthly marketing budget, broken down by quarter and week, along with a suggested split across marketing channels. Results update instantly, with no email signup required.

Sources indicate that "Business owners need clear, data-driven insight into what it truly takes to scale in today's digital landscape. This tool was built to provide exactly that. Having spent two decades in digital marketing, I can say with confidence that the level of competition we are seeing right now is unprecedented," said Caleb Tennenbaum, Founder & CEO of Marketing for the Future.

Home service businessesâincluding those in pest control, HVAC, plumbing, electrical, roofing, landscaping, garage doors, cleaning, pool service, painting, and remodelingâoften struggle to know whether they're underspending or overspending on marketing relative to their growth goals. The calculator addresses this gap by calibrating budget recommendations to typical investment levels within each trade, accounting for factors like competition and customer acquisition patterns specific to that industry.

In a recent development, ad agencies and marketing firms can embed the calculator on their own websites at no cost. Every embed includes the Marketing for the Future logo and a link back to mktg4thefuture.com, giving agencies a useful client tool while extending the company's brand reach. Embedding requires only downloading the calculator file, uploading it to a website, and pasting a short code snippet onto the desired page.

Industry observers note that marketing for the Future positions the calculator as a starting point for a broader conversation about marketing investment. The company encourages business owners and agencies alike to use the tool to benchmark their current spend, blueprint for growth, and avoid the common pitfalls of underfunding or overfunding their marketing efforts.
