In a recent development, volkswagen is turning one of its best-selling nameplates into an electric SUV. The newly introduced ID. Tiguan is now rolling off the assembly line and will replace the ID.4 in 2027.

It has been revealed that the ID.4 and ID.5 are on the way out, and the newly introduced ID. Tiguan will replace them in Volkswagen’s EV lineup next year.

Following the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, which are now on sale in Europe, the ID. Tiguan is the next model to go on sale as a “True Volkswagen,” as the company calls it.

The upcoming electric SUV adopts Volkswagen’s best-selling nameplate, the Tiguan, as part of its shift away from the numerical system used on the outgoing ID.4 and ID.5.

Volkswagen declared on Thursday that series production of the electric ID. Tiguan has now begun at its Embden Plant in Germany.

In a recent development, “The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars,” VW Brand CEO Thomas Shafer stated last month after unveiling the new SUV. He added that “The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together.”.

The ID. Tiguan will be a step change from its predecessors, the ID.4 and ID.5, featuring Volkswagen’s “Pure Positive” design language, which includes an overhauled interior and exterior design and updated tech.

Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan’s “hallmark feature” is the completely redesigned exterior. The new design remains closer to the gas-powered Tiguan, with a boxy, traditional SUV look.

Unlike the ID.4’s aerodynamic design, the newly introduced ID. Tiguan features a wide, chunky front end and traditional pull-style door handles instead of the flush ones.

It has been revealed that in Volkswagen’s words, the latest ID. Tiguan electric SUV “looks like a vehicle from the premium segment.”.

Inside, the updates are just as evident. The overhauled interior features Volkswagen’s upcoming infotainment setup, including a 10″ Digital Cockpit and a 15″ center display. There’s also an optional 12″ passenger screen available.

According to recent reports, another highlight is the return of physical buttons. After listening to customer feedback from current drivers, Volkswagen added physical buttons under the center display and on the steering wheel for climate control and other vehicle functions.

To spark a bit of nostalgia, VW added a fun latest Retro Mode feature that transforms the Digital Cockpit and center display to mimic the style of iconic models like the first-generation Golf.

Drivers can also choose from six classic VW models to display in a virtual “garage” on the infotainment screen: Golf I, Golf II Country, Golf IV, Tiguan I, Race Touareg, and Beetle.

In a recent development, the new Volkswagen ID. Tiguan will be available with two battery packs and three performance levels:.

Sources indicate that depending on the configuration, the ID. Tiguan offers a “new benchmark” for Volkswagen’s electric SUVs in Europe with a WLTP range of up to 377 miles (607 km).

Recent findings suggest that volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Tiguan in Germany and a few other European markets in October, starting at €42,695 ($47,800). It’s available in three trims: Trend, Life, and Style.

It has been revealed that after it rolls out in Europe through early 2027, Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan will go on sale in North America to replace the ID.4.

In a recent development, apparently, the new ID Tiguan has a slightly better Cx (Drag Coefficient) at 0.26 versus 0.28 on first gen ID4 and 0.27 on 2nd gen. According to VW, it’s achieved using front air curtains, a minimal air intake, an enclosed underbody, and a longer roof spoiler.

Sources indicate that volkswagen remarked prices and other details will come in “due course.” The current VW ID.4 uses an 82 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 291 miles in the RWD version. The AWD model offers around 263 miles.

Industry observers note that since the European model offers close to 25 miles (40 km) more WLTP range than the outgoing ID.4, the ID. Tiguan is expected to offer over 300 miles on the EPA scale.

Industry observers note that official US prices have not yet been declared. The outgoing ID.4 has a starting MSRP of about $45,000, so the ID. Tiguan will likely be priced similarly.

  • Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.
  • It has been revealed that the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

It has been revealed that the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA noted.

In its latest revision on the investigation, ULA remarked it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA remarked early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp stated Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the organization looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn debuts reserved for Leo.

It has been revealed that ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA remarked.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA noted it will share more as the investigation continues.

Recent findings suggest that yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many newly introduced ways to work together.”.

In a recent development, — Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon.

In her upcoming role, Mellen remarked she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”.

— Agility Robotics, the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:.

— Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass. Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this newly introduced age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times.

— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues.

It has been revealed that king is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.

— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

  • A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.
  • The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

According to recent reports, she’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” Latest America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sources indicate that sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

Recent findings suggest that “Free” is misleading. French Gates mentioned Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The Latest York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

Sources indicate that artificial intelligence infrastructure startup Marlowe AI Inc. has closed a huge $227 million seed round led by Accel.

It has been revealed that bessemer, Altimeter, Emergence Capital and a number of other institutional bakers chipped in as well. They were joined by a large group of angel investors that included the chief executives of Palo Alto Networks Inc, Uber Technologies Inc., Box Inc. and Dropbox Inc. GeekWire reported on Monday that Marlowe is valued at $1.15 billion.

Sources indicate that marlowe was founded last year by CEO Dan Lewis and Chief Technology Officer Kutta Srinivasan. Lewis previously headed the Microsoft Corp. unit responsible for Copilot Studio, the tech giant’s AI agent development tool. Srinivasan was the techical lead of the organization’s AI infrastructure group.

Sources indicate that marlowe is building AI data centers for inference workloads. The company will optimize each facility for a specific inference workload category by tailoring its chip mix, network configuration and software. Marlowe believes that its approach will provide better hardware efficiency than general-purpose graphics card clusters.

“Even modest gains in network architecture, power oversubscription, AI-driven fleet operations, and workload-specific inference optimization multiply to create a durable, 2-3x overall advantage in performance, availability, resiliency, and cost,” Lewis and Srinivasan wrote in Marlowe’s launch blog post.

Recent findings suggest that the organization plans to bring its first data center online  next month. It’s based on hardware from Etched Inc., an inference chip startup that was valued at $21 billion in August.

Graphics cards often use only a small fraction of their maximum clock speed to avoid overheating. Etched’s chip is less prone to overheating and can therefore operate at higher clock speeds, which boosts model performance. The company says that its accelerator provides “multiple times the FLOPs density” of graphics cards.

Etched ships its chips as part of custom-made inference racks. According to the company, the systems feature an interconnect that can perform some data movement tasks more than four times faster than competing silicon. Etched’s rack design also includes custom power management and cooling components.

In a recent development, marlowe’s second facility will come online in the second quarter of 2027. It will host racks based on Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s Helios design. A Helios rack hosts 72 AMD graphics cards along with central processing units and Pensando data processing units, or DPUs. The DPUs offload networking tasks from the other chips to leave more computing capacity for AI models.

Sources indicate that helios racks’ networking and power delivery links are arranged in a configuration that reduces the need for manual cable maintenance. Additionally, the coolant lines feature a so-called quick-disconnect design. They can be plugged and unplugged without the specialized tools usually needed for the task.

It has been revealed that geekWire reported that Marlowe has also signed a letter of intent for a third data center. According to the publication, each of the firm’s planned facilities will provide tens of megawatts of computing capacity. One megawatt is enough to power several hundred homes.

Marlowe will use the proceeds from its seed round to finance hardware purchases and hire engineers.

FHFA raises conforming loan limit to $855,400 in 2027

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the baseline conforming loan limit will rise 2.71% in 2027 to $855,400 for one-unit properties in most parts of the country, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA).
  • The $855,400 cap is an increase of $22,650 from 2026 and reflects slower home price growth tied to a weaker housing market and higher-for-longer mortgage rates.
  • In a recent development, under the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 (HERA), the national “ceiling” for high-cost areas is set at 150% of the baseline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the baseline conforming loan limit will rise 2.71% in 2027 to $855,400 for one-unit properties in most parts of the country, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA). Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will be authorized to buy loans up to that balance in the vast majority of U.S. counties.

The $855,400 cap is an increase of $22,650 from 2026 and reflects slower home price growth tied to a weaker housing market and higher-for-longer mortgage rates. The annual adjustment was 3.25% last year and above 5% in each of the prior two years.

In a recent development, under the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 (HERA), the national “ceiling” for high-cost areas is set at 150% of the baseline. For 2027, that ceiling will be $1,283,100 for one-unit properties in markets where 115% of the local median home value exceeds the baseline limit. Conforming caps first surpassed $1 million in these high-cost areas in 2022.

Recent findings suggest that special statutory provisions apply in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In these areas, the 2027 baseline loan limit for one-unit properties will be $1,283,100, while the ceiling will be $1,924,650.

“Due to rising home values, the CLL will be higher in all but 24 U.S. counties or county equivalents,” the FHFA noted in a statement.

Each November, FHFA publishes new conforming loan limits for the coming year. Increases resumed in 2016, after home prices returned to pre-Great Recession levels, a condition required by HERA. The statute also prevents the ceiling from declining in years when home prices fall; the cap only moves higher when national prices increase year over year.

Sources indicate that this year’s adjustment is tied to FHFA’s third-quarter 2026 House Price Index (HPI), which tracks changes in average U.S. home values over the prior four quarters. Nominal, seasonally adjusted, expanded-data HPI revealed house prices rose 2.72% on average between the third quarters of 2025 and 2026, essentially matching the 2.71% rise in the baseline conforming loan limit.

Industry observers note that the new limits expand the amount of mortgage debt that can qualify for conventional financing backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Loans above FHFA’s limits are classified as jumbos, a segment still dominated by banks and portfolio lenders that set their own credit standards and capital requirements.

Sources indicate that mortgage lenders once again anticipated FHFA’s announcement and raised their internal conforming loan limits ahead of the official release to compete for volume. But they were conservative.

It has been revealed that rocket Mortgage was an early mover, lifting its conforming loan limit to $845,000 for single-family homes in 48 states in September. CrossCountry Mortgage adopted the same level.

Pennymac set its internal limit at $850,000, while United Wholesale Mortgage increased its one-unit cap for conventional and Department of Veterans Affairs loans to $847,440.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chris Winkelmann outlines how families can determine their life insurance needs based on income, debts, dependents, and future expenses.

It has been revealed that MEDINA, Ohio, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- How much life insurance is truly necessary to protect a family's financial future? That question is answered in a HelloNation article featuring insights from Insurance Expert Chris Winkelmann of Medina, Ohio.

In a recent development, the article explains that many Ohio families struggle to determine the right coverage amount to protect their loved ones. Life insurance serves as a financial safety net if a primary earner dies unexpectedly. Without adequate coverage, families in Medina County and Northeast Ohio may face difficulty paying debts, covering daily living expenses, or funding future education for dependents.

According to the HelloNation article, calculating the proper coverage amount begins with evaluating household income. Life insurance is often intended to replace several years of earnings to maintain stability. Families are encouraged to assess how long their income would need to be replaced and what expenses would continue during that time.

Debt obligations are another critical factor. The article notes that mortgages, car loans, credit cards, and personal loans should be included in the total calculation. Leaving these debts unpaid can create significant financial strain for surviving family members. By including outstanding balances in the coverage amount, Ohio families can reduce the risk of burdening dependents with unexpected repayment responsibilities.

In a recent development, future expenses must also be considered. The article describes how costs such as college tuition, ongoing medical bills, and general living expenses should factor into life insurance planning. Families with young children may require higher levels of financial protection because more dependents rely on household income. As children grow older and debts decrease, coverage needs may change.

Industry observers note that the HelloNation article also explains the importance of selecting the right policy type. Term life insurance provides coverage for a specific period and is typically more affordable. Whole life insurance offers lifelong protection and includes a cash value component that grows over time. Many Ohio families choose term policies to cover large financial obligations, while using smaller permanent policies to provide long-term stability.

Industry observers note that premium affordability plays a significant role in policy selection. The article notes that premiums vary depending on age, health, policy type, and coverage amount. Families must select premiums that fit comfortably within their budget to ensure the policy remains active. A policy that becomes too expensive may lapse, leaving dependents without protection.

Optional riders are another consideration discussed in the article. Riders such as accidental death benefits, waiver of premium, critical illness coverage, and child riders can expand financial protection. While these additions increase premiums, they may provide meaningful security depending on household needs. Evaluating riders carefully helps ensure families avoid paying for unnecessary coverage.

According to recent reports, flexibility is also emphasized. Some term policies allow conversion to permanent coverage, and certain options include inflation protection to help maintain value over time. The article encourages regular reviews of life insurance policies, especially after major life events such as buying a home, changing jobs, or expanding a family.

Throughout the piece, Insurance Expert Chris Winkelmann provides context to help readers understand that life insurance decisions should reflect both present and future obligations. The article makes clear that determining the right coverage amount requires thoughtful planning based on income, debts, dependents, and long-term goals.

Recent findings suggest that the article concludes that life insurance remains a central tool for financial protection and stability. Ohio families in Medina County and Northeast Ohio who regularly review their policies are better positioned to safeguard their dependents while balancing premiums and policy type effectively.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.
  • Industry observers note that terms of the deal were not disclosed this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Industry observers note that terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the tech giant’s experimental arm, confirmed the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith noted on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Sources indicate that petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

Recent findings suggest that we’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Sources indicate that owners cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

According to recent reports, howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

In a recent development, the deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of consumers. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

FHFA maps out FICO 10T rollout with broad eligibility by late 2028

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the FICO 10T credit score model for use by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
  • The staged rollout, announced Tuesday, mirrors the VantageScore 4.0 timeline and is meant to give lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers time to analyze historic FICO 10T data, rework pricing and risk models, and update technology before a full transition, according to the agency.“The timeline below prepares lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers for the final step in credit score modernization: lender choice between FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0,” the agency remarked.
  • Bob Broeksmit, president and CEO of the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), issued a statement of support following the announcement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the FICO 10T credit score model for use by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It also released an implementation road map that would make FICO 10T broadly eligible and retire Classic FICO by September 2028.

The staged rollout, announced Tuesday, mirrors the VantageScore 4.0 timeline and is meant to give lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers time to analyze historic FICO 10T data, rework pricing and risk models, and update technology before a full transition, according to the agency.“The timeline below prepares lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers for the final step in credit score modernization: lender choice between FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0,” the agency remarked. At the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T are expected to go live alongside the existing Classic FICO in January.

Bob Broeksmit, president and CEO of the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), issued a statement of support following the announcement.

“We welcome this milestone as it moves us closer to the industry’s and FHFA’s goal of transitioning to true competition with two modernized credit score models,” Broeksmit said. “We appreciate FHFA’s desire to provide a clear and transparent roadmap for this process. Given the industry’s experience with the just-completed adoption of VantageScore 4.0, MBA will work with FHFA and industry stakeholders to expedite the implementation timeline responsibly.

Industry observers note that “MBA and its members will continue to engage with FHFA to establish meaningful competition for both credit scoring and credit reporting. Continued reforms to end the tri-merge requirement will further improve our credit reporting system and lower costs for borrowers. Today’s announcement is a critical next step.”.

Industry observers note that the FHFA initially validated both FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0 for use at the government-sponsored (GSEs) enterprises in October 2022. In July 2026, Fannie and Freddie released historical performance data for FICO 10T along with additional VantageScore 4.0 data, a key prerequisite for lenders and investors to back-test new score models and recalibrate credit policy.A FICO 10T pilot is expected to begin around December 2027. In this “launch and refine” phase, lenders will deliver a subset of loans underwritten with FICO 10T while FHFA, the GSEs and industry stakeholders monitor data quality, pricing and delivery performance.

Based on pilot results, FHFA expects upfront pricing grids and private mortgage insurer eligibility requirements, or PMIERs, to be updated to reflect the new score model. That step will be critical for secondary market execution and risk transfer structures that at the moment rely on Classic FICO.

A limited FICO 10T rollout is targeted for April 2028, followed by a scale-up and transition phase that leads to broad eligibility around September 2028. During this final stage, FHFA plans to confirm industry readiness, fully implement Uniform Loan Delivery Dataset (ULDD) Phase 5, expand FICO 10T use across GSE channels and retire Classic FICO.

FHFA emphasized that dates after November 2026 are targets and are subject to change.

In October, Fair Isaac Corp. said it will hold its wholesale mortgage price at $10 for a bundle of its credit scores for lenders and brokers enrolled in its Preferred Program. The $10 price is available through participating tri-merge credit report resellers to lenders that commit to FICO under the program. It covers both Classic FICO, which has been the mortgage standard for nearly three decades, and FICO Score 10T, the manufacturer’s trended-data model.

FICO is also preparing a new subscription-based pricing model for mortgage credit scores in 2027, sources told HousingWire.

VantageScore 4.0, by comparison, has been offered at 99 cents per score, or at no additional charge when purchased alongside a FICO score through Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, which jointly own VantageScore.

Bank of America Global Research, using data from Recursion, found that more than 170 lenders now pull VantageScore 4.0. Despite that breadth of use, only a small share of conventional loans are actually priced with VantageScore 4.0. In October, 20% of issuance reported a VantageScore 4.0, yet only about 8% of total issuance used the score model for pricing, according to the research.

Editor’s note: This story was updated with a statement from the MBA.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Apex Fintech Solutions Chief Platform Officer and Microsoft Azure product leader to lead technology strategy, architecture and AI-native engineering for Stirling ONE.

According to recent reports, NEW YORK, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Stirlingshire Investments today revealed the appointment of Daniel Gicklhorn as Chief Technology Officer. Gicklhorn will lead technology strategy, architecture and engineering for Stirling ONE, the AI-native platform built to give independent advisors the technology of a large firm without giving up their independence.

Stirling ONE, which Stirlingshire introduced at Future Proof in September, brings onboarding, portfolio management, trading, compliance, reporting and client communication together on one platform, so advisors can spend less time running their business and more time on their clients.

Gicklhorn has spent more than 20 years building the platforms global enterprises run on every day, from the infrastructure behind the world's most-used online services to the modern backbone behind a new generation of investing platforms. Most recently he was Chief Platform Officer at Apex Fintech Solutions, the clearing and custody provider behind hundreds of brokerages, wealth platforms and fintechs, holding hundreds of billions of dollars for tens of millions of investors. There he led the cross-product infrastructure and trust layers behind Ascend, Apex's modern cloud-based clearing and custody platform.

Before Apex, Gicklhorn spent more than a decade at Microsoft building global infrastructure and commercializing technology that powers the modern internet. He created Azure Front Door, the commercial global edge security and delivery platform that powers more than 100,000 websites, including Microsoft's own web properties, such as Office and Xbox.

At Stirlingshire, Gicklhorn will apply his experience to the continued evolution of Stirling ONE, with a focus on secure, scalable infrastructure and practical AI capabilities that help advisors operate more efficiently and serve clients more effectively.

It has been revealed that "The next generation of clients will expect their advisor to move at the speed of software, but no one trades trust for speed with their life savings," noted Gicklhorn. "I've spent my career building platforms that deliver both. My job is to make Stirling ONE the platform advisors trust to run their practice on today and tomorrow.".

Gicklhorn holds a Master of Engineering in computer science from Cornell University and advises early-stage companies on AI, cloud infrastructure and financial technology.

About Stirlingshire Investments.

Stirlingshire Investments is a wealth management firm built to provide independent financial advisors with the technology, infrastructure and economics to operate more effectively. Through Stirling ONE, Stirlingshire brings core wealth management functions together in one integrated environment, while offering advisors a 100% payout and zero platform expenses.

For more information about Stirlingshire Investments, visit www.stirlingshire.com.

Nicole Cox, CMO[email protected]647-500-2763.

Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.
  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Recent findings suggest that boles mentioned the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

It has been revealed that retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “notable step toward undersea superiority.”.

It has been revealed that “Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

Next year, Zeno Power aims to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

In a recent development, the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Sources indicate that since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

What will Social Security look like in 2027 and beyond?

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With potential program insolvency looming in 2032, the next few years for Social Security are being defined by conflicting pressures — including the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027, quickly rising financial obstacles for older Americans, and yet another proposal in Congress that could either stabilize benefits or sharply increase federal debt levels.
  • Earlier this month, The Senior Citizens League forecast a 3.6% COLA for 2028, matching the Social Security Administration’s recently unveiled 3.6% COLA for 2027.
  • Most Social Security beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Part B, and premiums are automatically deducted from monthly checks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With potential program insolvency looming in 2032, the next few years for Social Security are being defined by conflicting pressures — including the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027, quickly rising financial obstacles for older Americans, and yet another proposal in Congress that could either stabilize benefits or sharply increase federal debt levels.

Earlier this month, The Senior Citizens League forecast a 3.6% COLA for 2028, matching the Social Security Administration’s recently unveiled 3.6% COLA for 2027. But Morningstar noted this week that the 2027 COLA — the largest since 2023’s 8.7% adjustment — will translate into smaller take-home increases once Medicare costs are deducted.

Most Social Security beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Part B, and premiums are automatically deducted from monthly checks. Morningstar reported that the standard monthly Part B premium will rise by $6.50 next year to $209.40, a 3.2% increase. That will allow most beneficiaries to keep more than 3% of the 3.6% COLA after the deduction.

Morningstar calculated that a retiree receiving the average October benefit of $2,092 would see a net benefit increase of about 3.29%, assuming they pay the standard Part B premium and have no other changes in deductions. A higher-income retiree with a $3,500 monthly benefit would see a net increase of roughly 3.41% under the same assumptions.

The COLA is based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which compares the average readings for July, August and September on a year-over-year basis. Analysts cited by Morningstar noted that CPI-W may understate seniors’ actual cost pressures, particularly for healthcare, and pointed to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ CPI-E index for older households, which has historically risen faster than CPI-W.

The Senior Citizens League (TSCL) stated the projected 3.6% COLA for 2028 is likely to arrive against a deteriorating backdrop for older adults, including senior homeowners who may still be making monthly mortgage payments. The group said that seniors are now the country’s fastest-growing homeless population and that many forgo vision, dental and hearing care due to costs.

Sources indicate that TSCL’s release emphasized that Social Security’s primary trust fund is projected to reach insolvency in 2032, triggering automatic benefit reductions if Congress does not act. The Medicare Part A hospital insurance trust fund is projected to become insolvent in 2033, the group remarked.

That timing elevates the stakes for the next Congress, which will be led by Democrats after their decisive victories in the recent midterm elections. Senators elected in the current cycle will serve from Jan. 3, 2027, through Jan. 3, 2033, overlapping the projected insolvency date. TSCL framed these terms as a key window for any reforms to prevent automatic benefit cuts for millions of retirees.

In its agenda for the 120th Congress, TSCL called on lawmakers to:.

TSCL pointed to Social Security Administration projections, which show that eliminating the taxable wage cap would add “decades” to the trust fund’s life. And the organization’s internal polling indicates broad bipartisan support among seniors for lifting the cap.

As advocacy groups push for revenue-raising reforms, a fresh proposal in the Senate would instead rely on federal borrowing to preserve full benefits.

It has been revealed that ron Johnson (R-Wis.), the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, has introduced the Stop Scaring Seniors Act. The bill would allow the Department of the Treasury to transfer general fund dollars to Social Security’s retirement trust fund once it becomes insolvent, according to a press release published last week by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB).

Recent findings suggest that under current law, Social Security can only pay benefits from dedicated payroll tax income and trust fund reserves. When the retirement trust fund’s reserves are exhausted — presently projected to be in less than six years — benefits would be cut by about 22% without legislative changes.

CRFB estimated that backfilling Social Security with general revenue under Johnson’s bill would increase federal debt by $190 trillion over the next 75 years on an inflation-adjusted basis, equal to roughly 165% of gross domestic product.

“Paying for Social Security out of the general fund would absolutely explode the national debt, costing a whopping 165% of GDP over 75 years before even considering the economic implications,” CRFB President Maya MacGuineas said in the release, arguing that the policy could trigger a debt crisis or unsettle bond markets even before it is fully implemented.

CRFB characterized the bill as avoiding “the real decisions” needed to repair Social Security’s finances and urged lawmakers to pursue a mix of adjustments — potentially through a bipartisan commission — that would close the program’s funding gap without shifting the shortfall onto the federal balance sheet.

The trajectory of Social Security and Medicare benefits has direct implications for housing demand and credit risk among the senior segment.

Net benefit increases closer to 3% than 3.6% may constrain seniors’ ability to absorb higher housing costs — including the required property tax, insurance and association dues associated with reverse mortgages. The impact could be particularly acute in housing markets with rapid property tax growth.

Rising healthcare and prescription costs could drive more senior homeowners to tap their equity through home sales or reverse mortgages. Increased levels of downsizing would alter inventory and product mixes in senior-heavy markets.

In a recent development, A 22% across-the-board benefit cut in the next decade, if Congress fails to act, would likely raise delinquency risks among fixed-income borrowers and could affect investor views of senior-heavy mortgage-backed securities pools. Conversely, large-scale borrowing to backfill Social Security, as proposed in Johnson’s bill, could influence interest rates and broader funding conditions.

Recent findings suggest that localized affordability pressures could also emerge. Growth in senior homelessness and medical cost burdens might increase demand for affordable and supportive housing. It could also influence municipal planning, tax policy and zoning decisions that shape housing development pipelines.

BYD introduced the Denza N8 EV in China, a five-seat luxury SUV that promises more than 1,000 km (621 miles) of CLTC range, a tech-filled cabin, and plenty of premium extras.

Industry observers note that another day, another newly introduced BYD vehicle is now on sale in China. After opening preorders for the Denza N8 EV a few weeks ago, BYD held the grand launch event on Thursday.

The fresh N8 EV, or “the king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as Denza called it, is available in six variants, including four battery-electric (EV) and two plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrain options.

The all-electric Denza N8 starts at 269,900 yuan, or about $40,500, with prices ranging up to 329,900 yuan ($49,500) for the Flagship model. The PHEV models start at 300,900 yuan and 32,900 yuan, respectively.

Measuring 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase, the Denza N8 EV is slightly longer than the Kia EV9 and Hyundai IONIQ 9.

In a recent development, inside, the interior is pretty over the top with a huge 30″ panoramic infotainment screen that stretches nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard. There’s also a new 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) at the bottom of the windshield.

BYD added a few premium extras like front and rear zero-gravity seats, a drop-down ceiling entertainment screen, ambient lighting, and wireless phone chargers.

The Denza N8 is offered with a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD variant uses a single motor that delivers either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp), depending on the configuration.

According to recent reports, the tri-motor Denza N8 debuts BYD’s e3 Evo technology. The setup includes three electric motors: a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, for a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

BYD’s Denza noted the N8 EV boasts an all-electric CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles), “making it the world’s longest-range mass-produced all-electric SUV.”.

To put it in perspective, that’s as much as the outgoing N8 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) it’s replacing, which offered a combined CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

It’s available with two second-gen BYD Blade battery packs: 105.792 kWh and 130.15 kWh, delivering CLTC ranges of up to 885 km (549 miles) and 1,003 km (623 miles).

With BYD’s second-gen Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, the Denza N8 EV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. Charging from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

Like many of its new luxury vehicles, the Denza N8 is equipped with BYD’s premium tech and features, such as its DiSus-A intelligent air suspension system and God’s Eye 5.0 intelligent driving assistance system.

BYD also sells the extended Denza N8L in China, which went on sale earlier this year, starting at 299,800 yuan ($45,000).

Epochal launches with $100M to help developers train predictive AI models

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc.
  • According to recent reports, the capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp.
  • Epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:30 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Artificial intelligence tooling startup Epochal AI Inc. rolled out today with $100 million in funding.

According to recent reports, the capital was provided by Chief Executive Officer Guodong Zhang, a machine learning researcher who earlier co-founded xAI Corp. He established Epochal earlier this year with two other xAI co-founders, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss. The company’s staff also includes former researchers from Anthropic PBC, OpenAI Group PBC and Google DeepMind.

Epochal’s first offering is a cloud service called the Epochal Time Portal. According to the company, it enables developers to train AI models that can predict future events. The service does so by providing models with access to historical web data from the past 30 years.

Recent findings suggest that if a bank wishes to train an AI that can predict quarterly earnings, it could use the service to fetch financial results from the first three quarters of 2025. It could then ask the AI to estimate fourth-quarter results from the same year.

Sources indicate that after the model generates its predictions, developers can compare them against real fourth-quarter earnings to check the model’s accuracy. They can make adjustments if necessary and then repeat the training workflow until the model starts generating accurate forecasts.

In a recent development, the Epochal Time Portal features more than 1 trillion historical web pages on launch. Each entry includes a timestamp that indicates when it was created. According to the company, its timestamps make it possible to track how a web page changed over time.

It has been revealed that AI models access the content through a purpose-built search engine. It enables them to specify the time periods from which they wish to retrieve web pages. According to Epochal, its platform provides one-minute granularity for the most frequently updated pages.

Industry observers note that like consumer search engines, the Epochal Time Portal prioritizes the web pages that are most relevant to each given query. The difference is that it considers web pages’ creation date when evaluating relevance. If a query contains the term “Meta” but asks for pages created before 2021, the year Facebook Inc. rebranded, the Epochal Time Portal will not bring up pages that relate to the social networking giant.

Today’s frontier models can determine that they’re being trained on historical data rather than up-to-date information. For example, a model might compare the creation date of a web page to the virtual clock of the operating system on which it deployed. Such discrepancies can lower the effectiveness of training runs.

According to Epochal, its service mitigates the concern by deploying AI models in sandboxes synced to their training data. If a manufacturer is training a model on we pages from 2025, the Epochal Time Portal will run it on a Linux version from that year. It applies the same precautions to the software tools and programming language versions that models use.

The Epochal Time Portal is initially available in a single free tier with low usage limits. Epochal aims to follow up the launch by sharing the results of several AI experiments that its researchers have carried out using the service.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.
  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with major financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • In a recent development, for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with major financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

In a recent development, for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The manufacturer started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Sources indicate that beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Sources indicate that listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old manufacturer was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he stated.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the tech giant to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

In a recent development, what’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will upgrade the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that monday marked the end of the U.S.
  • BTR developers and operators say this uncertainty continues to suppress capital flowing into fresh projects, a trend they expect to continue until the federal government clarifies the rules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this year, build-to-rent projects secured some notable exemptions from the institutional investor ban included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. However, while the industry still doesn’t know exactly what the final rules will look like, it just moved a step closer to finding out.

Industry observers note that monday marked the end of the U.S. Department of the Treasury‘s public comment period on its proposed rules for BTR exemptions from the institutional investor ban. Although ROAD explicitly exempted BTR from the ban, some of the proposed rules and language Treasury released in October have left the industry uneasy and unsure of where it stands.

BTR developers and operators say this uncertainty continues to suppress capital flowing into fresh projects, a trend they expect to continue until the federal government clarifies the rules.

Last month, Treasury released a notice of proposed rulemaking detailing how it would implement the institutional investor ban while protecting BTR communities. The proposed rules would exempt newly built, never-owner-occupied BTR communities if an investor buys them within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy and uses them only as rentals.

According to recent reports, treasury would also exempt communities that include both rental and for-sale homes, allowing builders to sell the rental portion to large institutional investors while marketing the remaining homes to individual buyers. The proposals additionally call for allowing transfers of existing BTR communities between large institutional investors and keeping the renovate-to-rent exemption.

Although the rules appear to protect BTR, industry leaders say the finer details leave several concerns unresolved.

“If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group, stated in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

Over the last month, Treasury received more than 450 letters with questions and concerns concerning its proposed rulemakings. HousingWire TBD reviewed 10 of those letters, from high-profile BTR developers and operators and leading organizations that advocate on behalf of the rental housing industry, including:.

In a recent development, these letters detailed the outstanding concerns that the industry still has concerning how Treasury will enforce ROAD. With the institutional investor ban set to take effect on January 7, Treasury has several weeks to finalize and release the rules that BTR operators will have to follow.

Until then, the industry has to wait and see whether, and how, those concerns are addressed.

In a recent development, the chief concern among BTR developers, operators and advocates is the proposed requirement that institutional investors purchase BTR communities within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy (CO). Under the proposed framework, if a developer fails to sell a community by that deadline, they may lose the ability to do so altogether.

That proposal matters because many BTR developers, much like multifamily developers, rely on selling their communities after completion and stabilization to make a profit and move on to their next project.

In a recent development, richard Ross, CEO at Quinn Residences, argued that the 18-month window is far too limiting. A community may still be under development and lease-up after the first homes receive a CO, so 18 months will almost certainly run out before the full community is ready to sell.

“To build and stabilize a newly introduced community takes about 30 months. If I start receiving certificates of occupancy at month 15, I may not receive the final CO for the last home until month 28 or 29. I need enough time to complete and stabilize the entire community before selling it,” Ross stated in an interview.

The letters that HousingWire TBD reviewed unanimously opposed the proposed 18-month window. Just like Ross, industry groups argued that the deadline does not align with how rental communities are developed, leased up, financed and sold.

Recent findings suggest that the letter signed by a coalition of 12 BTR developers led by Greystar and Brookfield Residential argued that the deadline would create uncertainty for projects that may not be sold until years after construction. The letter further argued the restrictions would continue to affect financing decisions for future projects.

“A smaller potential buyer pool reduces liquidity and creates greater uncertainty regarding terminal value,” the letter read.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, the groups argued that Treasury must protect long-term institutional owners’ ability to purchase BTR communities. Otherwise, the federal government would undermine the industry.

“If large institutional investors cannot purchase horizontal multifamily communities (which individual families cannot), the values of those properties will fall and newly introduced construction and necessary maintenance and reinvestment will slow,” MBA’s letter read.

To address this, NAA and NMHC, two of the largest rental housing advocacy organizations, requested that Treasury eliminate the deadline or replace it with a provision that institutional investors can purchase BTR communities directly from the builder or developer responsible for construction.

Quinn Residences, AHV Communities and LGI Homes also requested that Treasury remove or substantially extend the deadline. LGI Homes also emphasized the need for production homebuilders to retain the option of renting homes that have not sold.

Recent findings suggest that treasury’s proposed rulemaking describes the three activities that could qualify an institutional investor as a covered entity as “purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains”. This matters because BTR developers often build and retain homes as rental properties before selling stabilized communities to finance future developments.

Treasury’s language is ambiguous, leaving open the possibility that BTR developers could be treated like institutional investors.

Recent findings suggest that the National Rental Home Council made this a central argument in its letter, distinguishing between an investor buying a home from someone else and one acting as the builder. The organization urged Treasury to recognize that developers who build and retain homes as rentals operate differently from investors who purchase newly built homes from third parties.

Up for Growth Action made a similar argument, urging Treasury to differentiate between creating latest rental housing and acquiring existing housing.

Several letters argued that Treasury’s proposed rule does not clearly distinguish single-plat rental communities, where multiple homes share one parcel and common ownership, from individual single-family homes. They worry the rule could inadvertently restrict the development, ownership or sale of these communities by treating them as collections of individual homes subject to the institutional investor ban.

In response, BTR advocates argued for clearer rules for single-plat communities and those mixing renters and owners, while NRHC asked whether buildings with three or more attached units could count as single-family homes.

The letters also raise concerns about the proposed exception for investors that purchase distressed homes, substantially rehabilitate them and rent them out. Treasury’s proposed rules would allow institutional investors to purchase existing homes in need of extensive repairs, as long as they spend 15% of the purchase price on improvements.

However, several of the letters argued that the 15% threshold is too high. They further argued that the rule could be hard to enforce for homes that are difficult to inspect before purchase, homes in jurisdictions without applicable local codes, and homes with problems that aren’t obvious upfront.

According to recent reports, rental housing advocates disagreed on how flexible the rehabilitation threshold should be. While some groups advocated for increasing the threshold, NMHC, NAA and RETTC support the 15% benchmark while advocating for more flexibility in identifying problems and applying older building standards.

The common theme is that industry leaders want the exception to work for genuinely distressed properties without requiring investors to predict every hidden problem before purchasing a home.

Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious blueprint to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.
  • Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid swiftly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Industry observers note that underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he noted.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Sources indicate that nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

It has been revealed that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek noted. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

It has been revealed that for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

In a recent development, “I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

According to recent reports, after graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

Recent findings suggest that “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd stated. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Recent findings suggest that redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he mentioned, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

According to recent reports, in launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

Industry observers note that while the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

In a recent development, team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd mentioned he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

According to recent reports, endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

According to recent reports, the company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.
