#122843. 7 US work permit changes in 2026 and the immigrant groups they hit

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1924 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

7 US work permit changes in 2026 and the immigrant groups they hit

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that work permits now expire sooner and no longer stay valid during renewals.
  • For many immigrants in the U.S., the right to hold a job depends on a work permit card that has to be renewed, and for years renewal was a routine chore rather than a threat to their income.
  • Many workers haven't felt the change yet, because neither rule reaches back to people already in the system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that work permits now expire sooner and no longer stay valid during renewals. See how 3 rule changes affect 4 immigrant groups in 2026.

For many immigrants in the U.S., the right to hold a job depends on a work permit card that has to be renewed, and for years renewal was a routine chore rather than a threat to their income. That changed at the end of 2025, when the federal government put two separate rules into effect within weeks of each other. USAGov reports that since Oct. 30, 2025, a pending renewal no longer keeps a worker's expired card in force. Before that date, a worker could stay on the job while waiting for a replacement card. A second rule, which took effect before the year was out, made the card itself expire sooner. As a result, 2026 is the first year in which workers renew under both rules at once, and every renewal becomes a point where a paycheck can stop.

Many workers haven't felt the change yet, because neither rule reaches back to people already in the system. Renewals filed before Oct. 30, 2025, are not affected, according to E-Verify. El Cronista reports that a worker who already holds a five-year card can keep using it through the date printed on it. Workers will therefore lose the old protections at different times through 2026 and beyond, as each person's card comes due. When a worker filed matters as much as what kind of immigration status they hold. Two people doing the same job with the same status can face very different risks this year, depending on where each one stands in the renewal cycle.

Industry observers note that the American Immigration Council identified which 2026 work permit changes hit which immigrant groups, from people waiting on green cards to H-4 spouses and holders of Temporary Protected Status. The same change can mean little to one group and cost another its income. People who already live on the shortest and least secure terms have the least room to absorb a delay, so a missed renewal does them the most damage.

According to recent reports, workers renewing a work permit no longer have a safety margin while they wait for the government to act. Until late 2025, workers in certain categories could keep working for up to 540 days past the expiration date on their card while a renewal was pending, according to the American Immigration Council. That period was long enough to cover most government delays. The Department of Homeland Security ended the grace period on Oct. 30, 2025, and for a covered renewal, the expiration date printed on the card is now the last day of legal work unless the upcoming card is approved first.

Recent findings suggest that workers and employers had no time to prepare. DHS confirmed the rule on Oct. 29, 2025, E-Verify reports, and it took effect the next day. The rule came out as an interim one, with a final rule expected to follow. Workers should not plan on the change going away.

The burden falls on employers as well as workers, because the employer has to verify that each employee can legally work. A receipt showing that a renewal is pending does not prove a worker's authorization, E-Verify reports, and a business cannot keep someone on the job just because the application is in. When a decision comes late, the employer loses an experienced worker for as long as the government takes to decide, through no fault of either side.

For anyone renewing under this rule, the question is no longer whether they filed on time but whether the government decides on time.

A work permit used to be a document that some immigrants could file away and largely forget for years at a time. For several categories of workers, the card now lasts no more than 18 months, down from a maximum of five years before the change, according to the American Immigration Council. Workers in these categories now go well under two years between renewals instead of several, and they have to strategy around the card far more often. Renewing the permit is no longer an occasional errand but a regular obligation on a worker's calendar.

The new limits are not the same for every worker. Some categories now receive cards valid for up to 18 months, while others receive cards valid for only one year. A worker in the one-year group must renew every single year, and the work on the next application begins soon after the last one is finished. Each worker's schedule depends on which of the two limits applies to that worker's category.

Sources indicate that the shorter card is most dangerous in combination with the end of automatic extensions. By itself, a shorter card would mostly mean more paperwork. Apart from a few limited exceptions, workers can no longer keep their jobs on an expired card while a renewal is pending, so for most of them every renewal carries the chance of a stretch without legal permission to work. More frequent renewals give workers more of those chances to fall into a gap. Employers who rely on these workers now have to keep up with the same shorter schedule, and they face the possibility of losing staff at each renewal.

Workers in these categories should treat the expiration date on their card as a standing deadline to watch, not a distant date to remember later.

It has been revealed that the American Immigration Council reports that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has issued a newly introduced edition of Form I-765 and added stricter screening, which makes renewing a work permit less of a formality. No card gets shorter and no worker loses authorization under this change alone. With tighter background checks and wider discretionary review, approval depends more on an officer's judgment and less on filing the right paperwork. That uncertainty carries more weight now that a pending renewal no longer keeps a worker on the job.

Under proposals still under discussion, people whose status is already the least secure would face the most added scrutiny. Tougher requirements for people on parole or deferred action are under consideration, though officials have only suggested or argued over them so far, and none of the proposals is final.

Applicants should initiative around the rules in force today and keep watching the proposals.

People waiting on a green card are partway to permanent residence, and their work permit is what keeps them on a payroll while the case is pending. With the 540-day buffer gone, an applicant whose renewal is still pending when the card expires has no legal right to work, even though nothing about the green card case itself has changed, according to the American Immigration Council. These applicants also face that risk on a shorter cycle, because their cards are now capped at 18 months.

Industry observers note that the federal government's general guidance does not tell these applicants plainly whether the new rules apply to them. "Check for updates from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to find out if this new rule affects your case," USAGov advised. The page was revised on March 17, 2026, but what it indicates about how long a card lasts may not reflect the shorter limits that took effect in December 2025, so an applicant who relies on it could expect a card to last longer than it will.

The safer course is to assume the stricter rules apply and strategy each renewal as a possible gap in pay.

People whose place in the U.S. rests on a claim of protection now have to renew their right to work again and again, whatever stage their case has reached. The group is wider than the word "asylum" suggests. Alongside asylum applicants, refugees and asylees, the changes reach people seeking withholding of removal, cancellation of removal or relief under the Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act (NACARA), according to El Cronista. Work permits for everyone in this group now last no more than 18 months, according to the American Immigration Council, including refugees and asylees whom the government has already recognized.

In a recent development, the real danger for this group is that a card now expires on its printed date whether or not the replacement has arrived. Without the old extensions, a person whose renewal is still pending when the card runs out loses legal permission to work. That gap comes from processing time alone, not from any finding against the person or the case. Someone can file on time and do everything right, then still have to stop working until the government decides. Employers who rely on workers in this group should track their renewal dates rather than assume the card covers them.

Industry observers note that new asylum seekers could also wait longer for their first permit under a proposal that has not taken effect. It would allow a waiting period of up to 365 days before an asylum seeker can receive a work permit. If officials adopt it, asylum seekers would wait longer for a first card and then hold it for a shorter time. The rules already in force tighten the end of the process, and the proposal would tighten the start as well.

People in this group and their employers should watch the proposal while planning now around the 18-month limit that already applies.

According to recent reports, H-4 spouses who renew their work permits can now lose the legal right to work on the day the old card expires if the renewal is still undecided. Under the old rule, a spouse could keep working for up to 540 days past the expiration date printed on the card, according to E-Verify, and could file a renewal without watching the date on the old one. Without the extension, the same wait now means time off the job and time without pay.

For H-4 spouses this year, the question is not whether they remain eligible to work but whether they receive the latest card before the old one expires.

Holders of Temporary Protected Status and humanitarian parolees face the strictest form of each upcoming work permit limit, because their right to stay in the U.S. already has an end date. Their work permits last one year at most, TPS designations for certain countries are being terminated, and they have limited exceptions to the end of automatic extensions, according to the American Immigration Council. These workers face all three pressures at the same time: a short card, little cushion when it expires, and a status the government can end. At each yearly renewal, the government decides again whether they can keep working legally.

According to recent reports, A one-year card is the longest these workers can get, and some may get a shorter one. The permit lasts one year or until the person's status or the country's designation ends, whichever comes first. A worker whose country's designation ends within the year therefore holds a card that ends with it. With TPS being terminated for certain countries, some workers from those countries hold cards backed by protection that is running out. For this group, the work permit cannot outlast the status behind it. The less secure a person's status, the more their income depends on deadlines they do not control.

Anyone in these groups should track two dates: when the card expires and when the protection behind it ends.

StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.
  • In a recent development, stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft.
  • Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.

In a recent development, stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a newly introduced round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

In a recent development, stepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The manufacturer has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

Sources indicate that the problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”.

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

Sources indicate that it gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer noted an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has stated the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

Sources indicate that it also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor noted up to 5,000 users may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity claims it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

Industry observers note that how it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

Recent findings suggest that more than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the manufacturer says, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

Sources indicate that stepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a tech giant’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-newly introduced releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Industry observers note that along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

It has been revealed that growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

According to recent reports, the organization has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

According to recent reports, what’s next: StepSecurity plans to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The company says it also plans to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chris Murray compares embroidery and screen printing based on durability, fabric type, appearance, and cost.

HONESDALE, Pa., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- When is embroidery a better choice than screen printing for custom apparel? That question is answered in a HelloNation article featuring insights from Chris Murray of Platform Industries in Honesdale, Pennsylvania.

The article explains that both embroidery and screen printing are widely used for customizing garments, but the better option depends on how the apparel will be used. Embroidery, which uses thread to stitch designs into fabric, offers long-lasting results with a raised, textured look. It is especially well-suited to thicker garments such as polos, jackets, hats, and work uniforms. Because the thread is sewn in rather than applied on top, embroidery resists fading, cracking, and peeling, even with frequent wear and washing.

It has been revealed that screen printing, on the other hand, involves pressing ink directly onto fabric. This allows for large, colorful designs and is typically the more cost-effective option for high-volume orders. The article notes that screen printing works best on lightweight materials like cotton t-shirts and is ideal for bold graphics or event apparel. However, printed designs may wear down over time, especially when washed often or if the curing process was incomplete.

Industry observers note that according to the HelloNation article, the decision between embroidery and screen printing often comes down to durability. For businesses in Northeastern Pennsylvania that need custom apparel to last, such as work uniforms or branded jackets, embroidery provides a more resilient finish. Thread maintains its shape and color better than ink, which can be affected by temperature, washing methods, and fabric quality.

Embroidery is also preferred when a more formal or polished look is required. The article explains that a stitched logo conveys professionalism and is commonly used for corporate uniforms and staff apparel. This can influence how a brand is perceived by customers, especially in roles with direct client interaction.

According to recent reports, that stated, the article outlines clear limitations of embroidery. It does not perform well on thin or stretchy fabrics, where the tension from stitching can cause distortion. Embroidery is also priced by stitch count, so larger or more complex designs can become costly. Logos with gradients, small text, or great detail are often better reproduced with screen printing, which handles intricate digital artwork more effectively.

Recent findings suggest that screen printing shines in situations where visual impact and cost-efficiency are key. The HelloNation article highlights that schools, sports teams, and community groups often choose screen printing for spirit wear or event t-shirts. It allows for vibrant, eye-catching graphics over a wide area of the garment. While screen printing is generally more affordable for large batches, its durability is not as strong as that of embroidery for heavy-duty use.

The article advises considering the intended use of the garment when selecting a method. Embroidery is ideal for long-term wear and garments that need to endure frequent laundering, such as custom work uniforms in Northeastern Pennsylvania. Screen printing works best for short-term or promotional use, where appearance and volume matter more than extended durability.

Cost considerations also factor in. The article notes that while embroidery may cost more for larger designs, it adds value when lasting quality and professional appearance are key. By contrast, screen printing offers budget-friendly options for temporary or casual apparel.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the HelloNation article concludes that each method has distinct strengths. Embroidery offers superior resilience and a refined look, making it the preferred choice for apparel that must hold up under regular use. Screen printing offers flexibility in design and volume, especially for simpler, short-term projects.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage applications increased 6.1% from one week earlier, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) weekly mortgage applications survey for the week ending November 20, 2026.

On an unadjusted basis, the Index increased 3% compared with the previous week.

The refinance index increased 1% from the previous week and was 51% lower than the same week one year ago. The seasonally adjusted purchase index increased 10% from one week earlier. The unadjusted purchase index increased 5% compared with the previous week and was 16% lower than the same week one year ago.

In a recent development, “Mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.38%, its highest level in five weeks. While mortgage rates increased slightly on a weekly average basis, rates declined over the course of the week, which likely spurred purchase application activity,” said Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace.”.

Industry observers note that kan added that a larger share of borrowers gravitated to ARM loans. The ARM share of activity accounted for 11.5% of applications, the highest share in more than a year, Kan noted.

In a recent development, “At 6.39%, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week. Refinance activity was flat over the week with conventional applications showing a small increase while VA refinances dropped more than 11%,” he remarked.

The refinance share of mortgage activity decreased to 40.1% of total applications from 41.1% the previous week. The adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) share of activity increased to 11.5% of total applications.

By product, the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) share of total applications decreased to 15.9% from 16.1% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) share decreased to 12.4% from 12.8% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5% from the week prior.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances ($832,750 or less) increased to 7.38% from 7.35%. Meanwhile, the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with jumbo loan balances decreased to 7.29% from 7.31%.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages backed by the FHA decreased to 7.05% from 7.06% while rates for 15-year fixed-rate mortgages increased to 6.79% from 6.64%. The average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs slightly increased to 6.39% from 6.38%.

Xactus’s Mortgage Intent Index — which analyzes aggregated, anonymized credit-pull activity across the Xactus Intelligent Verification Platform — increased week-over-week to a reading of 97.8.

“Mortgage intent edged up approximately 2.2% week over week,” stated Thomas Lloyd, chief strategy officer at Xactus. “The uptick follows last week’s Veterans Day-suppressed reading, suggesting underlying borrower demand remains present even in a challenging rate environment.”.

Lloyd continued, “Early readings from the Daily Xactus Mortgage Intent Index offer some cautious optimism heading into Thanksgiving week — Monday’s reading of 65.9 reflects expected seasonal softness, but the year-over-year gap of approximately 16.5% is a notable improvement from the roughly 25% deficit seen in recent weeks.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk’s companies are moving faster than expected on a Tesla-SpaceX combination.
  • Tesla holds its annual shareholder meeting on December 3, and the same directors who would sign off on the deal are up for re-election.
  • According to recent reports, according to Bloomberg’s sources, it’s now a negotiation over price and control, with boards and advisers on both sides involved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk’s companies are moving faster than expected on a Tesla-SpaceX combination. A deal could be announced as soon as December, which would make it the largest merger ever, according to Bloomberg.

Tesla holds its annual shareholder meeting on December 3, and the same directors who would sign off on the deal are up for re-election.

According to recent reports, according to Bloomberg’s sources, it’s now a negotiation over price and control, with boards and advisers on both sides involved. December is the target, but early 2027 is also on the table.

Sources indicate that one of the variables on the table is how many SpaceX shares Tesla investors would receive. So, as expected, this is shaping up as SpaceX absorbing Tesla, not the other way around.

That fits the valuations. SpaceX is worth over $1.9 trillion after its June IPO, while Tesla sits around $1.5 trillion. For scale, the record for a single deal has long been Vodafone’s $183 billion takeover of Mannesmann in 2000, and even SpaceX’s roughly $250 billion purchase of xAI (a private organization at the time) earlier this year would be dwarfed.

Neither manufacturer commented. Tesla stock rose as much as 1.9% on the report.

We’ve been tracking this since May, when Musk first floated merging the two companies weeks before the SpaceX IPO. At the time, we called it the fourth time Musk would make a more than $1 billion self-dealing transaction, after SolarCity, Twitter/X, and Tesla’s $2 billion xAI investment that turned into SpaceX stock.

Sources indicate that then, in October, Tesla’s proxy filing read like a board getting ready for a SpaceX merger. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees, has sat on SpaceX’s board since February. The ballot for the December 3 meeting is limited to re-electing Musk, chair Robyn Denholm, and JB Straubel to terms through 2029, plus a say-on-pay vote and the auditor.

A day later, Musk confirmed that both boards had formed special committees to explore a merger.

The governance piece is where Tesla shareholders should pay the most attention.

Musk owns about 20% of Tesla but controlled roughly 85% of SpaceX’s voting power through super-voting shares, according to its S-1. Swapping Tesla shares for SpaceX shares means trading one-share-one-vote for a organization where Musk’s control is effectively locked in.

Industry observers note that and the deal itself pays Musk. Under the change-in-control terms in his 2025 CEO award, the operational milestones drop out and the market cap test runs at the deal price, with earned shares vesting immediately. Based on the share count in the proxy, a deal valuing Tesla at $2 trillion (about a 33% premium to where it trades now) would clear the first market cap tranche on the spot. His 286 million restricted shares from the 2018 package also accelerate on a change in control.

Sources indicate that bloomberg reports that one of the main obstacles is how to ring-fence Tesla’s China business. A JPMorgan analyst described SpaceX’s defense and government work and Tesla’s China footprint as “key dynamics that are at odds with each other” for regulators and shareholders.

Recent findings suggest that that’s the same issue behind the Wall Street Journal’s July report that Tesla was weighing a sale or spinoff of its China operations, which Musk denied. Giga Shanghai is Tesla’s most productive factory and builds more than half of its cars. It shipped 67,829 vehicles in October alone.

Politics is the other wild card. Congress flipped to Democrats in the midterms, and they’ve said Musk’s companies and his political ties will get a hard look. Bloomberg previously reported the companies want to close before President Trump leaves office.

In a recent development, I suspected that the midterms might accelerate the timeline. The Dems don’t take office until January, and Musk likely wants to move this as far along as possible before then.

No rational independent board would offer $1.5 trillion (much less $2 trillion) for Tesla. It is a shrinking EV firm with a few fantasy projects that are not delivering. But endlessly diluting other stockholders is his thing.

It has been revealed that as for the “independent committees”, those are obviously a joke. No one believes that, but it’s not like Tesla’s shareholders would care at this point. Tesla’s stock has been a dud for 4 years, and shareholders’ best chance to see a return is another self-deal with Musk.

Tesla is a car and energy firm with falling car sales, and it would get folded into a rocket, satellite, and AI company that’s valued at a premium to it and controlled by one person.

It has been revealed that this is the end game. At least, it looks like Elon is running out of companies to fold together to hide underperformance.

If you’re following Tesla because of its energy business, the cheapest way to tap into that transition at home is still putting solar on your own roof. #122836. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • According to recent reports, it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • Recent findings suggest that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

According to recent reports, it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Recent findings suggest that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

Industry observers note that the disastrous update that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful fresh AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

Sources indicate that the question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the tech giant has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella stated Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella noted, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

According to recent reports, some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

Sources indicate that MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Blueprint) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a organization partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in major, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

In a recent development, over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

It has been revealed that what happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the manufacturer with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from latest finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

According to recent reports, moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

Industry observers note that since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

It has been revealed that in theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple users to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

The cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are crucial enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security issue involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he remarked, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

It has been revealed that managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It has been revealed that it’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

It has been revealed that what needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It has been revealed that it’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 21:36 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

It has been revealed that rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of latest capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different. Today came the ability to use Claude to create fully functional desktop applications for Windows and Mac computers with a single prompt.

It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.

In a recent development, the company said today that users can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop. Artifacts have been around for a while, and they can be almost anything, such as a simple order tracker or a meeting dashboard that pulls information from the user’s calendar and email inbox.

According to recent reports, however, until today, artifacts were a bit tricky to access. They could be opened up only from inside Claude itself, which meant consumers first had to open up the chatbot, login and then find the old conversation where they originally created the artifact they want to use.

According to recent reports, anthropic remarked people are using Claude artifacts all the time for various everyday tasks, and so it makes sense to mature the concept. “If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” the company said.

That’s why Anthropic is making it possible for people to use artifacts to create, run and share desktop applications with Claude’s new “Install as App” feature, which is available in beta now on Windows and macOS.

Sources indicate that in a video posted on X, Anthropic showed how straightforward it is to create a functional desktop app from a simple prompt. The user simply describes the tool they want Claude to create, click confirm and then sit back and wait for a few seconds as it slaps together the required code to bring that app to life.

You can now install Claude artifacts as desktop apps on Mac and Windows.

Sources indicate that ask Claude to build an artifact, click "Install as app", and open it like any other app. It can use your connectors and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item. pic.twitter.com/8CBgqe5OKq.

— ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs) November 24, 2026.

Industry observers note that because these are “real” apps, they come with their own app icons and they open in a dedicated Window, rather than running within the Claude interface. They also get the ability to send notifications to users, Anthropic mentioned.

As an added benefit, Claude artifacts that are transformed into desktop apps will be able to use Claude and various third-party connectors, meaning that AI agents will be able to interact with them autonomously, Anthropic said. However, the manufacturer did warn that any requests made by an app to Claude will count toward their monthly credit usage, which means it could become expensive if an app is used excessively.

In a blog post Anthropic showcased a number of examples of what its internal teams have built, including a fully featured image editing app called Linnet, a file manager with a cinematic design called Phosphor, and a terminal application that integrates with Claude, which is known as Tern.

According to recent reports, there is one major caveat to Claude artifacts-as-apps that sets them apart from traditional desktop applications. According to Anthropic, “you need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app.”.

That could be a pretty big downside, for many desktop applications are designed to work even if the computer is not connected to the internet. But those who lack a Wi-Fi connection will be unable to access their Claude-generated apps, even if they’re already built and configured.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What exactly does a bankruptcy trustee do, and why does it matter for someone filing for bankruptcy?
  • Industry observers note that the article provides a clear explanation of the bankruptcy trustee's responsibilities and how they help guide the bankruptcy process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Carla Vida and Behrooz Vida outline how bankruptcy trustees review financial information, oversee assets, and administer Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 cases.

FORT WORTH, Texas, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What exactly does a bankruptcy trustee do, and why does it matter for someone filing for bankruptcy? That question is answered in a HelloNation article featuring insights from Carla Vida and Behrooz Vida of The Vida Law Firm, PLLC.

Industry observers note that the article provides a clear explanation of the bankruptcy trustee's responsibilities and how they help guide the bankruptcy process. A bankruptcy trustee is a neutral party appointed by the court to oversee a bankruptcy case. Unlike a judge, the trustee manages the financial aspects, ensures that legal requirements are followed, and helps make sure that creditors are treated fairly.

The article explains that in a Chapter 7 bankruptcy case, the Chapter 7 trustee focuses on reviewing the debtor's financial disclosures, verifying property listings, and identifying which protected assets are exempt and which are not. If non-exempt property is available, the trustee may liquidate those assets to repay creditors. All debtors, both individual and business, are required to meet with the trustee to review the case. Creditors may also attend this meeting and ask questions about the filings. The article notes that understanding the trustee's role helps debtors know what to expect and how their property may be handled during the case.

In Chapter 13 cases, the trustee's role is different. The Chapter 13 trustee reviews the debtor's proposed repayment proposal, verifies income and expenses, and ensures the plan meets legal standards. The trustee does not act as a mediator between debtors and creditors, nor do they represent either party. According to the article, trustees help explain legal procedures, answer questions, and manage case administration. By maintaining impartiality, trustees help ensure that the process remains fair and legally sound for everyone involved.

The article emphasizes that debtor responsibilities are closely tied to the trustee role. Debtors must provide complete and accurate information about their income, debts, and personal property. The trustee is responsible for verifying those details and may take action if errors or omissions are discovered. The article advises that honest communication and cooperation with the trustee help keep the bankruptcy process on track and avoid unnecessary delays.

According to recent reports, trustees also play a central role in handling protected assets. In Chapter 7 cases, the trustee reviews exemption claims to determine which assets are shielded by law. If non-exempt assets are identified, the trustee may sell them and distribute the proceeds to creditors. In Chapter 13 cases, the trustee ensures that repayment plans are based on an accurate understanding of both exempt and non-exempt property. The article explains that this part of the trustee role is key to ensuring fair treatment for all parties.

Recent findings suggest that the trustee also acts as a link between debtors and creditors. According to the article, trustees help explain legal procedures, answer questions, and manage case administration. By staying neutral and enforcing the rules, trustees help protect the interests of both sides while keeping the process organized and fair.

Preventing fraud is another crucial part of the trustee's job. Trustees are trained to spot red flags, investigate questionable claims, and protect the integrity of the bankruptcy system. Their oversight ensures that bankruptcy relief is given only to those who follow the rules and meet the legal requirements. The article notes that when debtors understand the trustee role, they are better prepared to meet expectations and respond quickly to requests for documents or clarification.

In addition to managing individual cases, trustees are responsible for reporting to the court, maintaining records, and ensuring compliance throughout the bankruptcy case. They track payments, report distributions, and request proposal modifications when needed. This level of oversight provides added accountability and helps debtors stay on course as they work toward financial recovery.

In a recent development, the article concludes that the trustee role is essential in both Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 cases. Trustees enforce legal standards, oversee asset protection, and support a fair and efficient bankruptcy process. Learning how trustees operate helps individuals and business owners better understand their debtor responsibilities and approach bankruptcy with greater confidence.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Army detonated its Iowa lead azide stockpile.
  • Getting rid of the lead azide stored in Iowa forced the Army to choose among methods, and whichever one it picked would affect the people living around the plant.
  • Residents spent days planning around a date that kept moving while the Army's opponents fought the detonation in court.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Army detonated its Iowa lead azide stockpile. See why it acted, how barriers limit the lead, and what households near the plant did.

Getting rid of the lead azide stored in Iowa forced the Army to choose among methods, and whichever one it picked would affect the people living around the plant. The Army had a whole stockpile to destroy rather than a single bad drum, with 68 barrels of bomb-making material in all, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. With that much material, the way the Army destroys it matters to everyone who lives nearby. Army officials weighed gentler-sounding methods, including chemical neutralization and thermal treatment, before they settled on a blast. The Army's case is that the blast is the least risky of these methods. "In every instance, the answer is controlled detonation is safest," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle told PBS NewsHour. Once the Army chose a detonation, its neighbors no longer had to ask whether a blast would happen, only how to get through it.

Residents spent days planning around a date that kept moving while the Army's opponents fought the detonation in court. The date changed three times, PBS NewsHour reports, and the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals cleared the blast only on the Monday before it. The court did not find that the blast was harmless. It approved the detonation by pointing to the barriers around the storage area and to the weather restrictions, so a safe detonation day depends on those conditions holding. That leaves people nearby with three practical questions: why the Army couldn't wait, how much lead it can keep on site, and what they should do themselves.

According to recent reports, KWQC put together a guide for households around the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on the Army's strategy to blow up its lead azide, covering why the Army acted, how it planned to keep the lead contained and what families should do at home. A local outlet wrote the guide for the people who would have to act on it. Each part of the guide deals with the same trade-off from a different side. The Army acted because the drums were decaying, its barriers are designed to limit how much lead escapes, and residents' own precautions have to cover whatever gets past those barriers. None of these steps protects people on its own. Safety on detonation day depends on all three working together.

Sources indicate that the danger at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant has been building for years as old drums of lead azide slowly failed, and this year it reached a point where the Army could no longer leave it alone. Staff first noted deterioration in the barrels in 2009, and the decay since then has left them at risk of an accidental explosion, according to KWQC. The damage covered much of the stockpile, with several dozen degraded barrels found in March, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. The Army's question was no longer whether to act but how soon. Each month of delay meant more decay, not less.

The clearest warning sign was on the outside of the drums, and it made them dangerous to handle at all. Workers noticed crystals on the barrels' exteriors in March 2026. Army Col. Aaron Teller, a munitions emergency response specialist, warns that the slightest rubbing can break those crystals and touch off a chain of explosions, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. That reverses the usual intuition. Neutralizing the material with chemicals or treating it with heat sounds gentler, but in the Army's view workers would first have to lift and move the same drums that friction can set off. Leaving the drums where they sat offered no safe pause either, because doing nothing left the timing of any explosion to chance.

In a recent development, the explosion to fear is not the planned one but one that happens at a moment nobody picks. Army officials name a spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation as the danger. "The longer we wait, the longer the risk accumulates that they might have an accidental explosion," John Goodpaster, a chemistry professor at Indiana University, Indianapolis, mentioned, as reported by the Chicago Sun-Times. If the drums blew up on their own, nobody would choose the weather or warn the neighbors.

Acting now swaps an explosion no one can predict for one the Army controls, though a controlled blast still has to keep its lead from leaving the plant.

The Army is surrounding the blast with barriers because an open-air detonation with nothing around it has already shown how much lead can get away. In an open-air blast in the 1970s, 25% of the lead was released, according to KWQC. That is the one real-world result this strategy has to improve on. This time the Army is using sand barriers, a water wall, foam and soaked soil to cut how much lead dust reaches land beyond the plant. PBS NewsHour reports that the Army plans to use thousands of gallons of water. The Army's approach is to catch the dust at the spot where it forms, before any of it leaves the site.

According to recent reports, even the Army does not aim to keep all of the lead at the plant. "Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle remarked, as reported by PBS NewsHour. Army officials are only hopeful that these measures will bring the share of lead that escapes below the level of the 1970s blast. The barriers can make a leak smaller, but they cannot seal it. Any lead that gets through becomes a question of where it lands.

In a recent development, when the Army chose the day of the blast, it also chose which neighbors would be downwind. With the detonation set for 9 a.m. Wednesday, PBS NewsHour reports that the plume is projected to move toward Missouri instead of north, as the earlier plan had it. People who were out of the path before are now in it. The Army moved the date for the wind conditions expected on Wednesday, and those conditions are a forecast, not a guarantee. Missouri officials under Gov. Mike Kehoe are only now establishing additional air and water monitoring. On the side that is newly downwind, measurement is catching up to the risk instead of arriving ahead of it.

The lead that gets past the walls and follows the wind becomes a problem for the people living under it.

For people living near the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, the Army's trade-off became a set of household instructions, and distance from the plant decided which ones applied. Residents within five miles were first told to evacuate and those 5 to 20 miles away to stay sealed indoors, but an alert sent one hour before the 9 a.m. detonation reversed the evacuation advice, according to KWQC. The Associated Press reports that FEMA named Middletown, Augusta and Burlington, Iowa, in that final alert. Families who had been getting ready to leave home had to switch to staying in it, and the people closest to the plant were left with the same instruction as their neighbors farther out.

With evacuation off the table, residents' own homes had to provide the protection that the Army's barriers could not. Sealing a house means cutting it off from outside air through both the windows and the ventilation system. "STAY INDOORS with windows closed to block lead dust," FEMA mentioned in its emergency alert, as reported by The Associated Press. Households were also told to keep their heating and cooling systems moving only the air already inside. Dust was just one of the dangers named for people sheltering in the zone, and noise and vibration were the others. Residents can keep out the dust by closing up the house, but they can only wait out the noise and vibration. The guidance protects people who are under a roof.

A farmer can close up a farmhouse, but not the fields around it. The wind was expected to carry the plume southwest, away from Burlington and the Mississippi River, and farms lie in its projected path, according to The Associated Press. Fields and livestock cannot be moved indoors, and the shelter advice protects the farmer but not the farm.

The Army chose the blast it could schedule and built barriers to hold back what it could, but no one can seal the open ground in the plume's path.

In a recent development, lunar AI uses electricity prices, weather forecasts, and a property’s energy use to decide when to charge batteries or supply power. Adding the EV gives it another battery to coordinate with rooftop solar and household battery storage.

It currently operates VPPs in California, Hawaii, and Texas and is expanding in Utah, Nevada, and New Jersey. It also operates in Europe, the UK, and Japan.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.
  • A fresh baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night?
  • But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.

A fresh baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

“We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla noted. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”.

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

According to recent reports, birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has challenges with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

Gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”.

In a recent development, the platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for people.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

Recent findings suggest that birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on upcoming parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

In a recent development, how universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

In a recent development, it’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

It has been revealed that that “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

In a recent development, turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Recent findings suggest that earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

We’ll know our firm has made it when….

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

The news comes soon after a key breakthrough for Midnight in the United Kingdom, where Monument Bank started tokenizing customer deposits on the blockchain.

Industry observers note that per a Nov. 19 NADA NEWS report, Midnight Foundation President Fahmi Syed remarked the foundation had inked an MOU (memorandum of understanding) with a major Japanese payments manufacturer.

In a recent development, syed did not name the manufacturer. But the deal is a significant one for Midnight’s bid to establish a presence in Japan’s financial services sector.

However, it is just an initial agreement, and no commercial services have been rolled out in Japan yet.

It is also worth noting that the Midnight Foundation is talking to some major Japanese banks and companies working with intellectual property and medical data.

According to Syed, he spent two days in Tokyo meeting with major financial institutions and other companies.

Japan has been a key market for Midnight, along with the United States.

According to Midnight Foundation Japan country manager Taro Kimura, Japan is the only Asian country where the foundation has a local representative on the ground.

Midnight has been eyeing Japan more keenly due to the country’s sizeable Cardano community.

The Japanese push comes hot on the heels of a historic development in the British banking sector.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 18, British financial institution Monument Bank started tokenizing retail customer deposits on Midnight. It is the first UK bank to launch such a product on a public blockchain.

Industry observers note that the first phase of the venture involves up to £250 million in tokenized deposits. For this, the bank is offering customers a 12-month fixed annual interest rate of 5.2%.

It has been revealed that midnight employs zero-knowledge cryptography to safeguard sensitive transaction details, unlike traditional public blockchains. As a result, banks can meet compliance requirements while keeping their customers’ private information and transaction details out of public view.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that BYD just got some good news in its Defender-copycat court battle with JLR. After JLR had BYD’s Netherlands offices raided and documents seized, a Dutch court has now handed BYD an early win, ordering JLR to destroy the documents or face a penalty.

After BYD opened orders for the Ti 7 in Europe and the UK in late July, many (including us at Electrek) compared it to the iconic Land Rover Defender, with its boxy, rugged (yet still elegant) SUV design.

BYD even described it as having “an unapologetically boxy profile” that delivers “the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look.”.

In August, authorities on behalf of the British luxury automaker raided BYD’s offices in the Netherlands without prior warning and seized digital records.

On November 11, a Dutch court in The Hague ruled against JLR and ordered the company to destroy the seized documents, which included launch looks and other technical data, so they wouldn’t fall into anyone else’s hands.

JLR must destroy the documents within 24 hours of the ruling or face a fine of €50,000 ($55,000) for every hour it is delayed, with a maximum penalty of up to €500,000 ($553,000).

Industry observers note that within 24 hours of destroying it, JLR must also provide BYD with third-party confirmation that it has been destroyed. The court also rejected the British automaker’s request to pay a €500,000 ($553,000) fine.

According to Autoweek Netherlands, the ruling is based on the fact that JLR doesn’t need the documents, noting that the Ti 7 has not yet been sold in the European Union.

BYD won the ruling, and JLR is prohibited from taking any further legal action under the initial seizure order, but JLR has already begun summary proceedings over the infringement in Rotterdam and The Hague.

JLR claims that the Ti 7 SUV is a “slavish imitation” and infringes on the intellectual property of the Land Rover Defender and that BYD stripped down the Defender to reverse-engineer some of its technology.

Before the raid, BYD claims it fully cooperated with JLR’s requests. BYD’s lawyers called the British automakers’ raid a “fishing expedition” and claimed that “too many files were seized.”.

Industry observers note that the Ti 7 is on sale starting at £47,995 ($64,000) in the UK, on the road. That’s over £20,000 ($26,500) less than the plug-in Defender 110, which starts at £71,840 ($95,500) in the UK.

It has a seven-seat arrangement, which BYD mentioned was specifically designed for the European and UK markets.

As the first vehicle in the UK based on its DM-p (Dual Mode performance) powertrain, BYD said the Ti 7 “vastly exceeds the closest competition,” seemingly another jab at the Defender.

"JLR believes BYD stripped down the Defender to reverse engineer some of its technology".

Industry observers note that reverse engineering isn't illegal. Patent infringement is illegal.

According to recent reports, competition strip down each other's product all the time. As long as they don't use the "exact" same technology, it isn't a copy right problem.

The setup uses three electric motors and a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine, delivering a combined 402 hp (408 PS), enabling it to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph in 4.8 seconds.

The engine primarily powers a 35.6 kWh BYD Blade Battery, which provides a pure-electric WLTP driving range of up to 74 miles. In the city, it has an electric range of up to 102 miles.

Available exclusively in the UK in the flagship Excellence AWD trim, BYD claims that the Ti 7 offers “a level of equipment that exceeds anything that its rivals can offer at this price point.”.

We should learn more about the BYD and JLR legal battle soon. Check back for updates, as this story is still ongoing.

  • Recent findings suggest that microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:08 pm.

It has been revealed that microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal customers that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now it’s asking them to switch again.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

Recent findings suggest that the reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”.

Industry observers note that that’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft indicates Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The firm noted putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A fresh Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”.

Customers weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft unveiled Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Recent findings suggest that rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and noted it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the manufacturer in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist consumers may end up back with the people who built it.

#122823. Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off
