General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video company everyone used during the pandemic.
  • Total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters.
  • The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the tech giant outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 23:43 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

Zoom Communications Inc. has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video company everyone used during the pandemic. Its fiscal third-quarter results, posted Monday, indicated the strategy is working, though more work remains.

Total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters. Zoom raised its full-year outlook and confirmed its first quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share.

The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the tech giant outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.

According to recent reports, the concept of conversations to completion has enough merit that Microsoft used those exact words at its recent Ignite 2026 event. In fact, it held an entire session on the topic. Though having an 800-pound gorilla like Microsoft jump on a trend might seem threatening, Zoom has a significant lead and can use Microsoft’s marketing to add momentum to its current tailwind.

In a recent development, nearly all work starts with a conversation: a meeting, a call, a chat thread or a customer interaction. Then everyone leaves, and the real work begins: updating the customer record, writing the follow-up and scheduling the next step. Collaboration vendors have always owned the first step, leaving the second to someone else.

Industry observers note that zoom wants both. “We’d like to leverage AI to transform our business from a conversation-centric vendor to a system of completions,” Chief Executive Eric Yuan stated on the earnings call. He later put it more plainly: “Conversation is step 1. Step 2, AI will take over.”.

AI agents are promptly becoming a commodity, and so are the models behind them. What is scarce is context, the knowledge of what was decided, by whom, and why. Zoom sits on the richest source of it in most companies: what people actually mentioned to one another and to customers.

Recent findings suggest that “Any agent without context really cannot get work done,” Yuan said. That’s why the unified context layer Zoom showcased at Zoomtopia is central to the story. It links conversations to chats, documents and third-party systems, ensuring people and agents work from the same information.

Recent findings suggest that my Notes, the company’s AI note-taker, extends that reach to third-party and in-person conversations. Yuan mentioned it is nearing 2 million monthly active customers, with one financial services firm rolling it out to 80,000 wealth advisers. Chief Financial Officer Michelle Chang added that online customers using My Notes have been associated with a 50% reduction in churn.

That is what will create a deeper competitive moat for Zoom. The more context a customer stores with Zoom, the more useful its agents become and the harder it is to leave. Zoom’s moat is not the meeting. Think of it as the memory of the meeting.

According to recent reports, A context layer is only as good as the number of conversations it ingests, and this is where Zoom’s breadth of platforms matters. Meetings, phone, chat, contact center and now sales intelligence all feed into the same foundation, and each product gets smarter from the others.

It has been revealed that customers are consolidating. DSI Systems is replacing five separate products with Zoom. SolarWinds expanded its Zoom licenses while “recalibrating its Microsoft package,” according to Yuan. Enterprise net dollar expansion returned to 100%, its highest level in 11 quarters. “Strong RPO growth reflects our continued success in landing larger, longer-term multiproduct platform deals, demonstrating growing demand for our AI-first platform,” Chang mentioned.

In a recent development, customer experience is where completion gets paid for. Zoom CX recurring revenue grew in the high double digits for the seventh straight quarter, and all 10 of its largest CX deals included paid AI. More telling, Zoom mentioned at Zoomtopia that 90% of its top 100 CX deals in the first half were with customers latest to Zoom. Contact center is no longer a cross-sell. It is a front door.

Sources indicate that chang described the differentiation as “the ability to think about customer experience in a whole and fresh fresh way.” Specifically, she said, “to be able to seamlessly hand off from virtual agents to agents assisted with AI is a big winner for us.” AI-native startups have the virtual agent but not the human side. Legacy contact center vendors have the humans but not the pace of innovation. Zoom has both on one platform.

There is also an economic moat. Zoom runs most of its AI workload on its own small models and saves the expensive frontier models for harder tasks. “I fundamentally believe no single model can satisfy everything,” Yuan stated. Gross margin rose even as AI usage grew, a feat that a point product reselling another company’s tokens cannot easily match.

The quarter was strong, but analyst questions revealed several concerns.

According to recent reports, some will read the dividend as a sign of maturity. With more than $7 billion in cash and free cash flow margins above 40%, I see a manufacturer that can fund innovation and return capital at the same time.

Although these issues came up during the call, most of the investment community remains positive about Zoom. In his note, Arun Bhatia of William Blair wrote, “Churn and downsell rates are becoming more favorable, AI usage and monetization are increasing, and adoption of new products such as Phone and Zoom CX is strong. We are encouraged by these trends and see potential for a growth uptick in the future.”.

In a recent development, zoom’s headline growth resembles that of a mature software vendor, but the company is in transition, so it’s key to look beyond the numbers. The underlying enterprise business is built to be a platform that uses context to drive customers toward more products and longer commitments. Investors should watch enterprise growth, net expansion and CX AI attach rates rather than the top line.

Industry observers note that for information technology and business leaders, the lesson extends beyond Zoom. Conversation data is a strategic asset, so decide deliberately where it lives and which agents can act on it. Insist on openness so that context can feed the tools you choose. Start where completion is easy to measure, in the contact center and in sales.

Industry observers note that that is where Zoom is proving that the conversation was never the product. The outcome is.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#122822. Latest Update: sonnen’s fresh smart breakers help your home battery last longer

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (732 w)

EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: sonnen’s fresh smart breakers help your home battery last longer

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A home battery can do more during a blackout if it isn’t busy running nonessential, energy-hungry appliances.
  • The companies announced today that they’re integrating ADAPT Energy’s controls and Eaton AbleEdge smart breakers into the SOLRITE–sonnen virtual power plant (VPP).
  • The announcement doesn’t specify pricing, how many homes will receive it, or when existing customers can get it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A home battery can do more during a blackout if it isn’t busy running nonessential, energy-hungry appliances. sonnen and SOLRITE Energy are putting that same principle to work for the grid, adding smart breakers that can temporarily switch off selected household loads while batteries help meet electricity demand.

The companies announced today that they’re integrating ADAPT Energy’s controls and Eaton AbleEdge smart breakers into the SOLRITE–sonnen virtual power plant (VPP). The setup combines sonnenHub with breakers that manage power-hungry equipment, both during outages and when the grid needs help.

The announcement doesn’t specify pricing, how many homes will receive it, or when existing customers can get it.

Industry observers note that A VPP connects home batteries into a network so they can work together as a larger energy resource. This addition gives SOLRITE another way to respond: in addition to controlling the batteries, it can reduce the amount of electricity that participating homes use.

sonnen and SOLRITE used the example of a pool pump, as it’s energy-intensive, nonessential, and runs for longer periods. When an event begins, ADAPT temporarily switches off the pool pump while the sonnen battery sends electricity to the grid.

In a recent development, with less battery power going toward the pump, more can flow to the grid. Across participating homes, that gives the VPP more flexibility than relying on battery dispatch alone.

Homeowners have to opt in to that grid participation, and ADAPT will switch off only pre-approved household loads. Joining the VPP program doesn’t give the operator blanket permission to turn off anything in the house.

“Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home,” mentioned Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy.

The breakers also tackle a practical problem with home backup: Big appliances can drain a battery quickly, and the surge of power some equipment needs to start can overload a backup system just as an outage begins.

Recent findings suggest that ADAPT coordinates the smart breakers with the sonnen battery to automatically switch off large loads during backup operation. When grid power returns, it restores them, so homeowners don’t have to go around resetting individual circuits.

It has been revealed that that also gives homeowners more flexibility later. According to the companies, changing which smart-breaker-controlled loads are switched off during an outage doesn’t require rewiring those circuits.

The installation benefit matters, too. Some backup setups require electricians to move selected circuits into a separate panel. This system manages compatible circuits where their breakers already sit, which the companies say reduces installation complexity and inspection work.

Whole-home backup still has limits. Automatically managing large loads helps the available battery capacity go further; it doesn’t mean every appliance can run at once throughout an outage.

Sources indicate that SOLRITE finances, builds, and owns residential solar-plus-storage projects through what it calls Virtual Power Plant Agreements, with no upfront cost to homeowners. It says it operates in Texas, California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Illinois, with more markets planned.

Breaking: FAA rule changes: 6 flight delays airlines no longer pay for

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2076 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new federal rule takes effect Feb.
  • It has been revealed that when a flight sits at the gate for hours, most travelers assume the airline will at least buy them dinner and find them a bed for the night.
  • In a recent development, federal regulators expect travelers to come out behind, with airlines handing passengers less in perks and payouts overall, according to Insurance Business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new federal rule takes effect Feb. 1, 2027. See which delays no longer bring meal or hotel help, and which protections remain.

It has been revealed that when a flight sits at the gate for hours, most travelers assume the airline will at least buy them dinner and find them a bed for the night. That help can easily feel like a right. Even so, meal and hotel vouchers rest on goodwill rather than law. They remain voluntary commitments, according to Insurance Business, and travelers generally shouldn't expect them once a disruption is no longer classed as within the airline's control. A final rule required by the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 will take 10 kinds of disruption out of that category. Travelers $TRV will lose the meal and the room for those delays even though no passenger right has been repealed, because regulators changed only who is to blame.

In a recent development, federal regulators expect travelers to come out behind, with airlines handing passengers less in perks and payouts overall, according to Insurance Business. "These newly exempted causes of flight delays are not especially common, but we understand that the new rules might make travelers feel less protected when they fly," Robert Gallagher, chief executive for North America at Zurich Cover-More, told Insurance Business. The rule hasn't started yet, because regulators pushed back its start after Airlines for America asked for more time. Until then, today's commitments mostly still apply, and travelers have time to learn which delays will still earn a meal and a room.

Fox 5 DC laid out which disruptions airlines no longer must compensate passengers for, and which still count. The causes range from a sudden repair and a government system outage to a cabin that has to be cleaned after a passenger dies. Through all of them, a traveler's right to a cash refund stays in place. The new rule takes effect Feb. 1, 2027, after regulators moved it from its original start of Oct. 19, 2026, and it covers flights from Jan. 1, 2027. The categories sound tidy, but the line between what an airline caused and what it didn't is blurrier than the labels suggest.

A maintenance problem is the hardest of these delays to picture as beyond the carrier's control, because the airline owns, flies and services the aircraft. Once the newly introduced rule applies, sudden repairs, such as fixing overheated brakes, will count as outside the airline's control, Fox 5 DC reports, and travelers shouldn't expect meal or hotel vouchers for them. The permanent version of the change is a rulemaking titled "Revisions to Cause of Airline Delay Categories," according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. It sorts delays into categories and makes no finding about an airline's diligence.

According to recent reports, the rule has not taken effect, but travelers have already lost the perks for one kind of maintenance. On Nov. 28, 2025, the FAA required airlines to carry out specific maintenance through an emergency airworthiness directive, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. A federal safety order is the clearest case of work an airline did not choose to do. In a notice posted Dec. 10, 2025, the department said it would not hold carriers to their delay commitments for maintenance that directive required. That relief is enforcement discretion tied to a single directive, not a permanent rule. The permanent rule will reach further and cover sudden repairs of any kind, not only work done under one federal order.

This exemption covers planes and equipment physically damaged in extreme weather, not flights that bad weather merely slows down. A traveler who hears "weather" at the gate will probably picture a snowstorm holding flights in place, but an ordinary weather delay is not part of this category, Insurance Business reports. The category covers damage to an aircraft or the infrastructure it relies on from lightning, debris or sabotage, according to Fox 5 DC, so the deciding question is whether something was damaged.

Industry observers note that when a damaged plane is taken out of service, the cost of a stranded night becomes largely the traveler's own risk to manage. . The words "most" and "generally" matter, because coverage depends on the policy. A traveler who buys it still needs to confirm that the plan names delays caused by damage to an aircraft.

A delay blamed on cabin cleaning can now leave passengers with very different outcomes, depending on why the cabin needs cleaning. Cleaning a cabin after a passenger dies on board is among the 10 types of disruption newly excluded from the airline's control, according to Fox 5 DC. Travelers $TRV held up by that cleanup generally should not expect the airline to cover a meal or a hotel room. Ordinary cleaning delays stay the airline's responsibility, and only a death changes how the delay is classed. The exemption therefore gives airlines no general excuse for a slow turnaround between flights. When a gate agent notes the plane is being cleaned, that word alone tells a waiting traveler nothing about what the airline owes. The reason behind the cleaning decides it.

Sources indicate that travelers $TRV who lose a meal or a hotel room under the new rule keep one protection that has nothing to do with who caused the delay. Fox 5 DC reports that the reason behind a cancellation or a major schedule change has no bearing on refunds, and a passenger who refuses the altered trip can get the money back. Besides a long delay, a significant change includes a switch to another airport, extra connections or a downgrade to a lower class of seat, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. A switched airport counts the same way whether a storm or a mechanic forced the switch, and a traveler can collect the refund even when the cause is one the rule now exempts. The catch is that the traveler has to turn down the trip. Passengers who accept a rebooking and wait it out give up the refund, because this right offers a way out of the trip rather than comfort during the wait.

A mechanical delay declared at the gate will no longer be a reliable sign that the airline owes a traveler dinner and a room.

Industry observers note that what changes here is not a flight delayed by a storm but a plane damaged by one. Travelers worried about that second kind should initiative for it before they book.

In a recent development, A federal system failure is the easiest exemption to accept, because no airline runs air traffic control. Under the latest rule, travelers held up by a government outage that threatens safe flying should stop expecting meal or hotel vouchers, according to Fox 5 DC. The nationwide ground stop in November 2026 fits that description even though nothing actually failed. CNBC reports that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford noted the agency would not accept any risk that the problem might cut an air traffic center off from its planes. No FAA facility went dark, and the cause of the instability stayed unknown for about 45 minutes. Once the rule applies, a cautious decision by federal officials such as this one will cost travelers the airline's help without any fault on the airline's part.

In a recent development, the government label can also cover a failure that a private contractor may have caused. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated, as reported by CNBC. No answer to that question would move the delay back into the airline's column, because the airline neither ran the system nor installed the equipment. The traveler's claim depends on the category, not on whose mistake caused the trouble.

It has been revealed that the cancellations did not end when flights resumed. Friday's cancellations were the second-highest since the January blizzard, and roughly 6,500 more flights were canceled on Saturday, according to Cirium and FlightAware figures reported by CNBC. Disruption that runs into a weekend is when a hotel room and a meal matter most, and travelers caught in it will no longer get either from the airline.

An outage that seems to be no one's fault can turn out to be the most expensive kind for the traveler waiting at the gate.

It has been revealed that an airline does not cause a passenger's death, and it does not cause every medical crisis on board either. SF Gate reports that medical emergencies the carrier did not cause are also covered by the exclusion, and so are unruly passengers. In each of these events, a person in the cabin starts the delay, and the airline does not. That makes this exemption tightly drawn and hard to argue with on grounds of fairness. The airline did not create the problem, and the rule does not ask it to pay for a meal or a room because of it.

Even so, a delay after a death on board can still cost a traveler a connection and a night away from home, and the airline's voucher for that night is no longer part of the deal.

The fresh rule leaves the most familiar causes of delay with the airlines. Routine upkeep and crew scheduling problems remain the airline's responsibility, according to Fox 5 DC. A plane held for its regular checks, or a flight stuck because the crew schedule fell apart, still counts against the carrier. Maintenance and crew problems were among the Department of Transportation's examples of controllable delays, according to a CNBC report published in 2024. This is the part of the old bargain that survives for travelers. When the cause is plainly the airline's own housekeeping, its promises of meals and rooms still apply, but only as long as everyone agrees the work was routine.

In a recent development, the word "maintenance" can now either cost travelers their meal and hotel or keep those perks in place, and the difference turns on whether the work was planned. A carrier still owns the delay when it pulls a plane for planned work, but a repair that comes up suddenly or that regulators order now falls on the other side of the line. Airlines therefore have money riding on how they describe a delay, because under one description they still owe the vouchers and under the other they don't.

Sources indicate that even a delay that stays the airline's responsibility comes with no set federal payout, and what a stranded traveler gets is up to the carrier's own policy. "There is this kind of gray area where we're at the mercy of what the airline's policy is," Eric Napoli, chief legal officer at AirHelp, mentioned in 2024, as reported by CNBC. After a crew no-show or a scheduled check, the help a traveler receives still depends on which airline they booked.

When a delay is blamed on maintenance, travelers should ask whether the work was scheduled, and read the carrier's written commitments before they fly rather than at the gate.

In a recent development, A delay becomes a cash matter at a fixed point on the clock. The U.S. Department of Transportation defines a significant change on a domestic flight as a departure or arrival moved by more than 3 hours, and an international flight has to move by more than 6 hours to count. Travelers abroad have to sit through a bigger disruption before they can walk away with their money. The federal government set these lines, and no airline can decide on its own that a long delay was minor.

Refunds were once the main thing passengers fought airlines over. In 2020, when such grievances peaked, 87% of the air travel complaints filed with federal regulators concerned refunds, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. The department wrote refunds into a federal rule, while mandatory compensation and amenities were only at the proposal stage when it issued that rule. The refund right remains unchanged under the latest rule. "Passengers deserve to get their money back when an airline owes them — without headaches or haggling," then-U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg remarked.

Once a delay passes the threshold, the strongest move may be to decline the rebooking and claim the cash rather than wait for a voucher that may never come.

Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the manufacturer acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company indicates it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software upgrade that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

According to recent reports, the bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

In a recent development, so what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July patch was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Sources indicate that second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

It has been revealed that the preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate glitch.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft indicates it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft claims it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft states its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it aims to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft remarked the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it states. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

The fresh testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

According to recent reports, engwe has impressed us repeatedly with its value e-bikes at lower-than-believable prices. The Engwe M20 3.0 is a specs monster and blows away the original version of the bike released in 2023:.

According to recent reports, the M20 is fairly easy to assemble. At just over 100lbs, it is a bit hard to move around, but once assembled, it feels like a pretty impressive piece of machinery. I love the street tires on here instead of pretending to be an off-roader. Dual bright headlights and brake light with turn signals really give this thing some street cred. Adding to the safety roster, Engwe upgraded the quad-piston brakes with sporty red calipers and 202 mm rotors. This is not a value bike. The rear suspension is tight, which is great for 2 riders but might feel stiff out of the box for light riders. The seat is *chef’s kiss* even for 2 riders. Very soft and comfortable but not too soft. It even has a little ‘gas tank’ storage area aft the seat, which is keyed and enough to hold a few sandwiches, some riding gloves, or a small purse.

Sources indicate that one gripe: There are 3 sets of keys on here, the aforementioned storage area and one set each for each battery. We’d love to see these things keyed together.

The bike/moped/moto came with a huge 1.2 kW battery (or 2 in our case – unless you have a 80-mile commute, 1 should be plenty) that must be charged individually. But with a 60V 8A charger, each one only takes about 2-3 hours to charge, which is impressive.

I did not expect to like the ride of this thing as much as I did. We can dispense with the pleasantries here; it came set to Class 2 mode with a 20mph top speed and stickers to match; a quick Google search will show you how to open this up to 40mph open mode. I take responsibility for my own actions.

Recent findings suggest that the first thing you’ll notice here is that the motor is whisper-quiet, and with the street tires, there is very little road noise, even at 35mph. The half throttle is plenty responsive, a lot more so than the cadence sensor on the pedals, which are vestigial at best here. Those major brakes are a bit softer than I’d prefer, but given a good squeeze, those 203mm rotors and quad-piston hydraulic brakes are going to stop you, the 100lb bike, and your passenger/cargo fairly swiftly.

My girlfriend and I got pulled over for the first time in my e-biking life as I was picking her up at the coffee shop. The cop was immediately apologetic because “he thought we were kids” and not the 50-year-olds under the helmets he encountered. Then he noticed the pedals and noted that we’re all clear and that what we were on looked like a motorcycle and that a couple of e-moto kids had gotten into accidents recently, one hit by a drunk driver and who is still in a coma. While he was already letting us go, I pointed out the Class 2 sticker on the bike, and he gave me the thumbs-up as we sped off at 30mph. This M20 passed the local police test with flying colors. I can’t guarantee you’ll have the same experience in your jurisdiction.

Sources indicate that most of my gripes on this e-bike are inherent to the form factor. It is heavy at over 100 lbs, but you’d expect that with a 3.3kW motor, 2.4kW of batteries, and room for two. That said, don’t buy this bike if you need to take it up stairs or blueprint to pedal it without assist. In fact, this isn’t a bikepath bike or a put it on the back of your car bike. And, don’t buy this bike if you like to pedal. It’s too major and fast. This is a 35 mph roads bike. Also 3 sets of keys?

I did not expect to love this bike as much as I have. It is the perfect train station bike for me, and as a bonus, it is a great way to take my girlfriend to the coffee shop on the weekends. It has fat tires, great suspension, a cushy seat, and strong, smooth acceleration and confidence-inspiring braking. It looks cool enough for the cops to think I’m a kid picking up his girlfriend, and it has so much range that I probably won’t need to charge it monthly. At $1399-$1699 (10% off) depending on battery config, this is less than half the price of some of the pricier and admittedly more stylish Super73 options out there.

In a recent development, I understand that some will fault Engwe for selling a 3.3kW motor e-bike as a class 2 e-bike. But I genuinely feel safer on the road, being able to go at the 35mph speed that cars are going rather than forcing them to go around me. Plus, it isn’t like every single car on the road goes over the speed limit. So why not bikes too?

The Engwe M20 3.0 is over the limit but in all of the best possible ways.

  • 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- IntelliGRC, the cyber governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) platform built for managed service providers (MSPs) and managed security service providers (MSSPs), today announced Trust Center.
  • Trust Center is built to end the practice of sending security documents one at a time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Service providers can now publish a Trust Center for each tenant, gate documents behind access approval, and keep a record of who had access and when.

FAIRFAX, Va., Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- IntelliGRC, the cyber governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) platform built for managed service providers (MSPs) and managed security service providers (MSSPs), today announced Trust Center. The newly introduced capability lets customers design and publish a public web page for each tenant, where external organizations can find security documentation and request access to gated content. Trust Center is now available and is included with every IntelliGRC license at no added cost.

Trust Center is built to end the practice of sending security documents one at a time. Each Trust Center is hosted on IntelliGRC's domain and gives customers and prospects a single place to find certifications and audit artifacts. When a visitor requests access to gated content, an admin or designated user approves or denies the request. Approval sends the requester a magic link by email. Access can be revoked at any time, and the platform keeps a record of who had access and when. Customers can also add their own NDA for requesters to sign once they are provisioned access.

The feature is designed for providers that manage many clients at once. From the IntelliGRC Admin App, a provider can set defaults that establish a baseline for every client Trust Center under its license, upload documents once to a Shared Library and deploy them to all Trust Centers or only specific ones, and review pending access requests across every Trust Center from a single Approvals tab. Notifications alert admins to access requests and other Trust Center events.

"A compliance program only counts if you can prove it to the people asking," said Ozzie Saeed, Founder and CEO of IntelliGRC. "Our customers should not have to email documents one at a time and then lose track of who has them. Trust Center gives every tenant one page to point to. It puts the provider in charge of who gets in and lets them revoke that access at any time. For an MSP managing many clients, proof becomes something they can deliver the same way every time.".

Trust Center shipped in IntelliGRC release 3.52.0 on November 10, 2026. Existing customers can find it in the Trust Centers section of the Admin App. Latest to IntelliGRC? Schedule a discovery call with us to see it live.

IntelliGRC is a cyber governance, risk, and compliance platform built for MSPs and MSSPs to deliver high-caliber GRC as a Service (GRCaaS) at scale. Its multitenant architecture, asset-centric modeling, Intelligent Control Library, and practitioner-tuned AI automations help service providers turn complex, evolving compliance requirements into streamlined, repeatable, and profitable offerings for the Defense Industrial Base and other regulated markets. For more information, visit www.intelligrc.com.

Breaking: 10 things to know about filing an Army claim after a blast damages property

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How an Army claim for property damage works after a military blast such as the lead azide detonation in Iowa, from the Federal Tort Claims Act and SF 95 to deadlines, exceptions and fee limits.
  • Recent findings suggest that A blast from a nearby Army range, demolition site or training exercise does not, on its own, entitle a property owner to payment from the federal government.
  • The route to compensation is an Army claim for property damage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How an Army claim for property damage works after a military blast such as the lead azide detonation in Iowa, from the Federal Tort Claims Act and SF 95 to deadlines, exceptions and fee limits.

Recent findings suggest that A blast from a nearby Army range, demolition site or training exercise does not, on its own, entitle a property owner to payment from the federal government. Cracked plaster, broken windows and damaged foundations may all trace back to a military explosion. The government pays only when a claim meets conditions that Congress wrote into federal law.

The route to compensation is an Army claim for property damage. It is a formal demand for money presented to the Army, and it must come before any lawsuit. The main law behind these claims is the Federal Tort Claims Act. That law lets people seek money from the U.S. for property damage caused by the negligent or wrongful acts of federal employees acting within the scope of their jobs.

Recent findings suggest that army Regulation 27-20 governs how the Army handles claims. Army claims offices process them, and the U.S. Army Claims Service at Fort Meade, Maryland, sits at the top of that system. Two other laws, the Military Claims Act and the Foreign Claims Act, cover some cases the main statute does not reach.

Sources indicate that three requirements shape a claim under that statute. The claimant has to show fault, not only that damage happened near a federal operation. The claim has to reach the proper agency within a fixed deadline. It also has to name an exact dollar amount, and that figure limits what the claimant can later seek in court.

Sources indicate that the law also shields the government in other ways. Claims based on discretionary government decisions are barred, even when the discretion behind them was abused. Claims arising from combatant activities during wartime are excluded as well. The danger of explosives or blasting does not by itself make the government liable.

We cover each piece of the process below: the laws that apply, the form used to file and the filing deadline. We also cover the dollar figure a claim must state and the evidence that supports it. We also cover the fault requirement, the exceptions that bar some claims, what happens after the Army receives a claim and the caps on what lawyers can charge. Each entry describes how the system works rather than offering legal advice for a specific case.

In a recent development, the Federal Tort Claims Act is the main law a property owner uses to seek money from the federal government after an Army blast. It allows money claims for property damage caused by federal employees.

The law is usually shortened to FTCA. Most of it sits at 28 U.S.C. section 1346(b) and sections 2671 through 2680 of the same title.

That range covers more than liability. It also holds the rules for presenting a claim to an agency, the limits on attorney fees and the exceptions that bar some claims. Those sit at sections 2675, 2678 and 2680.

Industry observers note that three conditions sit at the center of the statute. The damage must trace back to a federal employee. That employee must have been acting within the scope of the job when the damage happened. The scope requirement ties a claim to the work the government assigned, not to what an employee does on personal time. The act itself must have been negligent or wrongful. A claim that fails any one of these conditions falls outside the FTCA.

Industry observers note that the FTCA borrows its standard of liability from state law. The law of the state where the act happened decides whether the government is liable. A claimant's case turns on how that state treats negligence and wrongful conduct, not on one national standard. A blast in Texas is measured against Texas law. A blast in Washington state is measured against Washington state law. Two similar incidents in different states can be judged under different rules as a result.

Army claims offices handle FTCA claims tied to Army activity. The U.S. Army Claims Service at Fort Meade, Maryland, sits at the top of that system. That puts the first stage of a claim in the hands of an Army claims office rather than a court.

Two federal laws besides the Federal Tort Claims Act can cover property damage tied to the Army. The Military Claims Act reaches certain claims from noncombat Army activities. The Foreign Claims Act covers damage caused by U.S. forces outside the U.S.

It has been revealed that the Military Claims Act appears at 10 U.S.C. section 2733. Its reach is limited to certain claims arising from noncombat Army activities. It does not cover every incident that involves the Army.

In a recent development, this statute can apply where the Federal Tort Claims Act does not. A property owner whose claim falls outside the tort statute may still have a route to payment under the Military Claims Act.

Whether the law fits a particular blast turns on the activity that caused the damage. The question is whether that activity was a noncombat Army activity of the kind the statute covers.

In a recent development, the Foreign Claims Act appears at 10 U.S.C. section 2734. It addresses damage caused by U.S. forces outside the U.S. Under this law, the location of the damage is the starting point.

Sources indicate that A blast tied to U.S. forces abroad raises different questions than one at a domestic installation. The overseas setting is what brings the Foreign Claims Act into play.

Industry observers note that the two statutes sort claims by different tests. The Military Claims Act looks at the type of Army activity behind the damage. The Foreign Claims Act looks at where U.S. forces caused it.

Army Regulation 27-20 governs Army claims, including those brought under these two statutes.

Service members' own injury claims are treated differently and follow separate rules.

Standard Form 95, titled Claim for Damage, Injury, or Death, is the federal form used to present a claim under the Federal Tort Claims Act. A property owner seeking payment for blast damage from Army activity can file it with the Army.

It has been revealed that the form is usually called SF 95. It is a standard federal form rather than an Army form. Claimants use it to present a Federal Tort Claims Act claim to whichever federal agency was involved. When the damage traces to Army activity, that agency is the Army.

It has been revealed that the title reveals the form's range. One form serves claims for damaged property, for personal injury and for death. A homeowner reporting a damaged roof after a blast uses the same document as someone reporting an injury.

The form is not the only accepted format. A claimant can also present the claim in a letter or another written document.

Any such writing must meet two conditions. It has to give the agency enough information to investigate the claim. It also has to demand a specific amount of money.

It has been revealed that the first condition supports the review itself. An Army claims office examines a claim before deciding on it. A writing that leaves out what was damaged, where it happened or how it happened gives the office little to investigate.

According to recent reports, the second condition rules out open-ended requests. A demand for fair compensation, or for whatever repairs end up costing, names no amount. A writing without a stated dollar figure does not meet the requirement.

Filing SF 95 or a qualifying letter starts the administrative stage of a federal tort claim. It does not decide the outcome. The Army still has to review the claim and decide whether to pay it.

A property owner seeking payment for Army blast damage under the Federal Tort Claims Act has two years to present a claim to the proper federal agency. Under 28 U.S.C. section 2401(b), a tort claim against the U.S. that misses that window is barred.

In a recent development, the two-year clock starts when the claim accrues. Accrual is the legal starting point for the period. The statute measures the deadline from that point. It does not run from the date an owner decides to seek payment.

The deadline applies to presenting the claim, not to filing a lawsuit. Presenting means delivering the claim to the agency responsible for the activity that caused the harm. For damage tied to Army activity, that agency is the Army. Army claims offices receive these filings.

Recent findings suggest that the word barred carries real weight in the statute. A claim that reaches the agency after the two-year period closes cannot go forward under the FTCA.

Recent findings suggest that the administrative claim is a required first step. An owner cannot bypass the Army and take an FTCA property damage claim straight to federal court. The claim must go to the agency first. Any lawsuit can follow only after that stage.

Section 2401(b) also sets a second, later deadline. That limit governs filing suit after an agency denies a claim in writing. An FTCA case therefore runs on two separate clocks. One governs reaching the agency, and the other governs reaching a courtroom. The two-year period covers only the first.

A Federal Tort Claims Act claim must name one specific dollar amount, known as a sum certain. That figure does two jobs. It tells the Army what the claimant wants paid. It also sets the most the claimant can later seek in court.

It has been revealed that under this requirement, a claim has to demand a definite amount of money. A property owner whose home, barn or fence was damaged by an Army blast cannot leave the figure open. The owner also cannot ask the agency to decide what the loss is worth. The claim has to put a number on the harm.

The requirement holds whether the claim arrives on Standard Form 95 or in a letter. A letter can describe the damage in detail. Without a dollar amount, it still falls short of a valid claim.

The ceiling matters most if the dispute reaches federal court. There, the claimant generally cannot sue for more than the amount stated to the agency. That limit comes from 28 U.S.C. section 2675(b).

According to recent reports, the same provision allows two narrow exceptions. The first covers newly discovered evidence that was not reasonably discoverable when the claim was presented. The second covers intervening facts relating to the amount of the claim. For that second route, the claimant must allege and prove those facts.

The first exception looks back at information that existed but could not reasonably have been found at filing. The second looks forward to facts that developed after the claim was presented. Neither gives a claimant a general option to raise the number later.

For blast damage, this structure puts weight on the valuation done before filing. A known repair left out of the figure does not become newly discovered evidence because it was overlooked. The same applies to a damaged item the owner knew about but did not include.

Sources indicate that the sum certain is the claimant's own valuation of the loss. It reflects the claimant's estimate of what repairs and replacements will cost.

A property owner who files an Army claim carries the burden of proving it. A well-supported file usually combines dated photographs and repair estimates with receipts, proof of ownership and records showing the property's condition before the blast.

Industry observers note that none of this comes from a single checklist in the statute. It reflects general claims practice. The formal floor is simpler: a written claim must give the agency enough information to investigate. Evidence is what turns that floor into a claim an investigator can verify.

In a recent development, dated photographs record the damage itself. Pictures taken soon after the blast capture cracked walls, broken windows or shifted foundations before weather, cleanup or repairs change them. A date on each image helps tie the damage to the time of the event rather than to an earlier or later cause.

Industry observers note that repair estimates translate visible damage into money. A written estimate from a contractor describes the work needed and what it should cost. Having more than one estimate gives an investigator a way to check whether a figure is reasonable.

It has been revealed that receipts do a related but separate job. They document money already spent, such as emergency repairs, a temporary cover for a damaged roof or a replacement for a broken item. An estimate predicts a cost. A receipt shows a cost that was paid.

Proof of ownership answers a threshold question: whether the person filing has a stake in the damaged property. A deed, a vehicle title or a bill of sale can establish that link.

In a recent development, records of the property's condition before the blast fill a gap that post-blast photos cannot. Older photos, inspection reports, appraisals or maintenance records can show that a crack or leak was not already there. Without them, an investigator has no baseline against which to measure what changed.

Gaps in the record fall on the person who filed. Missing or undated documents weaken the claimant's case, not the agency's.

Recent findings suggest that an Army blast that damages property does not create a right to payment on its own. Under the Federal Tort Claims Act, the claimant must show fault — a negligent or wrongful act by a federal employee — not simply that the activity was dangerous.

In a recent development, that fault requirement sits in the statute itself. The law permits money claims for harm caused by the negligent or wrongful acts of federal workers. It does not open the U.S. Treasury to every loss that follows government activity.

In a recent development, negligence, in general legal terms, is a failure to use the care a reasonable person would use in the same situation. A wrongful act is conduct the law treats as improper. Either one can support a claim. Without one of them, the claim has no footing.

The Supreme Court took up this question in Laird v. Nelms, decided in 1972. The case involved property damage blamed on a sonic boom. At glitch was whether the government could be held liable for that damage without proof of a negligent or wrongful act.

The court answered no. It held that the FTCA does not impose strict liability for ultrahazardous activity. Strict liability means responsibility for harm regardless of fault. Under the ruling, the act reaches fault-based claims, not claims resting on the danger of the activity alone.

For explosives, the consequence is direct. A claimant generally cannot recover just by showing that a detonation or blasting operation carried risk. The hazardous nature of the work does not stand in for proof of a careless or wrongful act.

According to recent reports, state law still matters to these claims. The FTCA generally looks to the law of the state where the act happened. Laird v. Nelms means a state rule that imposes liability without fault does not carry over to a claim against the government under the FTCA.

It has been revealed that A claim built on fault therefore points to conduct. It identifies what a federal employee did, or failed to do, that fell short of reasonable care and led to the damage.

The discretionary function exception, at 28 U.S.C. section 2680(a), bars claims against the federal government that rest on the exercise of a discretionary function or duty. The bar applies even when the discretion was abused.

Recent findings suggest that section 2680 is the part of the Federal Tort Claims Act that lists its exceptions, each in its own lettered subsection. Each one removes a category of claims from the law's reach. A claim that falls inside one of them cannot succeed under the FTCA, however much damage the property suffered.

It has been revealed that the discretionary function language covers choices made by a federal agency as well as those made by an individual government employee. It also covers a failure to exercise or perform such a function. The same subsection separately bars claims based on an employee's use of due care in carrying out a statute or regulation, valid or not.

The wording of section 2680(a) does not turn on whether a decision was sound. A choice can be a poor one. It can even be an abuse of discretion. If the conduct counts as a discretionary function or duty, the exception still covers it.

Industry observers note that that feature sets the exception apart from an ordinary fault inquiry. A property owner may be able to point to careless conduct behind a blast. The claim can still fail if the conduct falls within the exception.

Industry observers note that dalehite v. United States, decided by the Supreme Court in 1953, is the standard early authority on the discretionary function exception. The case is known as the Texas City disaster case.

A second carve-out sits at section 2680(j). It excludes claims arising from the combatant activities of the military or naval forces, or the Coast Guard, during time of war. This exception looks at the setting of the conduct rather than the kind of decision behind it.

It has been revealed that damage tied to wartime combat therefore falls outside the FTCA. Whether an exception applies is a separate question from whether negligence can be shown. A claim has to clear both.

If the Army has not made a final decision within six months of filing, the claimant may treat that as a denial and take the claim to federal court. A written denial starts a separate six-month clock to file suit.

Industry observers note that the first window comes from 28 U.S.C. section 2675(a). It gives the Army a defined stretch of time to investigate and decide. The statute frames the deemed denial as an option for the claimant, not an obligation. A claimant who would rather keep waiting for the Army's answer is not forced to sue at the six-month mark.

The second window works differently. Under 28 U.S.C. section 2401(b), a claimant who receives a written denial has six months to file suit in federal district court. That clock starts on the date the denial was mailed. It does not wait for the letter to arrive. A suit filed after the window closes is barred.

Together, the two six-month rules mean the path to court opens either through the Army's silence or through its written refusal.

A denial does not have to end the administrative process. The Justice Department's regulations at 28 C.F.R. section 14.9 allow a claimant to ask the agency to reconsider a denial. That request keeps the dispute with the Army rather than moving it straight to a courtroom.

Industry observers note that A lawsuit, if one follows, runs differently from many civil cases. Under 28 U.S.C. section 2402, a judge decides an FTCA case, not a jury. The claimant presents evidence and argument to the court. The judge then rules on both the facts and the law.

The money available in court is also limited. Section 2674 bars punitive damages against the U.S. A claimant can seek payment for the property loss itself. The court cannot add an award meant to punish the government for its conduct.

It has been revealed that federal law limits what a lawyer may take from a Federal Tort Claims Act recovery. Under 28 U.S.C. section 2678, attorney fees cannot exceed 20 percent of an administrative settlement. The cap rises to 25 percent for a judgment or for a settlement reached after a lawsuit is filed.

The two caps track the two stages of an FTCA claim. The 20 percent limit governs a claim settled at the agency level, before anyone goes to court. For property damaged by an Army blast, that means a settlement reached through the Army claims process.

The 25 percent limit applies once the dispute moves into litigation. It covers a judgment entered by a federal district court. It also covers a settlement the parties reach after the lawsuit has been filed.

According to recent reports, the ceiling depends on when the case ends, not on the size of the payment. A settlement reached at the administrative stage falls under the lower cap. The same dollar amount agreed after a suit begins falls under the higher one. The two ceilings sit five percentage points apart.

In a recent development, the caps are written into the statute, so they apply to fee arrangements in FTCA matters. A claimant can compare the percentage in a fee agreement with the ceiling for the stage the claim has reached.

A lawyer is not required to file. A property owner can prepare and present an administrative claim personally, without hiring counsel. The claim goes to the same Army claims offices that handle submissions prepared by lawyers.

A claimant who files alone handles each step of the process. That includes describing what happened, gathering records of the damage and putting a dollar figure on the loss. No attorney fee comes out of the payment when no lawyer is involved.

The caps apply only to money actually paid through a settlement or judgment. They limit a lawyer's share of a recovery. They do not guarantee that any recovery will be paid.

Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.
  • Sources indicate that in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down.
  • Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.

Sources indicate that in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley stated that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals issue ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal enhancement at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

According to recent reports, A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”.

It has been revealed that last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella indicates his manufacturer’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

Sources indicate that A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a organization’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It has been revealed that it will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t enhancement for the next five to 10 years.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

According to recent reports, there’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty.
  • Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.
  • Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, the OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

Industry observers note that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

According to recent reports, the Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any organization planning to glitch under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management.".

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:.

It has been revealed that the OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:.

Industry observers note that on diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Sources indicate that redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

In a recent development, under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

It has been revealed that the Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Sources indicate that concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:.

In a recent development, the difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

Recent findings suggest that the Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:.

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:.

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set.
  • Curve also figures in how Sequent got started.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 02:00 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today unveiled that it has raised $2.2 million in new funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

In a recent development, founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

Sources indicate that following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who remarked AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

It has been revealed that for now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

In a recent development, for two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Sources indicate that along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor intends priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”.

XRP on Track to Post Worst ETF Month Ever

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The XRP ETF market might be bracing to close a record-breaking month of outflows as demand for the XRP-based investment product has remained on hold all through the month.
  • This comes as the prolonged and intense market volatility has extended to the ETF ecosystem, causing institutional investors to withdraw their capital.
  • With November just about three weeks gone, the latest data from SoSoValue shows that XRP ETFs have already recorded a total of $30.76 million in net outflows this November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The XRP ETF market might be bracing to close a record-breaking month of outflows as demand for the XRP-based investment product has remained on hold all through the month.

This comes as the prolonged and intense market volatility has extended to the ETF ecosystem, causing institutional investors to withdraw their capital.

With November just about three weeks gone, the latest data from SoSoValue shows that XRP ETFs have already recorded a total of $30.76 million in net outflows this November.

Previous ETF data indicates that March remains the only month in which spot XRP ETFs have recorded net outflows since their launch.

While it still stands as the record outflow month for XRP ETFs, investors withdrew about $31.16 million from the funds during that month.

This means that the persistent withdrawals seen this month have brought the November outflow dangerously close to its previous monthly record seen in March.

Apparently, the spot XRP ETFs are on track to close November as their worst-performing month since launch, with just about $1 million left to hit the record.

Further data also shows that the spot XRP ETFs have yet to record a single day of net inflows throughout November, as the persistent price decline has caused investors to slow down their purchases.

As such, the influx of fresh capital into the spot XRP ETF market has remained on hold amid growing market uncertainty and a shift in investor sentiment.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (485 w)
