General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

Russia's oil exports are on pace for highest year since Ukraine war

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (485 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russia has shipped crude abroad at a pace of 3.65 million barrels a day this year, its strongest annual figure since it launched its all-out assault on Ukraine in 2022, according to Bloomberg.
  • Seaborne shipments averaged 3.92 million barrels a day over the four weeks through Nov.
  • Oil ministers from OPEC+, whose leadership is shared by Russia and Saudi Arabia, will gather Sunday to agree on the first production targets for 2027, according to Bloomberg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russia has shipped crude abroad at a pace of 3.65 million barrels a day this year, its strongest annual figure since it launched its all-out assault on Ukraine in 2022, according to Bloomberg.

Weekly flows have eased. Seaborne shipments averaged 3.92 million barrels a day over the four weeks through Nov. 22, a decline of 30,000 barrels a day from the updated number covering the span ending Nov. 15, according to Bloomberg's tanker data. Over the seven days ending Nov. 22, 35 tankers took on 26.17 million barrels, versus an adjusted 31 million barrels carried by 40 vessels the week before. Weekly shipments shed 700,000 barrels daily, leaving them at 3.74 million.

Oil ministers from OPEC+, whose leadership is shared by Russia and Saudi Arabia, will gather Sunday to agree on the first production targets for 2027, according to Bloomberg. The levels will use fresh baselines drawn from outside evaluations of how much each member can sustainably produce.

Russian exports are compounding the growth in output from Persian Gulf producers. Goldman Sachs $GS, JPMorgan $JPM Chase and Sanford C. Bernstein are among the firms predicting that the oil market will swing back into global oversupply, according to Bloomberg. Brent crude is down nearly 25% from the peak it reached at the end of October.

Ukrainian strikes on refineries are feeding the export stream. Moscow sends overseas the crude that damaged plants cannot process, according to Bloomberg. Russia has also had trouble lifting production enough to match the larger quota it holds under OPEC+.

Ukraine had struck 15 Russian refineries between Nov. 1 and Monday, according to a Bloomberg tally. Those plants have nameplate capacity totaling over 3.6 million barrels daily, which exceeds half of the national total. Two additional refineries have come under attack since then. Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed on Tuesday to retaliate for the attacks.

It has been revealed that the gross value of Russian shipments averaged $2.27 billion a week over the 28 days to Nov. 22, a two-month low, according to Bloomberg. Urals prices fell $8 a barrel and ESPO prices dropped $5. The value for the latest week dropped to roughly $1.94 billion, its weakest showing in 11 weeks.

In a recent development, china and India continue to be the largest purchasers of Russian crude. Over the 28 days through Nov. 22, shipments to Asian customers, counting cargoes with no final destination listed, edged down to 3.79 million barrels a day from a revised 3.83 million barrels a day in the previous period, according to Bloomberg's tanker data.

Ukraine paused refinery strikes for two weeks in October before resuming attacks on major plants, including Kirishi, which is geared toward exports, and Omsk, Russia's biggest.

The capacity review behind the 2027 targets was delayed by the war involving Iran. It was originally due by the end of September and was not expected to finish before mid-November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Zonveer ZX3 is one of the best values I’ve seen in electric off-road riding, and one of the most fun things I’ve ridden to date – value for the dollar. Its Black Friday sale brings the 2,800W electric dirt bike down to $1,299, $500 off its $1,799 list price.

According to recent reports, for that money, you get a 1,200Wh battery, dual hydraulic disc brakes, and full suspension in a 130 lb package. That’s a great entry point for beginners.

Zonveer is a young brand. It launched in the US in March with two bikes, the kid-sized DX1 and the ZX3, and it’s run by United Mobility, which lists its address in Dover, Delaware. It sells direct and ships from US warehouses, and Zonveer also sells the ZX3 across Europe under its own brand through its EU store.

Here’s what the ZX3 brings, according to Zonveer’s product page:.

A hub motor means there’s no motor chain to maintain, and the NFC card and PIN unlock mean there’s no app to fight with. I like that.

According to recent reports, zonveer sent me a ZX3 to test, and I’m impressed with what they shipped, knowing the cost. It isn’t trying to be a race bike. And it doesn’t need to be. Here’s my first ride review:.

With 2,800W peak, it’s somewhat modest by e-moto standards. That’s exactly what makes it approachable for someone who has never ridden a dirt bike: the power is enough to have a blast on trails without being intimidating.

My girlfriend had never ridden a dirt bike before, and she got comfortable within a few minutes, and she was hooked as soon as she got the hang of it.

It has been revealed that and while testing with my girlfriend, it was clear this bike makes the most sense for lighter riders. Zonveer claims it climbs slopes of up to 30 degrees, which is optimistic for anyone over ~175 lbs, like myself. It still climbed some of the worst slopes on my land, but it did so with some difficulty, which wasn’t the case for some of my lighter friends who also rode it.

In a recent development, range is the other claim to take with a grain of salt. Riding 45 miles on 1,200Wh means using under 27Wh per mile, which is e-bike efficiency on a 130 lb dirt bike with knobby tires. It’s still a lot of energy, and you can ride this long distances at lower speeds. Just expect less if you ride it hard, and that’s where the fun is at.

Zonveer’s Black Friday sale has the ZX3 at $1,299, and the firm gave Electrek readers the code ELECTREK for an extra 5% off, which brings it down to $1,234.05.

The sale also includes a free water bottle and lock, and can be combined for a two-pack of ZX3s for $2,599. Shipping is free, the warranty is one year, Zonveer told us it accepts returns within 30 days on bikes ridden less than 10 miles, with a $200 restocking fee. Here’s the full refund policy.

We’ve ridden a lot of electric two-wheelers, and the ZX3 is one of the most fun per dollar. At $1,299, or about $1,234 with our code, it’s hard to find another 1,200Wh electric dirt bike with dual hydraulic disc brakes and full suspension from a brand that ships from US warehouses.

It’s not fast by e-moto standards, and the range and climbing claims are optimistic. But for beginners, and especially lighter riders, the power lands right in that sweet spot of manageable fun. It’s a bike you can learn on without scaring yourself, and it’s cheap enough that a family can buy two for less than one Sur-Ron.

It has been revealed that dogecoin co-founder Billy Markus, known on X as Shibetoshi Nakamoto, reacted to the recent market decline, which saw over $2.56 billion in liquidations. He hinted at weak demand as a possible reason behind the massive sell-off.

Markus earlier wrote in a post that "Black Friday came early." This came as the broader financial markets dropped, not just crypto: tech stocks, gold, copper, and Asian equities all fell.

Markus’s post garnered attention from the Dogecoin community and the wider crypto community. A Dogecoin community member responded: “Am I retarded for thinking crypto is about to go up?”.

@alphadoge777 well it always goes up and down 🤣 but the market has been looking pretty low demand for awhile now.

"Well, it always goes up and down," Markus remarked, pointing to crypto's inherent volatility and adding that the market had been experiencing "pretty low demand for a while now.".

His comments come as the crypto market continues to crash, highlighting concerns about the lack of buying interest needed to prop up prices.

Markus did not point to a specific catalyst for the decline, but his remarks highlight an key ingredient for a bullish comeback in the market: demand.

The crypto market selloff deepened on Saturday, with Bitcoin hitting its lowest level since September 2024 and extending a brutal run for risk assets. Dogecoin was trading in the red, down 8.13% in the last 24 hours to $0.528 and down 16% weekly. Dogecoin fell to $0.05 earlier on Saturday, a low not seen since June 2022.

Data from Coinglass at press time show that $2.56 billion was liquidated in crypto positions over the past 24 hours; longs accounted for 89.2% of this total, at $2.28 billion, while short liquidations came in at $276,040.

In a recent development, analysts pointed to rising real, or inflation-adjusted, U.S. Treasury yields as a key driver of the ongoing sell-off, which extends a bear market that began in October of last year.

Crypto investors are searching for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026. The broader crypto market has dropped since the Clarity Act faced a setback in September.

Breaking: Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.
  • Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.
  • The outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The upcoming funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of major names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the manufacturer-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis stated in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”.

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis remarked the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight firm acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis mentioned.

In a recent development, since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making upcoming data centers harder to build. The tech giant cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The manufacturer isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders noted. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Recent findings suggest that both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company claims it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Recent findings suggest that srinivasan stated that at the massive tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a latest AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he stated.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe notes gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Industry observers note that competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

It has been revealed that marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The tech giant’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

In a recent development, much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders remarked. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe looks to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis mentioned. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Sources indicate that angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Industry observers note that past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Recent findings suggest that marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis noted the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one substantial customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”.

Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • exchange and the app shows the balance.
  • Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

In a recent development, for the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

It has been revealed that the CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

Recent findings suggest that that is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks indicates where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

According to recent reports, the letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#122799. 9 everyday sources of lead exposure and the steps that reduce each one

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3150 w)

9 everyday sources of lead exposure and the steps that reduce each one

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lead reaches children through dust, soil, water, toys and work clothes.
  • In a recent development, household dust and peeling paint are one hazard at two stages.
  • Lead paint hazards are widespread in American homes, with approximately 29 million U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lead reaches children through dust, soil, water, toys and work clothes. See 9 sources and the steps EPA advises to lower the dose.

In a recent development, household dust and peeling paint are one hazard at two stages. Lead paint that chips, peels or gets rubbed down around doors and windows becomes fine dust, and in that form it ends up in a child's lungs or mouth. The U.S. EPA advises families to damp-clean once a week and keep paint in good shape, because dust and deteriorating paint may hold lead. The two chores share a target: families clear the dust before a child takes it in, and they maintain the paint before it breaks down into more dust. A weekly schedule assumes latest dust will build up and need clearing again as long as worn paint remains. A clean floor this week claims nothing about how much dust will gather by next week.

Lead paint hazards are widespread in American homes, with approximately 29 million U.S. housing units affected. About 2.6 million of those homes have young children living in them, and those families are the ones a weekly cleaning routine is meant to protect. Lead-based paint was banned for use in homes in 1978, so a house built before then is more likely to have it on its walls. A construction date is only a clue, though, and it can't show whether the paint in any one older house is a hazard.

Parents can't always control what a toddler puts in their mouth, but they can control what goes on the plate, and a child who eats well absorbs less of the lead they do swallow. The U.S. EPA reports that nutrient-rich meals reduce how much lead the body absorbs. Food can limit the lead a child takes in, but it is not a treatment for lead already in the blood. Iron, calcium and vitamin C are the nutrients the agency singles out. A parent can turn general advice about healthy eating into a simple check of whether those three show up regularly in a child's meals. Families already cook these meals, so better nutrition is one of the cheapest steps a household can take.

A well-fed child is better protected, but no diet makes up for a dusty windowsill or a lead pipe. "Good nutrition is one way to protect children from lead," Michigan's WIC program , as reported by USDA WIC Works. Better meals lower the amount of lead a child's body keeps, while paint, dust and water go on supplying more of it. Diet belongs beside the steps that remove lead at its source, and a box of fortified cereal does not replace any of them.

A backyard or a city park looks like the healthiest place a child can spend an afternoon, and nothing about the dirt warns a parent away. The risk depends on what has stood nearby. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency advises families to have children play on grass or on bare soil that isn't contaminated, because soil near roads, junkyards and old buildings may contain lead. The warning signs are therefore in the neighborhood rather than in the ground: traffic, scrap yards and older structures close to where a child digs. Steering children toward grass is a sensible precaution based on where lead is likely to be. It can't tell a family whether its own bare patch of ground is contaminated or clean.

Children carry yard soil indoors on their shoes. A child coming in from play should clean the soles and take the shoes off at the entrance, which keeps the play area's dirt off the floors where a toddler crawls. Like the grass rule, this habit lowers how much lead reaches a child without answering whether the soil needed avoiding at all.

Recent findings suggest that parents who have checked the paint and the pipes in their home can still bring lead into it themselves. The U.S. EPA reports that adults can carry lead home from worksites and hobbies on their skin, hair, clothes and shoes. A house with no lead paint and no lead pipes can therefore end up with lead dust inside, brought in by the adults who live there. The lead starts in places the family doesn't control, such as a job site or a workbench. The adult who was there, though, decides where that lead gets left. Families can cut off this route at the door, through choices the adults make every day when they come home.

The EPA recommends a shower after any activity with possible lead exposure, because showering removes lead dust from skin and hair. A child touches an adult's skin and hair most directly during a hug or a ride on a hip. A shower does nothing for the work clothes and boots that came home from the same job, however. Lead left on them can spread to floors, furniture and laundry after the adult is clean. A child who crawls across the floor or climbs onto a lap can then pick it up there. For this reason, the routine has to treat clothes and shoes as carefully as the body, keeping them away from the spaces where children play.

It has been revealed that lead in tap water comes through the plumbing, out of sight behind walls and under the street, so a family can't judge the risk by looking around the house. Tap water can contain lead from old lead pipes, the US EPA says, and flushing the line, using cold water and filtering all reduce how much of it a child drinks. CDC names faucets and plumbing fixtures as lead sources alongside pipes, so the lead can be in the hardware at the sink as well as in the lines that feed it. "Lead service lines can be a major source of lead contamination in water," the EPA said. That makes the pipe connecting a home to the water main the first suspect, but a home without a lead service line can still have lead at the tap.

Many parents think of lead poisoning as a problem from an earlier era, one that regulators dealt with decades ago. Children's exposure has in fact fallen a great deal. "Blood lead concentrations have decreased dramatically in U.S. children over the past 4 decades," the American Academy of Pediatrics noted in 2016, as reported by ATSDR. The problem has not ended, though. Approximately 500,000 American children have enough lead in their blood to reach or pass the benchmark the agency sets, according to CDC, and behind that number are a large number of families still dealing with the problem. Children are exposed through the ordinary parts of home and neighborhood life rather than through one unusual source, and CDC sorts the common sources into six categories. No family can protect a child by fixing a single thing.

Recent findings suggest that children can take in lead in so many small ways that the useful question for a parent is how much of it a child takes in, not whether the child ever encounters it. Any amount matters. Health officials have yet to find any amount of lead in a child's blood that they consider safe, according to ATSDR, and CDC ties even small amounts to slower development, trouble learning and problems with behavior. Daily habits are therefore worth the effort, since each one lowers the amount of lead a child swallows or breathes. Cleaning and washing leave the paint, pipes and soil that produce the lead in place, however. Protecting a child takes two kinds of work. The first is the routines a family can do at home. The second is finding out what is hidden in the walls, the water lines and the yard.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency laid out simple steps families can take to prevent children's lead exposure, covering everything from a toddler's pacifier to backyard soil and a parent's work boots. Families can use the steps as a household to-do list for prevention, not as a scientific measure of risk. Some are chores that cut how much lead a child takes in. Others are checks that show where the lead in a home comes from, such as a soil screening, a call to the water utility or a blood test. The chores are cheap, and a family can start them this week. The checks take more effort and are easier to put off. They matter just as much, because only a check tells a family whether its home holds a source that no amount of cleaning will remove.

Recent findings suggest that cleaning manages the dust, but the paint the dust comes from stays in place. Whether that paint is a hazard, and what to do about it, is a question no amount of mopping can answer. A risk assessment identifies lead hazards and the actions to take. Until a family has one, it keeps up the paint without knowing what the walls contain.

The weekly damp mop is a family's first protection, and a risk assessment is how a family in an older home learns whether that protection is enough.

Industry observers note that parents can also add lead to a child's diet in the kitchen, often during the most routine tasks. Water for cooking and for mixing baby formula should come only from the cold tap. For a baby on formula, the rule covers the water in every bottle a parent prepares. Heating water to a boil leaves any lead in it untouched, so a parent who boils tap water for a bottle has not made it safer on that count. The EPA also advises families to know where herbs and "natural" ingredients come from before using them. A "natural" label does not tell a parent whether an ingredient contains lead.

Meals with enough iron, calcium and vitamin C, cold water at the stove and spices from known sources all help hold down the lead in what a child eats.

For a toddler, the lead in a house usually reaches the body on the child's own fingers. CDC's National Center for Environmental Health reports that lead dust is the most common source of exposure in young children, who put their hands and objects in their mouths. A toddler with dusty hands is swallowing lead a little at a time. The US EPA advises parents to wash children's hands frequently, especially after they play outdoors or with animals. A parent doesn't need to trace where the dirt on a child's hands came from to follow that routine. That makes handwashing especially valuable for the youngest children, who put their hands in their mouths the most.

Handwashing costs almost nothing, because plain soap and water is enough. What it requires is repetition. A crawling child picks up dust again on every floor and table, and a single wash before dinner doesn't cover the rest of the day. Each wash lowers the amount of lead that reaches the child, but it does nothing about the paint or soil that is the source of the dust.

In a recent development, adults need to wash too, because their own bodies can carry lead into the home. CDC names clothes and skin as the ways lead gets brought home, and the EPA advises adults to wash after activities that might have put them in contact with lead. A parent who washes up protects the child they pick up next, not only themselves. A child who scrubs at the sink while an adult skips it is still exposed. Even a household where everyone washes can't rely on washing alone. Clean hands pick up lead again from dust left on floors and furniture, so handwashing works only alongside the cleaning that removes that dust.

Washing gets a child's hands clean, and only a clean house keeps them that way.

A family can stop guessing by having its soil screened. ATSDR, the federal agency that runs the soilSHOP screening events, reports that the screenings are free. The grass rule works from where contamination is likely, while a screening settles the question for one specific yard. Because a federal public-health agency does the screening, a family gets a measured result rather than an estimate. Results come back the same day, so a parent learns right away whether to keep letting a child dig in that spot or to move play to the grass.

It has been revealed that taking shoes off at the door is the chore, and the soil screening is the check. A family that does only the first is still guessing about the ground its child plays on.

In an older house, lead becomes a danger to children when someone cuts, sands or scrapes its painted surfaces. For any home built before 1978, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency advises families to bring in certified professionals for that kind of work. The construction date marks where the advice applies, and it does not prove that a given house contains lead. Most houses from those years do have it, though, with lead-based paint in 83% to 86% of them. A family planning a project in such a house should assume the paint contains lead and test it or hire carefully before work starts, without waiting for chipped paint to raise the alarm.

The older the house, the greater the risk, because the earliest coats of paint held the most lead. ATSDR reports that white house paint made before 1955 could be 50% lead, and that the U.S. had about 23.2 million homes dating from before 1950 in 2006. A worker who sands or scrapes those early layers creates dust that is heavy with lead. The EPA's renovation advice therefore covers millions of ordinary homes along with the rare historic property. An owner of a house that old should treat even a small repair as lead work.

A fresh coat of paint does not make old lead paint safe, because the old layers underneath can still wear into dust wherever painted surfaces rub together. Routine repairs disturb that paint, so the choice of contractor matters as much as the project itself. The EPA advises families to hire a contractor who is Lead-Safe Certified, a credential a family can ask for by name. That certification comes from the EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule, so a family that asks for it is requiring a federal standard. Careful work still raises dust, and the EPA says residents should stay out until the work is done and the area is cleaned. For a family with young children, that means planning to stay somewhere else during the job.

In an older home, the safest repair is one planned around the lead before anyone picks up a scraper.

The habit protects a child only when it covers everything that came back from the worksite or the hobby: the person, the clothes and the shoes.

According to recent reports, A pacifier or a chewed toy is the shortest path between household dust and a child's body. The U.S. EPA advises families to keep these items clean because children handle and mouth them every day, and the dust they gather may contain lead. Dust on a rattle is a dose rather than a housekeeping problem. Chewing on toys and other objects is one of the ways lead dust reaches many young children, according to CDC. For that reason, the EPA tells parents to wash pacifiers, bottles and toys daily, on the same schedule as the child's chewing. The habit costs a family a sink and a few minutes, and it lowers the lead that reaches a young child who puts everything in the mouth.

A parent who washes a toy removes what sits on its surface but leaves what the toy is made of. The daily wash deals with the dust that settles on items a child uses regularly. Some toys carry lead in the object itself. The EPA advises keeping painted toys out of children's mouths, and CDC lists some imported toys as a source of lead. A child can take in lead from a painted or imported toy even after a parent has scrubbed it clean. Painted toys belong out of a child's mouth altogether, and parents should not assume an imported toy is safe because it has been washed.

In one small object, a family meets both kinds of work: a chore that lowers the dose and a source that no amount of washing can reach.

A family can flush and filter every day without ever learning whether its own line contains lead. Those habits lower the dose without revealing where the lead comes from. The answer belongs to the water utility, which families should contact both to check the service line and to test the water. That answer can also change while life indoors stays the same. Crews working near a service line may release more lead, so a family has good reason to call the utility again when the street outside is dug up.

Until the utility answers, the daily habits are the protection a family has, and they cost almost nothing to keep. A parent who runs the tap before filling a glass, drinks and cooks with cold water, and uses a filter has made the routine part of the day. That routine is worth keeping whatever the utility reports.

The habits lower the dose, but only the call tells a family whether it is guarding against a lead pipe it actually has.

A family that has mopped the floors, scrubbed hands, run the cold tap and hired a certified contractor still can't tell by looking at a child whether lead has reached the child's blood. "A child with lead in their blood may not have visible signs or symptoms and in fact many children who have lead poisoning look and act healthy," the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said. A toddler who eats, sleeps and plays normally gives a parent no assurance at all. The household chores lower how much lead reaches a child, but none of them shows whether any lead is already in the child's body. A blood test answers that question for one specific child.

In a recent development, whether a child gets a blood lead test depends on the family's health coverage. Children on Medicaid are required to have one at 12 and 24 months, the EPA states, while for every other child a test at those ages is a recommendation from the CDC. The schedule itself comes from the CDC, and the EPA passes it along to parents. A parent outside Medicaid can ask the doctor for the test directly. The EPA offers a postcard that parents can bring to the child's appointment to make that request.

At the 1- and 2-year checkups, a single blood draw tells a parent what a healthy-looking toddler cannot.

Bitcoin now trades well below $62,000, and this raises the question of whether the framework underpinning Timmer’s outlook still holds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.

According to recent reports, microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith remarked the president is “making an crucial point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he said most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

In a recent development, his reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

Recent findings suggest that he gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed organization that wants to build in Finland. Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, remarked he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a big technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

It has been revealed that rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the firm for a briefing.

Industry observers note that smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate company, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith said Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

Sources indicate that he put the ballroom donation in the first category, and stated the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered key.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He noted the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he mentioned much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

Smith noted the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange by volume, Binance is witnessing a rapid surge in its futures trading activity as the broader crypto market continues to face increased selling pressure.

While the market is still struggling with volatility and rapidly declining investor interest, the latest on-chain data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant highlights that futures traders have become extremely active on Binance.

The data shows that both Bitcoin and Ethereum have seen their perpetual futures trading volume on Binance surge to a combined high of $39.8 billion as of November 20.

Notably, this marks the highest level the metric has reached since September 21, indicating that traders are actively adjusting their positions to hedge against further losses as volatility continues to intensify.

Nonetheless, Bitcoin saw the highest increase in perpetual futures volume as it surged to $24.75 billion on the same day.

The data further indicated that the volume was slightly higher than the $24.57 billion recorded on September 21, when Bitcoin was trading above $87,000.

Ethereum, on the other hand, followed with a notable increase in the same metric, recording $15.05 billion in perpetual futures volume on the same day.

However, Ethereum did not entirely mimic Bitcoin in the trend as this was still below the $17.27 billion recorded during the September 21 trading period.

Further data reveals that the high futures trading activity recorded on Binance on November 20 has coincided with BlackRock’s record Bitcoin ETF outflow.

The data reveals that BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded $511 million in net outflows on that day, marking a sharp reversal from the positive inflows seen in September.

While this shows that investors are also pulling their funds from Bitcoin ETFs, it marked the highest single-day outflow BlackRock has ever recorded.

#122795. Breaking: Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3686 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.
  • That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality.
  • These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:59 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

According to recent reports, the popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

Industry observers note that “Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” mentioned Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”.

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” said Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

According to recent reports, devRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

According to recent reports, three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

Industry observers note that in September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

Enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the significant players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

Cost is currently the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.

Recent findings suggest that by most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

Industry observers note that “The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”.

According to recent reports, the pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

Recent findings suggest that in a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders said managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” said Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Sources indicate that experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” mentioned Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, stated open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

Industry observers note that “If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she mentioned. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

It has been revealed that they’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., said in an interview with the Financial Times.

In a recent development, sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing issue for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

Sources indicate that advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

An agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

According to recent reports, though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

According to recent reports, one is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” remarked Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”.

Although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

Evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

Baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

Finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

Recent findings suggest that organizations that blueprint to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

Recent findings suggest that lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software firm went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

If a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

“The core software engineering required to test and integrate latest models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” noted Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

Using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

In a recent development, cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” remarked Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

“On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” said Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”.

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data indicates that approach is usually a dead end.

Most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

Industry observers note that this interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

It has been revealed that “Every time a upcoming model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” stated Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

Though the open-weight option is viable for any organization, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as important as cost.

According to recent reports, compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

Industry observers note that training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

It has been revealed that but deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” mentioned TEKSystems’ Franco.

Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” mentioned Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”.

In a recent development, in contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” said David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

Sources indicate that “The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss remarked. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”.

According to recent reports, performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency problems can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

Industry observers note that executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

Industry observers note that hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

Complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

Google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

The corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” said TekSystems’ Franco.

Poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders noted dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

Continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because latest models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can swiftly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

In a recent development, rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

According to recent reports, “Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” stated Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”.

Lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate upcoming models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he said. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

Sources indicate that enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as crucial an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” said Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

It has been revealed that the shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

Sources indicate that at the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., said in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”.
