Latest Update: From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.
  • Since Grant Canary released his manufacturer a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • It has been revealed that the Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary released his manufacturer a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

It has been revealed that the Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

The company recently shifted again, adding a new line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary said, which benefits everyone.

Just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

High school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Industry observers note that humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the challenges.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

Industry observers note that when I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there rapidly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

It has been revealed that I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

Industry observers note that that ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

My personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally crucial: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [Latest York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do massive things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

In a recent development, in the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

It has been revealed that my hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as big an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

In a recent development, across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

According to recent reports, together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

Industry observers note that october was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

In a recent development, the coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest patch on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Industry observers note that small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. People need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

According to recent reports, the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

It has been revealed that that has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

In a recent development, every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

In a recent development, the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

America is approaching a “dangerous moment” for defense spending, according to a newly introduced report from Brookings. The think tank warns that rising outlays on Medicaid, Medicare, Social Security, and interest on the $40 trillion national debt are squeezing the military’s share of federal spending.The analysis, published at the start of this week, finds that since 1962 defense spending has been squeezed from 49% to 13% of the federal budget.Defense spending accounted for 2.8% of U.S. GDP in 2026 and is expected to remain at approximately 3% through 2030. This would put defense spending at its lowest share of GDP since World War II, Brookings—a nonprofit public policy think tank based in D.C.—said.

In a recent development, projections that spending will remain relatively constrained are particularly concerning, Brookings’ Jessica Riedl writes. The U.S. is engaged in a conflict in the Middle East with Iran and its proxy groups, and Russia and Ukraine are engaged in a land war that has continued since Russia’s 2022 invasion.

Three years ago, the RAND National Security Research Division—a Pentagon research advisor—warned that “in many ways, China is outpacing the United States and has largely negated the U.S. military advantage in the Western Pacific through two decades of focused military investment.”.

Without “significant change” in policy, the “balance of power will continue to shift in China’s favor,” the Congressional report found.

And yet, in the years since, the factors stacking up against increased defense spending are only getting weightier.

The Congressional Budget Office’s (CBO) latest roundup of government spending shows that $917 billion was spent on defense for fiscal year 2026, an increase of $48 billion from the prior year, and a 5.8% increase.

Industry observers note that the total for the government’s largest mandatory spending programs (Social Security benefits, Medicare and Medicaid) came in at nearly $3.5 trillion, a $217 billion uptick on the year before and a 6.7% increase. The government ran a total deficit of $1.9 trillion, the CBO reported, adding to the current national debt burden of $40.7 trillion, per the latest Treasury data.

Recent findings suggest that that debt comes at a cost. Interest payments rise as the government borrows more, particularly when borrowing costs remain elevated. The CBO noted that for fiscal year 2026, the Treasury paid $1.14 trillion in net interest on the public debt—an 11.1% or $114 billion increase on the previous fiscal year.

Interest payments on the debt are a growing concern for D.C. policymakers. The Joint Economic Committee (JEC) published a report in October that found interest payments in the future could consume more than half of available federal tax receipts by 2036.

Recent findings suggest that JEC chairman David Schweikert noted: “Under this higher interest rate scenario, we could spend $23 trillion on interest alone over the next decade. That is spending not on Social Security, not on Medicare, not on national defense, but simply paying for yesterday’s borrowing.”.

Industry observers note that the next Congress faces difficult choices: The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget has a countdown to when the combined trust funds of the Social Security system will be forced to start cutting benefits. The countdown at the moment stands at seven years and six months.

Sources indicate that “The newly elected Congress—which controls the purse strings—faces difficult fiscal choices that will persist into the next presidential administration,” the Brookings report claims. “Now, there is little headroom in the budget to increase defense spending to meet the proliferating defense challenges … something will have to give. The advocates of a robust military and American global leadership should prepare to make the most of limited budgetary resources.”.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.
  • Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.
  • According to recent reports, amazon didn’t disclose financial terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

According to recent reports, amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

The deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled aims to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy stated on the manufacturer’s earnings call last month.

Amazon declared the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

In a recent development, decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

Decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

Industry observers note that decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

The deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

Amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

Amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon noted last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

The deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other big buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

Industry observers note that “From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf said in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”.

It has been revealed that the deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin reportedly became available at a massive discount on Kraken after a sharp dislocation in Kraken's dollar trading markets.
  • Customers reported being able to purchase BTC for as little as 24,250 CAD, equivalent to $16,900 at that time.
  • Apparently, the incident has only affected the BTC/CAD trading pair on the platform, although some owners claim the disruption appeared across several CAD markets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin reportedly became available at a massive discount on Kraken after a sharp dislocation in Kraken's dollar trading markets.

Customers reported being able to purchase BTC for as little as 24,250 CAD, equivalent to $16,900 at that time.

Apparently, the incident has only affected the BTC/CAD trading pair on the platform, although some owners claim the disruption appeared across several CAD markets.

The incident might have involved thin liquidity problem in Kraken's CAD order books.

Large sell orders reportedly overwhelmed available buy orders, leaving insufficient demand to absorb the selling pressure.

According to some accounts, at one point about 20 BTC was being sold every 15 minutes, causing the imbalance to push BTC price against CAD further down.

Sources indicate that one such transaction resulted in BTC price at around C$24,250, or $16,900. Compared with Bitcoin trading between $57,000-$58,000, the discount amounted to a staggering 71%. Other owners reported BTC briefly trading around $27,000.

Industry observers note that kraken's status page continued to show its systems as operational during the incident. No official explanation from the exchange was available at the time of writing.

The reported dislocation highlights the risks associated with trading in markets with limited liquidity. When an order book lacks sufficient buy-side depth, even relatively large sell orders can cause prices to move sharply away from the broader market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has pulled the $41,990 Model Y All-Wheel Drive from its US online configurator. The cheapest dual-motor Model Y you can order now is the Model Y Premium AWD at $49,990, an $8,000 jump.

Recent findings suggest that the trim lasted just over nine months. Tesla released it in early February, and it’s gone without a word from the company.

Here’s what Tesla’s US Model Y design studio lists as of today (prices before the destination fee):.

It has been revealed that when Tesla launched the base Model Y AWD in February, it was basically the stripped-down Model Y with a second motor. It had 294 miles of range, did 0-60 mph in 4.6 seconds and kept the same cut-down cabin as the base RWD. At a $2,000 premium over the single-motor version, it was the most sensible AWD pricing Tesla had offered in years.

Industry observers note that and the AWD trim isn’t the only change. In February, the Premium RWD cost $44,990 and the Premium AWD cost $48,990. Both are now $1,000 higher.

According to recent reports, add it up and the cheapest all-wheel-drive Model Y went from $41,990 to $49,990 in nine months. That’s a 19% increase.

According to recent reports, the timing isn’t great for Tesla’s competitive position. Chevrolet’s 2027 Equinox EV LT 1 AWD starts at $40,295 before destination, with 307 miles of EPA range. Ford’s Mustang Mach-E Select AWD starts at $40,795.

Both now undercut Tesla’s cheapest AWD crossover by more than $9,000.

If you live somewhere it snows and you were shopping for a upcoming Model Y, the math just got a lot worse. You can still find some base AWD units in Tesla’s inventory, but once those are gone, that’s it.

This is also the latest cut in a year of Tesla shrinking its lineup. Elon Musk killed the Model S and Model X in January to free up Fremont for Optimus, and Cybertruck production is winding down. Meanwhile, the most recent upcoming Tesla is the $61,990 Model Y L, which sits at the top of the range, not the bottom.

We liked this trim. It was the first time in a long time that Tesla treated all-wheel drive as a $2,000 option rather than a huge upsell bundled with a nicer interior, and it put the Model Y right in the price bracket of the Equinox EV and Mach-E with AWD.

It has been revealed that now it’s gone, and the Premium trims went up $1,000 on top of that. Tesla didn’t explain either move. It rarely does anymore.

Recent findings suggest that there are two plausible reasons. Either Tesla is tight on Model Y build slots and would rather fill them with higher-margin Premium trims, or the cheap AWD simply wasn’t selling. We don’t know which. But both explanations land in the same place for buyers: a more expensive Model Y.

Tesla is not going to keep 6 different model Y trims especially when the most expensive trim in the Model YL is selling. They will definitely squeeze out as much money from selling more expensive trims so the lowest end trim will most likely be next to go.

And Tesla has a habit of this. The “Standard” name for its cheaper Model Y and Model 3 lasted a few months. The single-motor Cybertruck, the only version that made sense, was gone within days. Cheaper trims show up, get a news cycle, and quietly disappear.

That’s a problem for a tech giant whose consumer lineup is shrinking down to two cars. The Model Y is Tesla’s volume. Thinning it out at the bottom is the opposite of what you’d do if growing EV sales were the priority.

📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Companies selling robot-training video used to call about privacy once a month. Now it’s several times a week

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that earlier this month, India’s technology ministry probed home-services platforms about cleaners wearing head-mounted cameras inside customers’ homes.
  • Industry observers note that training robots this way is newly introduced (ish), but the questions aren’t.
  • Today I run Pimloc, which sells software to anonymize sensitive video.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that earlier this month, India’s technology ministry probed home-services platforms about cleaners wearing head-mounted cameras inside customers’ homes. The footage trains robots, and officials wanted to know how it was collected, what consent was obtained and whether it was going to AI developers overseas. They won’t be the last to ask.

Industry observers note that training robots this way is newly introduced (ish), but the questions aren’t. Over a decade ago, I helped build Autographer, one of the first wearable cameras. Back then, the focus was: “how do I know if I am being filmed?” so we designed privacy into the product. Today, because we’re filmed all the time, people (and their governments) ask: “Where is that footage, who has access and what are you doing with it?”.

Today I run Pimloc, which sells software to anonymize sensitive video. Much of our work involves police body-camera footage: shaky, often low-light and full of people who aren’t part of the incident. It’s remarkably similar to what robotics firms now collect. We’ve spent years developing technology to protect people in footage where they move promptly, turn away or appear at unusual angles.

A year ago we were approached by companies collecting or preparing footage for physical AI training roughly once a month. Now it’s several times a week – businesses working across autonomous vehicles, delivery robots, factories and drones.

It has been revealed that AI chatbots learned to communicate by reading the internet. A robot has as much chance of learning to fold clothes by trawling search engines as I have of becoming a Michelin-starred chef by reading Julia Child’s Mastering the Art of French Cooking.

So developers are recording real life instead. One startup recently told Fortune it had collected more than a million hours of first-person footage in its first month, and we’re hearing similar figures. Robotics and physical-AI companies had raised nearly $48 billion by early October, according to PitchBook data.

Many of the companies that first approached us were using open-source tools to try and redact footage – far from perfect, but it got them through non-public development and testing.

Now things are different in two ways. First, many of those companies are preparing to sell their footage to large AI developers with exacting standards. A buyer spending serious money on a dataset wants assurances about how it was collected, whether permissions cover its intended use and whether the people in it are protected. Suppliers know they will have to stand behind those claims.

Second, governments are paying attention. India’s inquiry is one example in one territory, of growing scrutiny over how AI training footage is collected and used. Big tech companies and labs looking to develop physical AI products and services have little choice but to push those same questions down to the organizations selling them the footage they need.

One manufacturer that approached us recently put it simply: “We need to solve this problem. Redaction is notable to us.”.

Some companies were created specifically to collect training footage. They can build consent and anonymization into their processes from day one. As India shows, that doesn’t settle every concern for workers or the people they film, but it gives them a headstart.

In a recent development, others have recorded video for years for a different purpose, and are only now discovering its upcoming value. But having captured the footage isn’t the same as having the right to sell it.

Recently, an established business that helps people with everyday tasks asked us about anonymizing years of footage captured by their customers for AI training. We had two immediate questions: could permissions realistically be established, years later, for a use nobody – not least the consumer – had envisaged when the footage was recorded? And could every identifying detail – from people in shot to letters on the fridge – be reliably found and protected?

That discussion is still on-going, but it reveals how difficult it can be to turn an archive into an asset after the fact.

For any business sitting on a digital archive, my advice is to start by asking: did the people you meant to film agree to the footage being sold? And is everyone else in it protected? You can’t assume the value without identifying those gaps and addressing them.

It has been revealed that buyers are best placed to make those checks standard. Privacy rules and expectations differ from country to country, as India’s scrutiny of overseas transfers reveals, and footage is already crossing borders. If the AI companies paying for it insisted on the same proof of permission and protection wherever it was recorded, every supplier would have to meet that bar.

I’m optimistic about what physical AI could do. But the footage that is increasingly being used to teach it captures far more than the task – people nearby, inside homes, documents, voices and screens in the background. Autographer taught me that what a camera picks up by accident matters as much as what it’s pointed at. Physical AI is learning that lesson at a far greater scale, and buyers have both the power and the incentive to act on it.

#122786. Tech Report: 9 things airline passengers can and can't recover after long delays under new U.S. rules

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3043 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: 9 things airline passengers can and can't recover after long delays under new U.S. rules

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cash refunds hold whatever caused a delay, but meals and hotels depend on blame.
  • Sources indicate that anyone who has spent an afternoon stuck at a gate tends to assume the airline owes them something for the lost hours.
  • Because care depends on blame, the question that decides a stranded traveler's night is who labels a delay and how.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cash refunds hold whatever caused a delay, but meals and hotels depend on blame. New DOT limits and an FAA rule shift that line. Here's what travelers can still recover.

Sources indicate that anyone who has spent an afternoon stuck at a gate tends to assume the airline owes them something for the lost hours. What a waiting passenger can count on is care rather than cash, and only when the airline is to blame. When a large carrier causes a delay, it usually offers help in kind, such as a newly introduced seat, food and sometimes a hotel room, but not one U.S. airline promised passengers money for a disruption in 2024, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. Each airline writes those promises into its own customer service proposal and can strike them out whenever it chooses, so a meal voucher or a hotel room is a favor rather than a right. The one protection that holds no matter what is the right to walk away from a disrupted trip and get the money back.

Because care depends on blame, the question that decides a stranded traveler's night is who labels a delay and how. Airlines make that call themselves. In 2024, airlines used differing methods to decide whether a disruption with several causes was within their control, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. New federal limits that take effect Feb. 1, 2027, and cover flights from Jan. 1, 2027, will stop airlines from counting 10 causes of delay as their own fault. The likely result is fewer delays that come with meals and hotels, while the right to a refund stays exactly as it is.

InsideFlyer laid out what travelers can recover when their flights are delayed or canceled, from turning down vouchers to the Montreal Convention, the FAA's line-up-and-wait rule and credit card insurance. Some of these are firm rights. Some are airline promises that the carrier no longer owes once a delay is ruled outside its control, and others pay only with proof.

A delayed traveler can get cash back without anyone deciding who caused the trouble. A passenger who turns down the trip after a cancellation or major delay is owed the ticket money, according to InsideFlyer. A storm, a crew shortage and a broken plane all count the same. After the traveler turns down rebooking and stays off the plane, the airline must matter the refund automatically, with no request from the passenger, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. A stranded traveler has two choices: keep flying on the airline's terms or take the money.

The automatic payment spares a traveler any argument with the airline, but the price of the refund stays the same. "Passengers deserve to get their money back when an airline owes them — without headaches or haggling," U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg noted in 2024, as reported by the U.S. Department of Transportation. A passenger who wants the cash still has to give up the flight, and in return gets back the full amount paid, including taxes and fees.

Before accepting a rebooking or airline extras, a traveler should compare them with the full price of the ticket returned.

A delay qualifies for a refund at a fixed point on the clock, not when the wait starts to feel unbearable. For a trip within the U.S., a traveler can claim their money back only once the delay reaches three hours, InsideFlyer reports, and on an international flight the wait has to reach six hours. A traveler who gives up and goes home before then has lost the trip without getting back the fare.

Recent findings suggest that most delayed domestic flights never reach the three-hour mark. Carriers that report to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics logged 85,892 domestic flights in 2022 that ran three hours or more late, a small share of all their delayed flights, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. A traveler who leaves after an hour or two at the gate has no right to a refund. The hour that matters is the one when the flight passes the mark, because that is when the traveler's options change.

A traveler whose flight passes three hours may be owed more than a refund. Airlines' own reporting tied 65% of the domestic delays that lasted at least three hours in 2022 at least partly to the carrier, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. Many travelers at the three-hour mark may therefore qualify both for the refund and for the care airlines promise when they cause a delay. They can't have both, though. The refund is paid only if the traveler declines rebooking and does not fly, and the choice comes down to one question: Does the traveler still need to get there?

Sources indicate that the three-hour mark is a trigger for getting money back, not a price on a passenger's lost time. In 2024, the U.S. Department of Transportation asked for public comment, through an advance notice of proposed rulemaking, on whether passengers facing a lengthy delay should receive services or compensation. The refund threshold is the only firm number a traveler can rely on, and any standard for amenities or pay remains an open question.

For now, a delay's length matters only for when a traveler can leave with a refund, and that is the moment to proposal around.

A refund helps a stranded traveler only if the airline pays it while the money can still cover a latest flight or the trip home, and airlines face a firm deadline to do that. An airline must refund a ticket bought with a credit card within seven days, and one paid for any other way within 20 calendar days, according to InsideFlyer. Paying by card puts a traveler on the faster clock. That matters most to someone who has to buy a seat on another airline the same day, because that traveler pays for two tickets until the first one is refunded. A card holder carries that double cost for a week or a little more, while a traveler who paid another way may carry it much longer.

In a recent development, the traveler doesn't have to file anything to get the money. The airline owes the refund automatically to a passenger who walks away from a disrupted flight, so the deadline is the only way a traveler can check whether the airline has done its part. If the refund hasn't arrived once the deadline has passed, the airline is late, and the traveler should call or write to press for payment.

The airline has to pay without being asked, but the traveler has to notice when it doesn't.

According to recent reports, A voucher offered at the counter after a canceled or badly delayed flight may look like a goodwill gesture, but it is the airline asking to keep a fare it already owes. Airlines may push credits, but eligible travelers can turn them down and demand cash, according to InsideFlyer. The U.S. Department of Transportation says that the refund is automatic and needs no request from the passenger, so accepting the credit is how a traveler would give the money up. The right to refuse a credit belongs only to travelers who qualify for a refund in the first place.

Sources indicate that some travelers will still want the credit, especially if they fly the same airline often. Airlines must honor such a credit for five years or more after issuing it, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. A long expiration date protects a traveler from losing the credit, but it does nothing for someone who needs the money for rent, a hotel or a ticket on another carrier. Miles need one more check. A traveler who paid for the ticket with miles gets miles back as the refund, but miles offered on a ticket bought with cash replace money the airline owes.

Before accepting anything, a traveler should ask one question: Is this my money coming back, or something offered in its place?

In a recent development, when an airline causes a delay, the big carriers commit to keeping the passenger's trip going, which is more help than a refund alone. InsideFlyer reports that these promises depend on whether the airline had control over what went wrong. That condition comes up often on long waits. Airlines listed at least one cause of their own for 62% of the domestic waits that ran three hours or longer in 2023, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. An airline cause in the mix doesn't settle how a delay is labeled, but on most long waits, the airline's share of the blame gives a passenger grounds to ask for help. A failure that looks like bad luck can also count against the carrier. In a proposal published in 2024, the department said it had told carriers that it considered the disruptions from Delta's IT outage controllable. In that case, regulators treated a computer systems failure as the airline's problem rather than as an act of nature. At the gate, a passenger's first question should be what caused the delay.

Sources indicate that the rebooking promise is narrower up close than it first appears. Airlines generally commit to rebooking a passenger for free, according to InsideFlyer, but a seat on another carrier is a different matter. Among the 10 largest airlines in 2024, five promised to move a passenger onto a partner carrier when they caused a long wait, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. A passenger on any of the rest had no such promise and might have to wait for that carrier's own next flight.

In a recent development, meals carry a condition of their own at some airlines. Carriers generally commit to meals or meal vouchers when they are at fault, according to InsideFlyer, yet that help can depend on the passenger speaking up. Southwest Airlines noted in its customer service plan that meals and hotel rooms were available "upon request," as reported by the U.S. Department of Transportation. On an airline with a plan worded that way, a traveler who knows the cause and asks is the one who collects.

Congress has ordered regulators to act on delays the airline causes, but passengers can't yet claim anything upcoming under that order. Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, the department must direct carriers to set policies for paying back travelers' meal and lodging costs after delays the airline directly causes, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. The department's proposal on these rights is an advance notice seeking public comment, not a final rule, and airlines have no new obligations under it. Until a final rule arrives, what a passenger gets at the gate depends on the commitments in that airline's own strategy.

At a controllable delay, a traveler gains more by knowing the cause and asking than by citing the law.

It has been revealed that starting with flights on Jan. 1, 2027, federal regulators will settle part of a delay's blame before any plane runs late. InsideFlyer reports that airlines can no longer code 10 causes of delay as their own fault on those flights, under a rule that takes effect Feb. 1, 2027. The U.S. Department of Transportation indicates that airline customer service prepares commit to care only for disruptions within the airline's control, so a delay from any of those 10 causes will come with no airline promise of rebooking, meals or a hotel room. Travelers $TRV flying through 2026 keep the current treatment, while a trip flown in early 2027 falls under the newly introduced limits.

It has been revealed that airline promises have depended on a delay's reported cause once before, during an emergency. During a shutdown-related FAA order in November 2025, airline commitments did not apply to disruptions caused by the national aviation system, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. That notice was guidance and did not bind airlines. The 2027 limits come instead from a rule the department published on Sept. 3, 2026.

The causes moving out of the airline's column include problems on the airline's own planes and in its own cabins, not only storms and other acts of nature. InsideFlyer reports that from 2027, hacking attacks, urgent fixes, government system outages and the ejection of a disruptive flyer are among 10 triggers that will no longer be blamed on carriers. To a passenger stuck at the gate, a rushed repair or a removed troublemaker looks like the airline's problem to solve. Yet a traveler delayed by either will have no airline promise of a meal or a room. Nor can that traveler know at the gate whether the airline will provide care, because a repair delay may or may not count as an urgent fix.

Regulators have already excused delays from one round of required repairs, well before 2027. On December 10, 2025, federal officials stated they would use enforcement discretion over delays from maintenance required by an emergency airworthiness directive from the Federal Aviation Administration, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. That notice covered only delays from that single directive. It also concerned the amenities airlines commit to, not refunds. Even before the 2027 limits take effect, a passenger delayed by repairs under that directive could not count on regulators to hold the airline to its promise of meals and a hotel.

When an agent blames a hack, a forced repair, a government system failure or a removed passenger, the traveler should stop waiting for a hotel voucher and weigh the refund instead.

Recent findings suggest that A upcoming federal rule about departures gives a delayed passenger nothing to claim. The FAA's line-up-and-wait rule went into force in late November 2026, and although it may add to delays, it creates no new right to cash, according to InsideFlyer. The FAA wrote the rule for its own workforce. The notice is addressed to the Air Traffic Organization's service units and facilities, according to the FAA, and its requirements bind those offices, so it is a rule in force rather than a proposal. Nothing in it addresses passengers or compensation. A traveler should count it as a possible cause of a delay, not as a remedy for one.

Industry observers note that the rule sets how the FAA supervises its controllers. It has no bearing on the people waiting at the gate. The agency turned advice into an order, and the wording of its guidance changed from "should" to "must," according to the FAA. Facilities now have to meet the requirement instead of treating it as a recommendation. A delay tied to the rule starts with an FAA requirement for its own facilities, though the airline still decides how to code the cause.

Sources indicate that A passenger still has a claim when the hold-up begins in the control tower. The FAA notice gives passengers nothing, but the refund rule does not ask whose staffing caused the wait. A traveler who declines a trip after the delay passes the thresholds is still owed a refund, whatever the cause. Once the wait runs that long and the trip is no longer worth taking, the traveler should turn it down and claim the money.

In a recent development, the notice also carries an end date, though that date does not settle how long the requirement itself will apply. The FAA notice is set to be canceled on June 9, 2027, according to the FAA, and it does not spell out what follows.

Whatever the FAA decides next, a traveler's leverage over this kind of delay is the refund right.

Industry observers note that A traveler who hears that an international treaty covers flight delays may expect a set payment for the hours spent waiting, but the Montreal Convention offers no such payment. Passengers flying abroad can seek compensation for proven losses from delays, though the treaty caps the amounts, according to InsideFlyer. What a passenger can claim is the money a delay cost them, not the time or patience it took. The treaty applies to international flights, so a delayed domestic trip gets nothing from it. A passenger who walks away from a disrupted flight can take back the fare under U.S. refund rules. A passenger who keeps going abroad and pays for a hotel, meals or a new connection along the way can try to recover those extra costs under the treaty, as long as they can show what they spent.

Because payment depends on proof, a passenger delayed on an international trip should keep a receipt for every cost the delay causes, from the airport meal to the extra night in a hotel.

A traveler's own insurer or credit card issuer may pay for a hotel room and meals during a delay when the airline won't, according to InsideFlyer. That makes such coverage something to try after the airline has stated no, not the first place to ask. It is a benefit that comes with a policy or a card, not a right the airline owes, so what a traveler collects depends on the plan's own terms. Weather and FAA disruptions are the delays where this coverage can matter most. An airline commits to care only for disruptions within its control, so a passenger stranded by a storm or an air traffic problem may have no airline promise of a meal or a room.

According to recent reports, an insurer or card issuer may also cover more than a room and food, including the costs of an interrupted trip. That matters when one late departure throws off every later leg of a journey. Each of these benefits is possible rather than certain, so only a traveler who has checked their own policy or card terms knows which ones they can count on. A passenger who learns the terms at the gate, after the airline has refused, may find out too late that the plan excludes the very delay they are sitting through.

After the cash refund, the airline's promises and the treaty, the last source of help is one travelers have to confirm for themselves by reading their policy or card terms before they fly.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still claims Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

According to recent reports, most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Recent findings suggest that embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

In a recent development, the schedule is fixed. Circle confirmed in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide claims "message limits will tighten over time until no fresh burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Recent findings suggest that circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the organization wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

Industry observers note that funds already in transit are protected. The guide notes "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

According to recent reports, the migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

It has been revealed that the main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle noted "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or revision integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

Industry observers note that the fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

Industry observers note that for everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electric truck operator Nevoya is expanding its deal with Meta with the fresh deployment of 25 Class 8 battery-electric trucks on the Interstate 10 (I-10) between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona … but Meta won’t be shipping any products.

It has been revealed that the second major trucking deal between Facebook parent company Meta and electric truck operator Nevoya will put 25 new battery-electric semis on I-10, running freight between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona. But Meta isn’t buying trucks, hiring drivers or shipping its own products. Instead, Zuck’s company helping pay for someone else’s cleaner freight through environmental attribute certificates (EACs), a carbon credit mechanism that lets companies claim the emissions benefits of electric trucking without operating the trucks themselves.

“Coming back to Nevoya for a second corridor reflects what we look for in our value chain work: partners that can scale, and agreements we can repeat, said Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta. “Freight is part of the emissions footprint of building and operating our data centers, and multi-year commitments like this help address our scope 3 emissions and make electric trucking available and competitive on the routes that serve the regions where we build.”.

Recent findings suggest that meta was one of several buyers in the DC-based Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) buyers’ alliance. The group’s collective EAC purchases supported Nevoya’s initial 63-truck deployment on the Houston–Dallas corridor back in May. This fresh Agreement, however, is a standalone deal between Nevoya and Meta only, and gives Meta an established framework to open more electric truck corridors in the future.

This clever application of these agreements is what makes the Dallas-Houston run stand out, with GMA calling it, “the first large-scale application of book and claim to zero-emission trucking.” The manufacturer adds that this arrangement helps client companies overcome existing barriers to EV adoption while enabling Nevoya to deploy new trucks, “where they deliver the strongest commercial and operational value.”.

Coca-Cola CFO John Murphy to retire. Here are his 3 pieces of career advice after nearly 40 years at the organization

💡 Key Takeaways
  • CFO turnover continues across the Fortune 500, and one of the latest changes is at The Coca-Cola Firm, where longtime finance chief John Murphy is preparing to retire after nearly four decades at the beverage giant.
  • It has been revealed that murphy, who has served as CFO since 2019 and president since 2022, will step down from his CFO role on April 2.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that good morning. CFO turnover continues across the Fortune 500, and one of the latest changes is at The Coca-Cola Firm, where longtime finance chief John Murphy is preparing to retire after nearly four decades at the beverage giant.

It has been revealed that murphy, who has served as CFO since 2019 and president since 2022, will step down from his CFO role on April 2. He will remain president until his retirement later that year, although a specific date has not yet been announced.

Industry observers note that to succeed Murphy, Coca-Cola has tapped another Fortune 500 finance chief: David Elkins, who has served as executive vice president and CFO of Bristol Myers Squibb since 2019. His previous roles include positions at Johnson & Johnson and AstraZeneca. At Coca-Cola, Elkins will oversee finance, global strategy and enterprise services.

Elkins has a “track record of success across complex, global companies,” Coca-Cola CEO Henrique Braun said in the tech giant’s announcement Monday. Braun also highlighted Elkins’ ability to develop future leaders.

Murphy, meanwhile, has been a transformational leader during his 38 years at Coca-Cola, Braun remarked.

In a recent development, although Coca-Cola selected an external candidate for its CFO role, Braun is a product of the company’s own leadership pipeline. He became CEO in March after spending 30 years at Coca-Cola, reflecting the company’s history of developing leaders from within.

Murphy, 64, joined the organization in 1988 and held a variety of general management, finance and strategic planning positions around the world. His roles included vice president of business systems for Coca-Cola North America, executive vice president and CFO of Coca-Cola Japan, and vice president of strategic planning for the company.

Industry observers note that I interviewed Murphy in September to discuss Coca-Cola’s planned $10 billion infrastructure investment from 2026 through 2030, which will span multiple projects across its system. Coca-Cola contributed $85 billion to U.S. GDP in 2025, or roughly $10 million every hour, according to an independent study commissioned by the firm.

After our conversation about the investment, I asked Murphy what career advice he would share with people early in their careers, drawing from his own experience at Coca-Cola.

Have the courage to get uncomfortable.

“The first thing I say to younger folks is to have the courage to get uncomfortable. I think you grow and learn more in positions where you are uncomfortable than when it’s easy, and sometimes it’s a tough decision for younger folks to make. Do that a few times, and you then start to differentiate yourself from those around you.”.

“The second thing I would encourage people to do is focus on today—and tomorrow will take care of itself. In other words, do the very best that you can with what’s on your agenda for today, and don’t worry too much about what comes tomorrow or next week. And then, in a strange way, the better you do today, the better tomorrow and next week and next month will be.”.

Industry observers note that “The last thing I say to people is, from early on, build your network. You can never have too many people in your network. And the last time I checked—I’ve never yet been punished for being nice to people.”.

As Murphy prepares to close a nearly four-decade career at Coca-Cola, his advice is a reminder that career growth isn’t necessarily about having a perfect plan. It’s about being willing to take on challenges, doing today’s work well and building relationships along the way.

Alex Berkett was named CFO at the PGA Tour, effective Feb. 1. Berkett joins from Citi, where he served as managing director and global head of media, entertainment and sports investment banking. Previously, he spent more than a decade at Paramount Global and its predecessors, rising to chief corporate development and strategy officer. He also co-founded Townsquare Media in 2010 and earlier spent nearly 12 years in investment banking at Bear Stearns and J.P. Morgan.

According to recent reports, ron Farnsworth was named EVP and CFO at NRC Health (Nasdaq: NRC), effective on or about Nov. 30. Farnsworth most recently served as CFO of Columbia Banking System from 2023 through December 2025 before transitioning to an advisory role in 2026. Previously, he was CFO of Umpqua Holdings until its merger with Columbia in 2023, following earlier roles as senior vice president of finance and interim CFO. He also served as CFO of Independent Financial Network and began his career in audit at KPMG.

Angela Simmons is expected to become EVP and CFO at Genworth Financial, Inc., (NYSE: GNW) effective Jan. 1. Simmons, presently CFO of Genworth’s Closed Block, joined the tech giant in 2002. Before assuming her current role in 2020, she served as controller for U.S. Life Insurance and spent more than a decade leading Genworth’s SEC reporting function. She will succeed Jerome Upton, who was appointed president and CEO following Thomas McInerney’s earlier-than-planned departure to focus on his health. Upton will continue as CFO through Dec. 31, leaving the timing of Simmons’ anticipated appointment unchanged.

Roger Smith, CFO of Ur-Energy Inc. (NYSE American: URG), an ISR uranium producer, will retire from the company effective Dec. 1, after a 45-year career in mining industry finance and accounting. Jade Walle, currently VP of finance, has been promoted to CFO, upon Smith's retirement. Walle joined Ur-Energy in September 2025. Most recently, he was an audit partner with PwC, having begun his career there in 1996. His technical background includes service in PwC's Global Capital Markets Group in London.

The annual survey released by the National Retail Federation and conducted by Prosper Insights and Analytics, estimates that 182.7 million consumers plan to shop over Thanksgiving weekend. That is slightly below last year's 186.9 million but still historically elevated.

It has been revealed that holiday shopping keeps starting earlier: 60% of shoppers begin by the start of November, up from 56% before the pandemic. Black Friday is still the most popular day, with 69% (126 million) planning to shop. Of those, 89% plan to shop online and 67% in stores. Cyber Monday follows at 36% (66.1 million).

Sources indicate that almost half of respondents noted deals are the top motivator, ahead of tradition (26%). About eighty-two percent said they are taking steps to control costs, such as buying cheaper gifts or buying for fewer people. About 59% plan to use AI for holiday shopping, mostly for product recommendations, gift ideas, and price comparison.

He Saw a ‘Weird’ Machine on Instagram, Got on a Plane to Try It and Built a $75 Million Fitness Empire

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (916 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that most people who see something odd on Instagram mutter “huh, neat,” and keep scrolling.
  • Ramsey shared how the STRONG brand came together, why some Pilates traditionalists hate it, and why he is totally okay with that.
  • Sources indicate that this wasn’t your original career path.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most people who see something odd on Instagram mutter “huh, neat,” and keep scrolling. Michael Ramsey bought a plane ticket to check it out in person. The former oil and gas marketer, who once ran an F45 studio in Port Melbourne, saw a post about an exercise machine called the Rowformer, and flew from Australia to Orange County to try it himself. Seven years later, STRONG Pilates has more than 130 studios across multiple countries and continents, 57,000 members and more than $75 million in net revenue over the past 12 months.

Ramsey shared how the STRONG brand came together, why some Pilates traditionalists hate it, and why he is totally okay with that.

Sources indicate that this wasn’t your original career path. How did you get involved in Pilates?I was working in oil and gas, and I was not enjoying my life too much. I wasn’t highly motivated in corporate. And on the weekends, I was actually running a nightclub with my business partner, Mark Armstrong, who I’ve been in business with for eleven years. And he tapped me on the shoulder and he noted, “Hey, I found this really unique boutique concept called F45 Training.” This was about twelve years ago. And so we actually brought the first F45 studio to Melbourne, Australia, and I quit my job in corporate, and for the first time in my life, I felt free, like I was in charge of my own destiny. Not only did I have financial freedom, but I had time as well. We scaled our F45 studios to six very swiftly, sold after about four or five years.

Sources indicate that what inspired STRONG?My housemate indicated me an Instagram post about this Rowformer machine that was created out of Orange County. And to me it ticked a lot of boxes — you’ve got rowing, and you’ve got the Reformer. So I jumped on a plane, took the class and it was one of the most exhilarating, endorphin-led kind of workouts I’d ever done. I’m looking around the room, and there are all these incredibly fit women in their forties and fifties that just looked incredible. And I’m like, “Wow, this, this is awesome. I need to take this back to Australia.” Mark tried it, had the same experience, and then we negotiated global rights for the machine and built a franchise model around it.

Most of us see something cool on Instagram and keep scrolling. We don’t jump on a plane. What does that say about you?Look, to be transparent, it was very opportunistic. I could see, and nothing against F45, but I couldn’t see the lifetime value of the customer increasing over time due to the impact of workouts. So I was on the hunt for something that was low impact, more longevity-focused. How do we keep our members for five, six, seven, ten years? That was a question that I had and the problem I was trying to solve.

How do you turn early adopters into paying clients and repeat customers?You need to respect your product and business enough to have people paying from the start. There’s this whole thing in the fitness industry about free trials, and do they work or do they not work? We are a premium product, and I think once the work is done and the product is ready, you need to respect yourself and your product by charging for every session.

According to recent reports, now, for anyone who’s starting in this space, I would say the first thing to do is just start. Just open, and then learn from your consumer and innovate like crazy. And that’s all we did. It’s a very different product today than what it was seven years ago, and in another seven years it’s gonna be probably even more different, because that’s how it works. If you don’t innovate, you will recede, and you will die.

Was there an innovation that came from customer feedback and made you think, “Oh yeah, that’s a good idea”?The massive one was the TV screens. Our male audience, as soon as we put TVs in, their trial-to-member conversion went through the roof. You’ve got to imagine, seven years ago, a lot of men hadn’t even experienced Pilates before. They were terrified to jump on a reformer. So the TVs, although they’re not liked by the traditionalists, gave us a huge uptake, particularly with male consumers. It was huge for us.

Your Instagram handle is just “Strong.” How on earth did you get that?Do you remember when domain names were getting really expensive? Like imagine strong.com. It’s probably worth half a million dollars. I had some friends that were trying to open businesses and trying to get these domain names, and I thought, “Well, I’m gonna start acquiring one-word Instagram names,” because Instagram was really taking off at the time. And so I had Strong, I had Cultivate, I had Ram. So I just held onto them. And then when I went to Orange County and I did the workout, I thought, “How does this workout make me feel? Not only do I need to be physically strong, but I need to be mentally strong to get through this.” And so it just made sense to call it STRONG Pilates, and now we’re here. At one point, it was getting tagged every 30 seconds all around the world, and I would just sit there watching it.
