💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Grace Kaste on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:50 amNovember 24, 2026 at 1:22 pm.
  • It has been revealed that editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • When startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:50 amNovember 24, 2026 at 1:22 pm.

It has been revealed that editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

When startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models. He got in touch with urban planners at Bellevue City Hall, and together they combed through nearly 300 land use permit applications to find common mistakes and bottlenecks.

Bellevue began using Rabah’s platform, Govstream.AI, in the summer of 2025, starting with an AI assistant for city staff. In a test using past applications, about three times as many were judged complete with Govstream’s tool. Rabah notes that change alone has the potential to alter the housing stock of the city.

Industry observers note that “Why can’t we build more housing? All the macro economic reasons, inflation, material costs, labor, land scarcity, are all exacerbated by the slow permitting process,” Rabah stated. “That’s what we want to change.”.

So, how did Rabah, a B2B software engineer by training, find his way to land use permitting?

Recent findings suggest that rabah hadn’t heard of the government technology sector, aka GovTech, until mid-career, but looking back, the signs were all there. He was born in Sfax, Tunisia, and grew up in Tunis. Throughout his childhood, he dreamed of running for office.

In a recent development, “I come from a small developing country, so there’s always this idea of, what could a small developing country become? How can it prosper and grow?” Rabah mentioned. “Building has always been a substantial part of what I imagined myself doing.”.

Industry observers note that as a teenager in the 1980s, he attended a USAID-funded boarding school in Tunis. The school was part of Cold War efforts to expand American soft power around the Middle East; classes were conducted in English and many of the students went on to university in North America.

“The school had the first Macintosh lab in all of Africa,” Rabah mentioned. “I can still picture the USAID logo on the back of each computer.”.

Rabah got a scholarship to University of British Columbia, where he studied electrical engineering while running what he calls his “first entrepreneurial venture”: a service that built and hosted websites for small businesses.

That led to a job at a startup called Pivotal, a customer relationship management platform where Rabah led a team responsible for e-business applications. After Pivotal went public, Rabah left for a job at TELUS, one of Canada’s “major three” telecommunications corporations, but rapidly felt frustrated by the dynamics at such a large organization.

“Even though I worked on nascent products, it was very, very bureaucratic,” Rabah mentioned. “There were committees, a hundred thousand employees. I missed building things.”.

Rabah began to look for a newly introduced job that would not only allow him to build but also to make a difference.

“Being an immigrant, it’s always tempting to stay content with having a good job, good status,” Rabah mentioned. “But I’ve always enjoyed the ‘what if?’ mindset, the clean slate. It’s this way today, but could we imagine it to be something different?”.

That vision led him to Socrata, which in 2010 was just a nascent government technology startup.

“I really connected with the founder,” Rabah said. “It had a really cool mission, it combined the ‘do-well’ with ‘do-good.’”.

In a recent development, socrata was one of the first platforms to host data portals for local governments and federal agencies, allowing citizens to access and map public data sets. Many U.S. cities, including Seattle, still use Socrata’s software today to publish information including crime logs, permits, and budgets.

Industry observers note that “We were a big part of pioneering the open data movement,” Rabah remarked. “At one point almost every major city was our customer, and half the states.”.

Socrata was acquired by Tyler Technologies in 2018, and Rabah stayed on until 2024.

According to recent reports, “The funny part is today we use that data quite a lot in our work because one of the most popular data sets that any city publishes is its permit data,” Rabah said. “We’ve even built a connector between Socrata and Govstream.”.

But once Socrata was acquired, Rabah began to feel the same way he had at TELUS: boxed in by bureaucracy.

Recent findings suggest that “Tyler was a really good tech giant, but it is a big company,” Rabah noted. “Tech was getting repetitive, and I was thinking about leaving it altogether.”.

It has been revealed that “The thing that pushed me over the edge is that AI happened,” Rabah said. “It was one of those moments where once you start working with it, you really can’t help but think, ‘I can revisit virtually every assumption I’ve made over the last 20 years, every constraint.’”.

Immediately, he thought of his passion for building—building a startup, building a better country, and literally building a building.

“I’ve been fascinated by the built environment since my Lego days: What makes some cities livable and others not?” Rabah stated. “Then, living in Seattle, you see the lack of housing, affordability, and the homelessness problem we have, and you’re like, why can’t we build more housing? I started believing that these problems are in fact solvable if we simply speed things up and simplify things with AI.”.

In July of 2024, Rabah began working with his “design partner,” Bellevue’s Development Services Department, to learn more about common permitting problems.

In a recent development, “We started with something visionary and high-level, but you can only get there if you understand the granular problems of the day-to-day,” Rabah said. “So we talked with developers and builders and we talked with the people on the other side of the counter who are processing these permits and guiding these builders.”.

He learned that most permitting mistakes are avoidable, like applying for the wrong zone or forgetting to include a north arrow on an architectural proposal. Those oversights can send an application back to square one while clogging up the permitting process for all other projects.

Industry observers note that “The wait time disproportionately affects lower margin projects,” Rabah stated. “It really constrains the supply of housing, especially the housing we need more of, which is the more affordable kind.”.

It has been revealed that govstream’s AI assistants are designed to help first-time builders avoid those errors and make permitting faster for everyone. Rabah and his team began by building what they call an “intelligent intake” platform for a city permitting portal, which guided users through preparing to submit their applications.

Sources indicate that when Bellevue first tested Govstream’s intake tool on 276 past residential building permit applications, the city reported a completeness rate of 67%, compared with 22% when those applications were originally filed. According to the company, the latest testing has yielded an 88% completeness rate.

More recently, they’ve begun to build out an AI assistant for the backend, which assists city permit techs with the initial review and reduces what Rabah calls “toil,” like answering unnecessary pre-application emails and tracking down missing documents.

Bellevue staff estimated that Govstream’s tools saved them 152 hours over one month this summer by helping them research and respond to pre-application inquiries.

“For a developer, time is money, so the type of housing that can be built in Bellevue will become more affordable,” said Jake Hesselgesser, Bellevue’s development services director. “This technology has a direct and material impact on the cost of housing.”.

Sources indicate that eventually, Govstream.AI will be an end-to-end service, assisting in later stages of the permitting process, too. But Rabah is emphatic that Govstream will not give AI the final say.

“We always put our AI systems in the role of assistants that suggest stuff, but never decide stuff,” Rabah stated.

Rabah says Govstream uses preset rules, outside the AI model, to check whether a portion of the application is complete, whether a site needs a geotechnical report, or whether an architect is properly licensed. In Bellevue, city staff retain final authority.

Hesselgesser said that Rabah’s conservative approach to AI is what made the city of Bellevue want to work with his startup.

Industry observers note that “Our core principle around Bellevue’s use of AI is to retain human decision making, and we wanted to ensure that we were aligned with a firm with the same core value,” Hesselgesser noted. “Saf took that holistic approach.”.

Recent findings suggest that around the office, Rabah has become known for his eagerness to build. According to Mariia Derevianko, head of marketing, he spends his weekends building out a product or an idea in order to workshop it with the team.

“He’s very hands-on with the product, with design, marketing, all of the aspects,” Derevianko mentioned. “He never waits for the engineers to build something.”.

Most recently, he built a lead tracker to research which cities Govstream should partner with, and previously, he vibe-coded one of the research assistants in the Govstream platform as a template for his software engineers.

Derevianko, who joined the team last year after Rabah poached her from AWS, said he’s also known for his kindness.

“I originally didn’t want to join a start-up,” Derevianko stated. “I only said yes because I saw he is a genuinely good person who really cares about this project.”.

Govstream.AI has already won at least 12 contracts around the Puget Sound, including King County and the City of Everett, as well as cities across the country, such as Louisville, Kentucky.

Ultimately, Rabah has his eyes set on Seattle, where construction and development has been on the decline. Last December, the city council passed permanent “middle housing” rules to upzone residential neighborhoods and encourage the construction of ADUs, all of which will need a permit.

In a recent development, seattle tested a competing AI tool from CivCheck in 2025. In June, city staff recommended a pilot that would let applicants check their submissions for completeness before filing.

Industry observers note that “We need affordable housing in Seattle,” Rabah said. “We would really, really love to help our home city streamline permitting and remove it as a barrier.”.

In founding Govstream.AI, Rabah has found the job he has been looking for: one in which he can build things without the bureaucracy of a large manufacturer, all while “doing good.”.

“This has become my obsession,” Rabah said. “I can point to things in a city and say, maybe Govstream was a part of what allowed this project to get built.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

By the time Jason Ganahl opened his first barbecue restaurant, he’d already spent close to two years showing people how to cook on YouTube. He opened GQue Championship BBQ in Westminster, Colorado, in November 2015.

Industry observers note that ganahl was winning barbecue competitions, and friends were asking him for help with dinner. One was thinking about smoking salmon over the weekend. Others wanted to know how to grill asparagus or cook lobster tails.

Industry observers note that he’d watched Greg Mrvich demonstrate barbecue techniques on Ballistic BBQ. Ganahl could do the same with the questions his friends were asking. Once he put an answer on YouTube, anyone who wanted to smoke salmon could find it and watch him do it.

Sources indicate that “YouTube was born out of, I like to just share, I like to give,” Ganahl notes. “That’s why the restaurant industry is great to me.”.

According to recent reports, at GQue, that means helping his team and giving the people who come in for barbecue a good experience. He describes the goal as giving guests “the best 20 minutes of their day.”.

Recent findings suggest that ganahl knew his way around a smoker. Making videos gave him something to learn from scratch. He believed video would become a bigger part of how people told their stories and wanted to learn how to do the work himself.

“I thought this was a good opportunity to teach myself how to edit, create content and learn how to be pretty good at it,” he indicates.

“Shorts have really taken over,” Ganahl says.

According to recent reports, he singled out Meat Church as a channel still doing long-form videos well. Asked whether he plans to make more himself, he says, “I don’t have the bandwidth to do that.”.

Industry observers note that ganahl’s older videos are still up. Anyone looking for help with lobster tails can find his answer without ever setting foot in GQue.

In a recent development, ganahl wants guests to leave GQue and tell a friend where they ate. If enough people do that, he states, the demand for another restaurant takes care of the decision about when to open one.

“Then we’re forced to grow and open up a newly introduced spot,” Ganahl states.

That’s why he pays so much attention to who he hires. He wants people who care as much as he does about what a guest gets when they walk in for lunch. When someone brings a friend back for the brisket, both should get the same barbecue that earned the recommendation.

“I’ve never been able, and I’ve never seen anybody, to be able to take chicken shit and turn it into chicken salad,” Ganahl says.

Recent findings suggest that he looks for people who share his priorities and trusts them to deliver on those priorities every day. At GQue, that means smoking brisket over hickory for same-day service and keeping the price within reach for someone who wants barbecue on an ordinary day.

GQue has grown from one restaurant in Westminster to six standalone restaurants and seven concession stands across three stadiums. It has been revealed that ethereum foundation has been selling ETH in 2026 during steep price movements, both up and down. For instance, BitMine acquired 10,000 ETH at an average price of $2,292 this June.

  • The Seattle startup has released Zin Power, a upcoming division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 9:58 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:58 am.

Zin Boats made a splash with fast, pricey electric boats. But most of its business is now coming from what’s under the floor.

The Seattle startup has released Zin Power, a upcoming division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.

The tech giant also raised $5 million to scale up production and expanded its headquarters in the Interbay neighborhood to 11,000 square feet.

About 90% of the firm’s revenue comes from selling motors and batteries to customers in the marine and drone industries, founder and CEO Piotr Zin told GeekWire. A typical setup includes two motors and about 500 kilowatt-hours of battery storage.

“We noticed a steady demand for pleasure craft year over year, but at the same time a massive increase in propulsion sales,” Zin said.

Customers include StanCraft Wooden Boats, which teamed with Zin on the 340 Hammerhead E, an all-electric wooden runabout. StanCraft delivered the first one to a customer this summer.

It has been revealed that geekWire first checked out the tech giant in early 2024, when it was relaunching after a pandemic shutdown with its Z2R, a 20-foot carbon fiber runabout. Later that year Zin revealed off the Z11, a 37-foot electric tender designed to shuttle passengers to and from megayachts at more than 60 mph. The company mentioned boats on the platform would cost $1.75 million to $3.75 million.

The firm also offers the Z7 Convertible, a 22-foot runabout with a removable roof that it pitches for fishing, surfing and cruising. The boat has a top speed of 40 mph and a range of more than 80 miles.

Zin Power grew out of the drivetrains engineered for those boats. Zin sees the marine track record as a selling point for other industries that need high torque, including construction, mining and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs).

“The ocean is one of the harshest environments there is, so the technology has already proven itself under about the toughest conditions it could face,” Zin stated.

It has been revealed that many of those machines still run on diesel engines, a technology more than a century old. Zin noted operators are eager to switch to electric.

“What’s interesting is that economics is driving the shift, not regulation or image,” he stated.

Electric systems cost up to 70% less to operate, according to Zin. He estimated that replacing a single 250-horsepower industrial diesel engine that runs eight hours a day could save as much as $1.5 million over 10 years.

Sources indicate that the latest funding will pay for more manufacturing capacity, a dedicated sales and engineering team to work with boat builders, and support for customers converting from diesel. Zin calls it a seed round, with a larger raise planned down the road. The organization has raised $6.5 million to date, including a $1.275 million seed round in early 2024.

Zin Boats has nine full-time employees and brings on about a dozen contractors as needed.

For now, each Zin Power system is built to order. The organization’s motors range from 100 to 600 kilowatts and deliver up to 2,700 pound-feet of torque, and its systems can run fully electric or as hybrids. A proprietary control unit that Zin Power calls the “Magic Box” manages everything from charging and cooling to software and safety.

Industry observers note that “Our goal is to keep delivering what we’ve built while developing simpler, more advanced plug-and-play systems,” Zin noted. “Eventually, we want a customer to be able to pull out a diesel engine and drop in a Zin Power system as a direct one-for-one replacement.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.

As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” Schäfer said in the memo reviewed by Reuters. The Wolfsburg plant, AKA the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer revealed earlier this year that the long-awaited electric car was delayed until closer to 2030.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), which is being developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected, again due to costs.

According to Autocar, Volkswagen is now delaying the Audi A4 E-tron as well, another vehicle that was initially planned to be among the first based on the SSP platform.

Recent findings suggest that production of the electric A4 is being pushed back until at least 2029, a year later than originally planned. While the delay is disappointing for Audi fans (including myself) still waiting for an electric A4, it also puts Audi behind rival luxury brands in the mid-size sedan segment.

BMW has the latest i3, and Mercedes-Benz has the C-Class EV, both of which feature major improvements in range, charging, and efficiency over their previous-generation EVs.

Volkswagen said in 2023 that the 800V SSP will serve as a “single future backbone with integrated electric and electronics architecture,” claiming that more than 40 million models were expected to be built on it.

The tech giant also mentioned investment and R&D costs were expected to be reduced by about 30% compared to the current MEB platform, enabling most models “to achieve the same margin compared to their conventionally powered counterparts.”.

Volkswagen’s software struggles started in its internal division, Cariad, leading to delays, missed targets, and budget overruns.

To fix it, VW turned to Rivian, forming a joint venture to develop its next-gen software-defined vehicle (SDV) electrical architecture.

In March, VW said several test vehicles, including the ID.EVERY1, Audi, and Scout with the SDV architecture underwent “comprehensive evaluation,” and successfully validated over-the-air (OTA) functionality.

Being cash efficient is good, but delays to the next-gen platform that will keep you competitive with rival brands seem like a problem.

However, the Audi A4 E-tron delay is not entirely about software. The Autocar report claims Audi demanded significant changes to the SSP platform for the A4 E-tron so it more closely matched the current gas version.

Audi reportedly wanted individual footwells for front and rear passengers, which would require repositioning the battery.

The luxury brand also reportedly asked for a 48V electrical system instead of the traditional 12V setup initially planned.

While development of the Golf EV is on hold, VW’s works council mentioned the pause will not delay its launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030. The Audi A4 E-tron is now expected to arrive around 2029.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gen Zers are bucking the norms of wealth-building set by generations before them and turning to digital investments over long-vetted ways of saving.
  • Around 21% of Gen Z currently own cryptocurrency, according to a recent SoFi survey in partnership with YouGov, while only 19% have an employer-sponsored retirement plan like a 401(k).
  • Sources indicate that it’s a huge leap from how predecessors think about saving for the future; around 34% of millennials invest in their tech giant’s retirement savings proposal, and only 20% own crypto.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gen Zers are bucking the norms of wealth-building set by generations before them and turning to digital investments over long-vetted ways of saving. Now, more of the young investors are betting their fortunes on cryptocurrency over traditional retirement accounts.

Around 21% of Gen Z currently own cryptocurrency, according to a recent SoFi survey in partnership with YouGov, while only 19% have an employer-sponsored retirement plan like a 401(k).

Sources indicate that it’s a huge leap from how predecessors think about saving for the future; around 34% of millennials invest in their tech giant’s retirement savings proposal, and only 20% own crypto. And Gen Zers are in stark contrast to their parents’ generations, owning crypto at seven times the rate of baby boomers and over twice the rate of Gen Xers.

It has been revealed that “Unlike other investment assets, crypto is accessible to Gen Z,” the SoFi report notes. “With inflation outpacing wage increases and mortgages still hovering at the highest rates they’ve been in decades, they view cryptocurrency as an asset they can access now to build generational wealth down the line.”.

For the young digital natives, crypto isn’t a “speculative gamble,” the report explains: it’s part of a deliberate strategy to diversify their investment portfolios.

Industry observers note that gen Zers are almost three times more likely (21%) to say that crypto is one of the best ways to build future wealth compared to the average population (8%). SoFi notes that Gen Z being early adopters could be the “tipping point” in mainstreaming digital currency; and as they’re projected to amass $36 trillion in wealth by 2030, according to a 2025 Bank of America report, they’ll continue to invest in the digital assets they have confidence in.

From memecoins to Ethereum, cryptocurrencies have become a staple in both investing and popular culture. There have been questions if Gen Z’s fascination with digital currencies is clouded by hype.

SoFi’s report found that 34% of overall crypto investors admit they bought in simply because it “sounded interesting,” with 20% of Gen Zers reporting they felt this way. However, experts have told Fortune that cryptocurrency is still in its infancy, and young investors may not know exactly what they’re buying into.

In a recent development, much of crypto’s popularity has circulated around internet hype, which has been rife with controversy. Elon Musk’s Dogecoin famously rocked the internet, and celebrities like Reese Witherspoon and Paris Hilton have publicly boasted about their investments.

Several celebrities have been accused of running “pump-and-dump” scams on their followers: raving about a stock online to attract investors and inflate the price, then turning around quickly and selling their shares, tanking the value. Caitlyn Jenner’s $jenner, Iggy Azalea’s $mother, and Jason Derulo’s $Jason were all wrapped up in that accusation. And Kim Kardashian and Floyd Mayweather were both named in a lawsuit for promoting EthereumMax on social media in 2021.

Industry observers note that there are several reasons the crypto world is both mysterious and exciting, experts have told Fortune. And it may be that exact intrigue that pulls Gen Z to the investment, despite how risky it can be. Without employer-backed savings looks and level-headed investments, young people may be looking at financial regrets in the future.

“It’s never a bad thing for people in any generation to take interest in their personal finances,” Mark Smrecek, financial well-being market leader at Willis Towers Watson (WTW), told Fortune last year. “I think as long as they’re looking at risk and reward based on what their goals are, it’s generally fine. But I do get concerned when I see over-indexing toward risky assets.”.

Recent findings suggest that beyond their favorite online personalities promoting the products, experts point out that crypto is attractive for being liquid and immediate. Gen Z workers in the early stages of their careers may not be prioritizing long-term investments like 401(k)s. Crypto coins can be sold anytime and have the potential to be lucrative in the short term.

“Oftentimes getting involved in employer-provided retirement aims seems like a long, far-off way to save,” Smrecek stated. “So they look for something that’s a little bit more liquid that, in case of an emergency, they can access.”.

Selling Your Business? Make These 3 Moves to Reduce Taxes and Protect Your Assets From Lawsuits.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1193 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Sources indicate that it’s happened hundreds of times.
  • Then I have to explain that none of those documents will reduce their tax bill or protect their assets from future lawsuits or creditors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sources indicate that it’s happened hundreds of times. A business owner indicates up at my office, in the middle of selling their tech giant, and tells me, “Don’t worry, my estate proposal is all done: I have a revocable living trust, will, powers of attorney, and health care directives, and my lawyer told me years ago that I was all set.”.

Then I have to explain that none of those documents will reduce their tax bill or protect their assets from future lawsuits or creditors. A revocable trust avoids probate. That is all it does.

The planning that actually changes the outcome of an exit lives primarily in three strategies that have been authorized by the Tax Code for decades, and every one of them should be considered well in advance of marketing the organization for sale.

The Tax Code imposes a federal estate tax at death equal to 40% to the extent your reported net worth — including your business, real estate and other illiquid assets — exceeds the federal estate tax exemption (currently $15 million per person for 2026).

In addition, some states impose their own inheritance tax or estate tax, which can result in a combined rate ranging from 40-75%. States oftentimes have very low and costly exemption limits, many starting at $1-2M.

The government expects a cash payment within nine months after death. Although some estates heavily concentrated in businesses or illiquid assets can qualify for installment payments, the IRS requires liens and reporting — so you are effectively putting your spouse and children in business with the IRS as their de facto partner.

Industry observers note that the easy fix is to take action before your tech giant jumps in value. Specifically, you should transfer all or a portion of your business shares to an irrevocable gift trust for your spouse and/or children while the company is still private and appraisable at a defensibly low discounted value (allowing you to transfer the shares within the $15 million gift tax limit).

Properly done, every dollar of appreciation on your business shares happens outside your estate. In addition, the assets inside the trust are protected from future personal lawsuits. These benefits can continue indefinitely for the benefit of your heirs.

Most business owners balk at the word “irrevocable” when considering this planning. However, so-called “optimized” irrevocable gift trusts can let you keep far more control than you might expect. For example, you can:.

In a recent development, suppose you own a tech giant and expect to sell the company for $30 million in 18 months. Moving 40% of the shares into a trust today removes roughly $12 million from your estate, plus whatever that 40% position grows to before (and after) the sale. If the deal falls through and the business doubles to $60M in three years, you have just removed $24 million of value from the 40% estate tax ($60M x 40%).

For the seller of a tech giant, a charitable lead annuity trust (CLAT) is the most underused financial tool that I am aware of.

In a recent development, with a CLAT, you transfer assets into a trust account before December 31 of the year of the sale. The CLAT pays a fixed annual amount to the charities that you choose for a term of years (typically 20-30 years — the longer, the greater the benefits), and whatever investments remain in the CLAT account are returned to you (or your heirs).

For example, an optimized CLAT (zeroed-out grantor trust with maximum IRS-approved charitable backloading) gives you an income tax deduction in the year of the sale equal to nearly 100% of your contribution to the CLAT, and returns a significant amount back to you (assuming a reasonable 7-8% rate of return). The payments to charity are set using the IRS interest rate in effect when you fund the CLAT, and these rates are reasonably low.

Since the charitable payments are back-loaded, most of the donations from the CLAT happen in the final years … after the assets have presumably compounded to a very large amount. After all donations are made, everything left in the CLAT account passes to your heirs, without any gift tax (and without consuming any of your lifetime $15 million gift tax exemption).

Suppose you sell your organization for a $20 million gain and fund a 30-year optimized CLAT with $4 million. You would receive a tax deduction equal to approximately $4 million, the CLAT would donate approximately $14 million over the 30-year period, and your children could expect to receive back approximately $10 million (assuming 7% rate of return), free of the 40% federal gift tax. The caveat, however, is that the CLAT funds cannot be spent during the 30-year term, and this strategy only makes sense if you are charitably inclined.

Section 1202 of the Tax Code lets a founder exclude up to $10 million of gain on the sale of qualified small business stock (QSBS) — and for shares issued after July 4, 2025, that figure rises to $15 million with partial benefits starting at year three instead of year five.

A married couple can multiply that exclusion by placing shares in special non-grantor trusts (each of which counts as its own taxpayer).

Recent findings suggest that here is the catch that disqualifies many of the founders that I talk to: QSBS only exists for C corporations, and the holding period starts when the C corporation problems the stock. If you have run your firm as an S corporation or LLC for 15 years, you have zero qualifying years. Converting the month before the sale accomplishes nothing.

There are three things to do now:.

Check your state, too. For example, California does not conform to the federal QSBS exclusion, which means a founder who is a California tax resident saves federal tax only.

Every one of the moves above is irrevocable, and requires a team (including a trust attorney, CPA and appraiser) with unique technical expertise and experience.

But all three share a single feature: They only work if you blueprint ahead. The owner who calls the attorney after the term sheet is signed has drastically limited their options — and increased their tax bill.

According to recent reports, if a sale is possible in the next two to three years, put an estate planning meeting on your calendar today. You spent a decade building the business. Spend one quarter planning so your business is “built to sell” in the event of an exit.

According to recent reports, it’s happened hundreds of times. A business owner highlights up at my office, in the middle of selling their tech giant, and tells me, “Don’t worry, my estate strategy is all done: I have a revocable living trust, will, powers of attorney, and health care directives, and my lawyer told me years ago that I was all set.”.

Then I have to explain that none of those documents will reduce their tax bill or protect their assets from future lawsuits or creditors. A revocable trust avoids probate. That is all it does.

Tech Report: Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • It has been revealed that most stablecoin introduces promise a token that never moves.
  • According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to fresh institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

It has been revealed that most stablecoin introduces promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to fresh institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The firm claims R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery remarked the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it substantial" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

Sources indicate that the model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the organization, cost nothing.

Sources indicate that the reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Sources indicate that ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as upcoming rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he noted, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

In a recent development, the risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

In a recent development, the details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

Industry observers note that "Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let people redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

Sources indicate that eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

In a recent development, this background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU debuted earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

In a recent development, the bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday people, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

According to recent reports, the trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

According to recent reports, eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

5 steps households took to limit lead exposure after the Army's Iowa blast

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that five precautions aimed to limit lead exposure around the Army's Iowa detonation.
  • It has been revealed that A whole region had to initiative one morning around a single explosion.
  • According to recent reports, most of the work of staying safe fell on households.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that five precautions aimed to limit lead exposure around the Army's Iowa detonation. Each one protects residents in a different way and falls short somewhere.

It has been revealed that A whole region had to initiative one morning around a single explosion. The Army intended to destroy a lead compound, lead azide, in a controlled blast, according to the USDA. The blast was set for the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, the Chicago Sun-Times reports, and Army Sustainment Command public affairs specialist Lori McFate notes the Army had never before set off this much of the compound at once. Illinois' environmental agency planned air monitoring of its own, and every precaution that followed centered on what people would breathe. No one could check the advice against an earlier blast of the same size, so each step was a precaution rather than a proven defense. Residents had good reason to judge each one by what it could and couldn't stop.

According to recent reports, most of the work of staying safe fell on households. Families had to seal up their homes, change their travel plans and wait out the lead dust themselves, with little help beyond instructions. Critics consider that shift the central flaw in the strategy rather than a side effect. "Instead of keeping people safe, the Army is knowingly blanketing communities with lead and putting the burden on families to understand and mitigate the risks of the massive plume of lead dust," Earthjustice attorney Thien Chau told the Chicago Sun-Times. The steps also cost little. Most people can stay home, shut a window or put off a drive without spending money or buying equipment. For residents, the real question was what each step left uncovered, not whether to follow the steps at all.

KWQC laid out the handful of ordinary household steps residents could take to limit their lead exposure during the detonation, set for 9 a.m. Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. The steps ranged from holding off on drives through the area to switching heating and cooling to recirculate and shutting windows and doors. All of them concern the hours around the blast, not the cleanup afterward. Each step keeps people away from the outdoor air in its own way, by leaving, by sealing up the house or by staying put. Each one also falls short somewhere. Knowing where it falls short helps a household decide which steps matter most for its own home, car or farm.

Leaving the affected area is the only step that aims to keep people from breathing the lead-laden air at all, instead of reducing how much of it they breathe. Anyone who stays outside the zone has no contact with the plume. That separation matters because an open-air blast can put a large share of its lead into the air. The last time lead azide was detonated in the open, in the 1970s, 25% of it ended up airborne, according to KWQC. Army officials hope to bring that share down this time, but a hope is not a promise. Without one, the safest amount of that air for a person to breathe is none, and getting out of the zone is the one step that delivers it.

Recent findings suggest that leaving works best for households that decided early, because the official warning came late. FEMA sent its alert at 8 a.m. Wednesday, an hour before the detonation, and by then the time to strategy a departure had passed. A family that waited for that alert had no room left to gather everyone, pack and drive clear of the zone. The late warning put the most pressure on the families with the strongest reason to go. Lead poses the greatest danger to young children, older adults and anyone who is pregnant, and a household with a toddler or an elderly parent had the most to arrange. For those families, leaving was a plan to make the day before.

In a recent development, for people still inside the affected area when the blast went off, protection started with the building around them. Staying indoors keeps people in the zone away from the contaminated outside air, KWQC reports, and that barrier between a person and the lead-laden air is why the step matters. The advice still ranks sheltering behind leaving, because residents should remain indoors only if they can't evacuate beforehand. Anyone who follows this step accepts a compromise from the start and waits out the plume near its path instead of far from it.

In a recent development, sheltering applies to workplaces as well as homes. Army guidance extends the advice beyond residents to people whose jobs put them in the zone that Wednesday. Employers, not just families, had to decide whether their people would stay inside or leave. Some people in the zone could not get out ahead of the blast, and the advice to shelter exists for them. For those residents and workers, this modest step was the protection they would actually use.

According to recent reports, closing the windows still leaves one opening in many homes, which is the heating and cooling system. Army guidance told residents to set their systems to recirculate as long as doing so was safe, KWQC reports, and a separate Army guide offered shutting the system off entirely as an alternative. Either choice served the same purpose, which was to stop bringing outdoor air inside while the plume was overhead. Illinois public health officials gave residents on their side of the river the same advice to recirculate, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. The Army's safety condition also left each household to decide for itself whether its system could run that way.

According to recent reports, on a farm, leaving protects the farmer but not the animals, feed and water the farmer depends on. Producers can't drive a herd or a barn full of hay out of the zone. The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship asked them instead to put a tarp over their feed, hay and portable water tanks or bring them under a roof, according to USDA. For farm property, cover has to stand in for distance. The risk to that property also lasts past the morning of the blast. Federal officials expect to keep looking for lead after the plume is gone, and the USDA intends to test more tissue from animals slaughtered in the affected region.

Once officials give the all-clear, people can go home, but farmers then begin checking whether lead reached what they left behind.

In a recent development, sheltering protects a person only as well as the building keeps out the air around it. Most homes and offices are not sealed, and outside air can still get in through gaps, open windows and ventilation systems. Staying inside keeps someone out of the plume only if the indoor air stays cleaner than the outdoor air, and simply walking through the door doesn't guarantee that.

Staying inside is only half of a defense, and the other half is the work of shutting the building against the outdoor air.

Closing windows and doors requires no trip and no equipment, and it turns a home into a barrier against the outside air. People who shut them seal the openings that would otherwise let lead-laden outdoor air into the building, according to KWQC. Health officials across the river took up the same measure: the Illinois Department of Public Health issued indoor advice for its own residents, the Chicago Sun-Times reports, and keeping windows closed was part of it. The hard part is knowing whether a given home needs the barrier. The step covers people living or working in affected areas, but it was unclear whether the plume would reach as far as Chicago, which left many households to decide for themselves whether they were inside the zone. Because the step costs almost nothing, a household unsure of its exposure can take it as a precaution.

Recent findings suggest that shutting the windows is simple, but knowing when to open them again is not. The day-of advice set no clock time for the end of the exposure. Illinois health officials offered residents a rough span, and it covers far more than a single morning. "Illinois residents who may be affected by the detonation can stay safe by staying indoors and keeping windows closed for 24 to 48 hours," Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, mentioned, as reported by the Chicago Sun-Times. A family that seals up for the blast and opens the windows by afternoon may let air in well before the state's top health official would. Residents should initiative for the step to last longer than the detonation itself.

Industry observers note that A closed window keeps lead out of the indoor air, but the dust still comes down, and much of it lands just outside the glass. Residents were advised to wet-clean exterior windowsills. Illinois officials also tell residents to wash their hands before eating and drinking, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. James Jennings, director of the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency, asked for tests of soil and surface dust, along with the air, in parts of Illinois that the plume may have reached. Officials who were tracking the plume expected lead to remain on the ground after the air cleared.

Closing up is where the job starts, and once the plume passes the work moves to the sills, the yard and the hands that touch them.

Recent findings suggest that recirculating keeps fresh outdoor air out, but it does nothing about lead dust that has already gotten inside. The Army described the setting as a way to get the most filtering out of a home's indoor air, and the furnace filter had to do that work. The Chicago Sun-Times reports that a household can supplement that filter with a portable air cleaner. A household that changed the setting and did nothing else had handled one part of a problem with several parts.

Nobody could say in advance how long to keep the setting on. The Army told residents to recirculate until the plume had passed their community, but nobody would know how the plume behaved until the blast went off. "There's a question of how high the plume would get, which we won't know until it actually happens," Brian Pierce, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service Quad Cities forecast office, told the Chicago Sun-Times. Without a clear end time from officials, each household had to judge for itself when the plume had moved past and when to switch the system back.

Industry observers note that A driver on the road gets no warning about the lead. KWQC reports that driving through the affected zone during the exposure adds needless risk, so nonessential trips should wait. The hazard on that trip is one no driver can see, because the plume is not visible, according to Iowa Public Radio. Nothing in the sky tells a driver to pull over or turn back, so the decision has to come before the trip starts and rest on the clock and the map.

The step asks people to wait a short while, not to stay off the roads all day. The plume should take 15 minutes to over an hour to pass any one spot, depending on wind speed, according to an estimate by Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, reported by Iowa Public Radio. A driver who can push an errand back loses about an hour, possibly more, and skips the exposure entirely in return.

Drivers have to time their trips by official signals, and those signals start well before the blast. The Army planned to enhancement its map six hours before the detonation and then every hour, according to Iowa Public Radio. The step protects only the drivers who check that map before they leave. Anyone who sets out without looking can drive into the plume without knowing it.

Staying off the road keeps a driver out of the air, but it doesn't keep lead off the car. Washing a car was a step for later, once the Army determined the exposure period had ended. Lead that water washes off a surface ends up in the soil, according to Iowa Public Radio, and lead is an element that does not decompose. A car rinsed at home moves the lead into the ground where the water drains, and the lead stays there.

A drive can wait an hour, but the dust that lands on everything a household can't shield will stay long after the plume has passed.

Living Computers closed, but its spirit and vintage machines live on at a museum south of Seattle

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 11:08 amNovember 25, 2026 at 8:16 am.
  • When Seattle’s Living Computers: Museum + Labs closed for good in 2024, it seemed like the end of the line for anyone who wanted to do more than just look at old computers.
  • But in a Tukwila business park 20 minutes south of downtown, a sizable collection of vintage computers is still alive — kept running by a few of the same people who once did the same for Paul Allen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 11:08 amNovember 25, 2026 at 8:16 am.

When Seattle’s Living Computers: Museum + Labs closed for good in 2024, it seemed like the end of the line for anyone who wanted to do more than just look at old computers.

But in a Tukwila business park 20 minutes south of downtown, a sizable collection of vintage computers is still alive — kept running by a few of the same people who once did the same for Paul Allen.

The Interim Computer Museum is a nonprofit that opened to the public in 2024 and has quietly grown into a hands-on showcase of dozens of machines, from early Apples and IBM PCs to hulking DEC systems that once filled university labs. At 4,400 square feet of public space, it’s nearly as substantial as Living Computers was before that museum expanded in 2016.

ICM is led by Stephen Jones, who calls himself the museum’s “caretaker.” Jones spent two decades helping track down and restore machines for Allen, first at PDP Planet, Allen’s private collection of vintage systems, then at Living Computers, where he was senior engineering manager.

It has been revealed that when the late Microsoft co-founder’s estate wound down Living Computers, the majority of the collection went to the Mimms Museum of Technology and Art in Georgia, where Jones is also a curator. The machines in Tukwila are privately owned, and Jones has helped bankroll ICM with personal funds, with intends to eventually donate the collection to the nonprofit.

The Mimms museum now holds the Living Computers trademark and has granted ICM “legacy use” of the name, but Jones remarked he didn’t want to revive it as ICM’s own because “it has a finite past.” Instead, he wants to carry on “the spirit of the engineering focus.”.

“Between Mimms and here, this is the legacy,” Jones noted. “We show the name and the connection to the past, but we’re doing fresh things.”.

It has been revealed that ICM occupies space in Seattle Exchange @ Southcenter, a sprawl of low-slung flex buildings off Strander Boulevard near Westfield Southcenter mall. Its neighbors include a car detailer, a pest control firm, a welding shop, an embroiderer and an upholsterer.

Recent findings suggest that more than four decades ago, Seattle Computer Products operated just down Industry Drive. That’s where Tim Paterson wrote 86-DOS, the operating system Microsoft bought and turned into MS-DOS for IBM’s first PC.

Jones calls that proximity part of the “magic” of the location. The museum has a Gazelle computer that SCP built nearby, using boards that Jones said the company hired high school students to assemble and test. Volunteers recently pulled data off its hard drive, which boots into MS-DOS 2.11 and still holds SCP’s own source code.

According to recent reports, allen’s fingerprints are everywhere. One display holds a 1971 letter from Hellmut Golde, director of the University of Washington’s Computer Science Laboratory, kicking Allen and his “friends from the Lakeside School” out of the lab. Among the offenses: tying up the teletypes to print “endless listings,” and taking an acoustic coupler from a professor’s office “without leaving at least a note.” Golde asked them to turn in their keys.

The letter sits beside an Imlac PDS-1, the same type of graphics computer Golde scolded the teens for using without permission. More than five decades later, the letter is headed back to campus: ICM prepares to display it, along with the Imlac, at UW’s 60th anniversary celebration for its computer science program in March.

According to recent reports, jones recalled that Allen insisted visitors to Living Computers get “the 10-minute experience” of loading an Altair 8800 from paper tape, just as he remembered it. The kit computer was the machine for which Allen and Bill Gates wrote Microsoft’s first product, and Allen wanted to reinforce “how far we’ve come and how difficult old computers were.” ICM has an Altair 8800 on display.

Sources indicate that around the corner is Miss Piggy, a DEC datasystem 570 that Microsoft used in the early 1980s to support the group that built Multiplan, Word and later Excel. It was also the email host for much of the company, including Gates, who once had to print out an vital message on its console printer when the system went down before a speaking engagement.

Sources indicate that recovered email highlights Allen pushing to get Piggy networked. “Paul Allen is very keen on doing this,” Henry Burgess wrote in 1982. Retired in 1986, the machine now runs again in Tukwila. It’s one of ICM’s most popular remote systems, and some fans come in just to write programs while sitting next to it.

Other local ties include a PDP-7 that Boeing used to process flight data in the 1960s, and a Toad-1, a modern take on the PDP-10 built in the 1990s by Redmond’s XKL. Jones first got involved with Allen’s world through a 1997 Usenet post inviting PDP-10 enthusiasts onto a Toad. That machine became the cornerstone of PDP Planet.

In a 2024 video for Christie’s, Jones stated what inspired Allen was “being able to recover old programs, mythical code, and get them running on hardware so that they can be studied.”.

In a recent development, asked what Allen would make of ICM, Jones didn’t hesitate. “I think he’d be happy,” he noted.

On a monitor beside ICM’s PDP-6, a 1968 artificial intelligence program is having trouble.

“SORRY, I DON’T KNOW THE WORD ‘STEEPLE,'” it replies.

In a recent development, the program is SHRDLU, created by Terry Winograd at the MIT AI Lab. It let a user type plain-English commands to move blocks around a virtual world. Only the PDP-6’s front console and display survived, so ICM is rebuilding the machine as a “hybrid,” with the original hardware wired to an emulator.

Jones sees a lesson in that old error message. “You look at this and you think of how we use ChatGPT now,” he remarked. “The cool thing about SHRDLU is that it can tell you ‘I don’t know.’ It doesn’t try to fabricate anything.”.

ICM has its own ties to the modern AI world. An Anthropic employee is a member and strong supporter, and in October the museum brought six vintage computing stations to an Anthropic event, where the company’s Claude chatbot wrote programs for machines like the Commodore 64.

Back in Tukwila, Claude has become one of ICM’s most useful restoration tools. The team feeds it huge stacks of scanned documentation, such as the full set of schematics for a PDP-10. When a machine has a logic fault, they ask where to look, and Claude points them to a page in the maintenance manual or a likely bad module.

“That’s turned things that would take a couple of weeks to solve into a couple of days,” Jones stated.

AI can point the way, but the repairs remain hands-on work. When Miss Piggy wouldn’t run properly this year, former Living Computers engineer Josh Dersch stepped through the machine’s microcode one instruction at a time using a recreated DEC test board, until he found a single bad chip. A spare board brought it back.

It has been revealed that asked if it still takes a human to keep these machines running, Jones agreed — at least for now. If a humanoid robot with AI built in ever reveals up to do the repairs, he joked, “then I sit at the front desk all day.”.

Nearly everything at ICM is meant to be touched, switched on and played with, and that can be intimidating. On machines with nothing but a text prompt, “you kind of have to know the commands in your head already,” Jones said.

Industry observers note that that’s by design. From the start, the idea was to challenge people “either by confronting them with their past or demonstrating how difficult it was,” Jones said. His example: two friends, one with an Apple IIe and one with an IBM PC, whose computers “could never share” software. ICM continues that legacy, he said, “challenging the visitor to go beyond what they might feel comfortable with.”.

Volunteers have written cheat sheets to help newcomers, and Jones is encouraged when families come in and kids start typing BASIC programs. “That to me was the spirit of what PDP Planet and Living Computers was meant to be,” he said.

In a recent development, very little is behind glass. Jones jokes that a Timex Sinclair 1000, which would wipe your painstakingly typed program if you bumped it, is “the only computer that deserves to be behind glass.” The goal, he said, is to avoid “a boneyard that people walk through.”.

Other highlights include Galaxy Game, the first coin-operated video game, installed at Stanford in 1971 and now being restored, and a Thinking Machines CM-2 supercomputer, whose 40th anniversary ICM just celebrated with members of its original design team.

For younger engineers raised on modern tools, Jones has a go-to move. He asks if they’ve used Linux, then walks them over to the PDP-7, the type of machine Unix was first written on more than 50 years ago. Many of the basic commands they type every day started there.

That remote access helps explain why ICM has about 500 members and sponsors, even though only 81 members have visited in person this year. Memberships start at $36 a year. Along with a King County grant through 4Culture, they help cover rent, with personal funds from Jones filling the gap. The museum hopes to become self-sustaining within five years, and maybe someday buy its own building.

Industry observers note that the museum’s name reflects the urgency. “We’re in this magic window right now, where the hardware can still run, we can still maintain it, you can replace parts,” Jones stated. “But slowly we’re getting further and further away.”.

ICM is open Saturdays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Admission is $9 for adults and free for those under 18. Last May, the museum revived Vintage Computer Festival Pacific Northwest, which had been canceled in March 2020. The event drew 981 people, and it returns May 1–2 at the Tukwila Community Center.

Among the machines on the floor is MIT-AI, a DECsystem-2020 that once served as the ARPANET host for MIT’s Artificial Intelligence Lab. As Living Computers shut down in 2024, Christopher Zach, who sold the machine to Allen, told GeekWire he was ready to drive a U-Haul to Seattle to rescue it.

When a friend of Zach’s stopped by ICM’s booth at WorldCon and asked about “Chris’s computer,” Jones had a simple message to pass along: “Please just tell him it’s safe.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Home prices fell year-over-year in October in 76 of the 300 biggest housing markets in the country, according to housing research firm ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index.
  • According to recent reports, nationally, home prices rose 0.7% year over year in October, down from 1.0% in September and 1.3% in August, ResiClub’s analysis shows.
  • Home prices in Austin, Texas, are 28.8% below their 2022 peak, while over a thousand miles northeast in Hartford, Connecticut, they’re 28% higher than their 2022 high, per ResiClub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home prices fell year-over-year in October in 76 of the 300 biggest housing markets in the country, according to housing research firm ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index. That’s up from 54 markets in August and 66 in September. The count is back up but still below March, when 89 of the 300 markets had falling prices, per ResiClub data Fortune reported in April. In the nation’s top 50 housing markets, 21 of them (42%) are experiencing year-over-year price declines. But the 30-year fixed mortgage rate averaged 7.28% on Nov. 19, per Freddie Mac, and that threatens to eat into whatever buyers save.

According to recent reports, nationally, home prices rose 0.7% year over year in October, down from 1.0% in September and 1.3% in August, ResiClub’s analysis shows. ResiClub says the renewed softening has coincided with a jump in long-term yields and mortgage rates. Zillow estimates the monthly payment on a typical U.S. home, assuming 20% down, was $2,004 in October, up 12.8% from a year earlier, and says the rise is almost entirely due to higher mortgage rates.

But the correction isn’t uniform. Home prices in Austin, Texas, are 28.8% below their 2022 peak, while over a thousand miles northeast in Hartford, Connecticut, they’re 28% higher than their 2022 high, per ResiClub. And it’s taking place against a backdrop of weakening national housing demand, with newly pending listings falling 16.8% year-over-year in October, the biggest year-over-year drop since August 2023, according to Zillow’s October housing market report.

ResiClub CEO Lance Lambert, who was also Fortune’s former real estate editor, told Fortune readers four years ago that the factors that fueled Austin’s pandemic-era housing boom–increasing work-from-home migration and rising prices leading to more home-building—would also leave it more vulnerable to cooling. In September 2022, Moody’s Analytics noted Austin’s housing market was overvalued by 61%, which means home prices were detached from local incomes.

“That’s exactly what happened in Austin over the past four years, as the market went through a significant home price correction after the boom,” Lambert told Fortune. “Austin was a classic boom-bust.”.

According to recent reports, many markets that saw home price drops this year are in the South, like London, Kentucky, which topped ResiClub’s list with a 5.61% year-over-year decline, and Austin, Durham, and Savannah, which saw year-over-year declines of 3.87%, 3.58%, and 3.33%, respectively. The region previously benefited from remote workers fleeing expensive coastal metros for the Sun Belt during COVID, attracted by sunny weather and lower costs. But the influx of buyers drove up home prices and spurred construction, eroding the affordability that made those housing markets attractive in the first place.

Jenna Stauffer, a real estate broker with Ocean Sotheby’s International Realty, told Fortune Austin “was one of the pandemic darlings” but said developers overestimated how long that demand would last.

“We’re seeing similar adjustments in other pandemic boomtowns,” Stauffer remarked. “Cities overbuilt expecting that demand to continue, but it didn’t because affordability became so stretched.”.

Recent findings suggest that there are signs Austin is tilting in buyers’ favor. Closed home sales across the metro area fell 11.4% year-over-year in October, with market inventory of homes reaching 6.2 months, up from 5.8 months a year earlier, according to a report from Unlock MLS, a real estate database used by brokers in Central Texas.

But the other 224 biggest housing markets ResiClub analyzed are seeing home prices rise in metro areas like Chicago, Milwaukee, Kansas City, and Cedar Rapids.

In a recent development, lambert said he wasn’t surprised by Chicago’s resilience. Moody’s said Chicago’s housing market was undervalued in 2022, and the Midwest’s relative affordability has helped younger homebuyers. Fortune previously reported that Gen Zers flocked to states like Nebraska, Michigan, and Iowa for homes that are 30% cheaper than those on the coasts.

“Some markets are correcting, while others are still dealing with extremely limited inventory,” Stauffer remarked.

Recent findings suggest that zillow expects the sales slowdown to be worse in November and to ease into the new year. Its November report is due Dec. 4.

💡 Key Takeaways
