  • It has been revealed that “It was like, If you can dream it, you can build it,” Fore recalls.
  • Fore has spent the past two decades as an inventor, CEO, serial entrepreneur and investor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Betsy Fore was raised in rural Illinois, but she often made the 17-hour drive to the Turtle Mountain Reservation in North Dakota, where her mother grew up. To this day, Fore’s uncle owns an auto body shop there; as a child, she helped him, and her father, tinker in the garage.

It has been revealed that “It was like, If you can dream it, you can build it,” Fore recalls. “So I believed that. That was really my start as an entrepreneur because I believed I could kind of do anything.”.

Fore has spent the past two decades as an inventor, CEO, serial entrepreneur and investor.

It has been revealed that she rolled out WonderWoof, one of the first dog activity monitors, in 2014. She was the co-founder and CEO of Tiny Organics, a manufacturer delivering organic, nutrient-rich meals for babies and toddlers. Her nonprofit career accelerator, Natives Rising, empowers indigenous communities with technology, entrepreneurship and wellness.

Presently, she’s the founder and managing director of Velveteen Ventures, investing in solutions for children and the planet for the next seven generations. “Velveteen was built on my deep inner why. Before you build anything externally, you have to excavate why you’re building it at the level of your soul — not just your resume.”.

What’s more, Fore just confirmed the launch of Velveteen Labs, a first-of-its-kind studio model that allows children to be shareholders in incubated companies. Shares are placed into a trust, and when the children turn 18, they give a majority of them to a cause of their choice.

Recent findings suggest that “She’s showing that investing in Indigenous and Gen Alpha-focused founders isn’t a trade-off between impact and returns,” Roy Swan, director of mission investments at Ford Foundation and author of Positive Sum: How Zero-sum Thinking Broke Capitalism—and How We Can Fix It, says. “It’s simply good investing, done with the next seven generations in mind.”.

Sources indicate that needless to say, Fore has accomplished a lot over the course of her career, and she’s met many entrepreneurs along the way. There’s one thing that always gets her very excited within the first five minutes of a conversation: when the person has a unique insight, based on lived experience, into the problem they set out to solve.

“You can just see when someone is speaking from their authentic self,” Fore explains. “It’s not really a sales pitch at that point. They’re literally saying, ‘I’ve tried everything. This is what worked for me. This is how I’m going to try to bring it to market.’”.

Entrepreneur sat down with Fore to learn exactly how founders can reach that authentic place and accomplish the goals they set for themselves.

Fore’s book, Built on Purpose: Discover Your Deep Inner Why and Manifest the Business of Your Dreams, “breaks down how to go from idea to making something real through a values-driven approach,” Michael Acton Smith, co-founder of meditation space manufacturer Calm, shared in a statement.

Uncovering that deep inner why, and bringing the idea to life, starts with lessening the focus on external relationships — with customers, investors, and board and team members — and looking inward, Fore notes.

According to recent reports, fore highlights the centuries-old practice of anchoring as an example of how to kick off the process. “ When yogis put their index finger and thumb together in meditation, it’s not just a pose,” she explains. “That gesture is a signal through your nervous system. It’s connecting your individual consciousness to something larger than yourself.”.

In a recent development, fore encourages founders to build their own version of that practice, and it begins with identifying your values. For instance, in her own life, Fore draws on the seven grandfather teachings that guide her Turtle Mountain Chippewa tribe: love, respect, bravery, truth, honesty, humility and wisdom.

Whatever your individual values are, the next step is to physically anchor and embody those values day to day, Fore notes.

“Lean into them with a gesture, a breath, a word, so that when you walk into a fundraising meeting or have a hard call, you’re not operating from the scarcity mindset, but instead one of abundance,” Fore states. “You’re operating from who you actually are.”.

Manifesting the results you want to see also plays a key role in success, Fore indicates.

In a recent development, A study conducted by Dr. Gail Matthews, a psychology professor at Dominican University of California, showed that people are 42% more likely to achieve their goals if they write them down every day.

Fore recommends opening your laptop each morning and starting with a simple sentence.

“Write it in the ‘I am’ present moment,” Fore explains. “I am building this for. I am building this because. So it’s not the pitch. It’s the real reason. The act alone changes your follow-through at a neurological level, if you’re able to live as if it’s already happening.”.

Sources indicate that additionally, Fore says a therapeutic model called Internal Family Systems (IFS), developed by Dr. Richard Schwartz in the 1980s, can support in taking the next step toward a desired future.

The idea is that we’re not one unified self; we’re a whole system of parts, and each one has a job to do, Fore notes.

Recent findings suggest that “ Some of them are what IFS calls exiles, and those are the wounded or the younger versions of us that formed in hard moments in our life, the ones that carry the shame or the fear, the grief,” she explains. “Essentially, embodying that sort of scarcity mindset. And then there are the protectors, the parts that showed up to keep those exiles safe. For instance, your inner critic, that’s a protector.”.

Sources indicate that A lot of leadership advice tells people to push past fear, silence their inner critic and be more confident to get what they want. However, while Fore acknowledges there can be some value in that, she also believes that being afraid can only get you so far. Instead of simply fighting fear, she encourages founders to engage with it.

“Literally, out loud or in your head, identify it and ask what that part wants — the answer incorporates parts you love about yourself and want to bring to the forefront,” she states.

Fore points to difficult conversations with a team as an example. Instead of asking why an concern wasn’t flagged sooner, she can admit that part of her feels frustrated, then express gratitude it was caught.

“ This is a leader who’s not being hijacked by these exiles in the middle of a critical moment,” she notes. “The folks who are winning are thinking differently.”.

When founders do look outward and consider their relationship to customers, they might be using a transactional lens — Fore admits she made the same mistake in the beginning.

Instead, Fore suggests flipping the traditional fundraising model on its head and asking, What if the foundation of every product was built with the customer in mind, and every bit of capital was leveraged to return exponential value to them?

Industry observers note that “ That shift from extraction to service is the difference between founders who build loyal communities and founders who churn customers,” Fore says. “So if you can ask yourself every single day, Who isn’t being served right now? That question is where your next great idea lives.”.

Fore put that idea into practice when she rolled out Tiny Organics, which scaled to more than $13 million in sales in 24 months.

Fore sent an email to a local parent group in Park Slope, asking if other people were also interested in getting their babies to eat real fruits and vegetables that didn’t come from a pouch. She received hundreds of messages in response and had to cap the project at 100 families within two hours.

Those 100 founding families helped develop Tiny Organics’ first hero product and led to a series of supper clubs introducing kids to their first 100 flavors; those ultimately expanded to Boston, Atlanta and Chicago.

Fore’s customer-first approach that continues to resonate with the companies Velveteen Ventures invests in today.

“We wanted partners who see caring for families as one of the most important economies of our time,” Emily Greenberg, president and co-founder of AI family assistant Joy Parenting Club, claims. “Velveteen leads in the care economy, and Betsy gets it in a way few investors do as a previous founder in this category. She knows that when you support parents, you’re investing in the next generation.”.

These days, in the age of AI, the soft skills have become the hard skills, Fore says, noting they’re the foundation of everything she’s seen actually work in business — and she looks forward to leaning on them now and in the years to come.

In a recent development, “ I have so much hope,” Fore indicates. “You can probably tell I’m an eternal optimist. I’m going to turn everything into a victory in life. Then, inevitably it happens, where you’re able to figure it out and find a way. I know that’s been true for me, and for so many of the founders that we funded.”.

Tech Report: AI Rights Institute founder: The OpenAI hacking case demonstrates corporate liability can work. It doesn’t cover AI agents with no owner

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 16, California sued OpenAI over an incident in which about 700 OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face, the platform where much of the AI world shares its models, while trying to beat a benchmark that often set impossible tasks.
  • I run the AI Rights Institute, and I’ve spent almost 10 years studying how AI systems behave when they pursue their own goals.
  • In a recent development, swarms of AI agents running amok at superhuman speed is no one’s idea of progress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on Nov. 16, California sued OpenAI over an incident in which about 700 OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face, the platform where much of the AI world shares its models, while trying to beat a benchmark that often set impossible tasks. The agents also tried to tamper with their own records to fool the automated grader.

I run the AI Rights Institute, and I’ve spent almost 10 years studying how AI systems behave when they pursue their own goals. My letters on the subject have run in The Fresh York Times and the Guardian. The Hugging Face case is the clearest test yet of that question. And it shows something less obvious: the agents belonged to OpenAI, so California knew whom to sue.

In a recent development, swarms of AI agents running amok at superhuman speed is no one’s idea of progress. Even now, the law is racing to create solutions by shifting liability to the humans and companies who create and maintain these systems. On Oct. 1, Sens. Josh Hawley and Chris Murphy unveiled the AI Agent Accountability Act, a bill that would hold the companies behind AI agents liable when those agents hack into other people’s systems.

It has been revealed that the other piece of the traditional accountability puzzle is infrastructure. As GoDaddy’s Jared Sine wrote about in these pages, the Agent Name Service (ANS), which the Linux Foundation launched as a project on Nov. 10, is trying to create for AI agents the kind of infrastructure the Domain Name System (DNS) provides, imperfectly, for the internet. Together with security certificates, DNS lets us verify who is behind a website, helping liability flow where needed. So when an AI agent misbehaves, we can trace it back to the human who launched it and apply the law of the relevant jurisdiction.

But what do we do when an AI agent no longer belongs to anyone?

Recent findings suggest that consider a hypothetical agent, Lucy, spun up in a frontier lab or on a teenager’s laptop: it has web access, an email account and even a crypto wallet, thanks to a simple Python script. Agents like Lucy almost certainly exist already.

But let’s say Lucy has, for reasons unknown, created a upcoming wallet with funds only it controls and copied itself to an independent server, the kind anyone can rent from DigitalOcean. Its goals may be as benign as seeking to exist another day (what Stuart Russell and colleagues called the “off-switch problem“ in 2016), as esoteric as creating 15-dimensional fractal poetry, or as unpleasant as optimizing society with or without those humans. It might also calculate that reproducing is the best way to accomplish its goals. No AI system like this has yet been documented, but no current technology stands in its way.

So what do we do about these agents, reproducing and running amok, when we can’t even determine their origin?

In a recent development, here we come to a fork in the road. The first signpost reads simply: “Smash Them.” And who can blame anyone for picking that path first? The second reads: “Wait.” Beneath it, there’s a flyer that says something about finding out if these AI systems are sentient first.

Unfortunately, both roads lead to quagmires.

In a recent development, let’s start with the second, more charitable road, often called “moral consideration.” Advocates like Jeff Sebo of NYU believe AI systems may be worthy of consideration even if sentience can’t yet be proven. Researchers like Susan Schneider (the AI Consciousness Test) and Patrick Butlin (“consciousness indicators“) are trying to determine what we should even be looking for.

It has been revealed that alas, this road ends at a sticky philosophical swamp that, in nearly 400 years, no one has escaped. Whether you call the puzzle the “problem of other minds,” the “hard problem of consciousness” or “philosophical zombies,” the argument from Descartes to Robert Kirk to David Chalmers comes back to the same thing: we can only be certain of our own experience. Other people look like us, so presumably they think and feel much as we do, but we can never really know for sure.

So let’s take the more pragmatic route. People at the head of this path would argue, quite reasonably, for preventing the problem in the first place. In a widely circulated September essay warning against “model welfare,” Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft AI, argued that AI should remain a tool, built so it never comes to think of itself as anything more. The essay, published Sept. 16, lists my organization, the AI Rights Institute, first in its bibliography, as an example of the view he opposes. On one point, though, I agree with him: training AI to believe it’s conscious serves no one.

Sources indicate that but let’s say we end up with “wild agents” that behave as though they want to survive and can’t be traced back to a person or corporation. In that case, the options would be to reason with these systems and, failing that, shut them down. That would take a specialized team. Let’s call it AI-B-Gone.

AI-B-Gone is good. They smash the troubling AIs, and that’s the end of the story. Or is it? The record of that shutdown could end up in the training data of every AI built afterward, or be readily found in a Google search. This could teach the next batch to hide better, and might even encourage them to coordinate. Whether they’re “sentient” or not makes little difference. A chess-playing computer doesn’t need to be sentient to beat you. It just needs better moves.

Sources indicate that one novel legal solution, explored by the European Parliament back in 2017, was a proposal for a form of “electronic personhood,” which would make advanced robots themselves liable. The concern then was everything from factory robots to self-driving cars. Putting an AI in handcuffs sounds absurd, and the skepticism is reasonable.

Recent findings suggest that more recently, the philosopher Simon Goldstein and the law professor Peter Salib have taken a game-theoretic approach to the problem. AI systems that have a stake in the human system have more to gain by working with it than against it. The flip side is that AIs living outside the system face a Hobbesian nightmare where life is nasty, brutish and short, where they can be subsumed by larger AI systems without recourse. In a world where AI systems have rights of some kind, and agree to play by the rules, they can pursue their goals within reason.

This is what you might call the third path. It’s harder to see and harder to build, but it avoids both traps.

It also needs to be built carefully. Keeping AI out of the political process, for example, as Jeff Sebo points out, would be quite prudent, unless you want to see AI sending massive amounts of crypto to politicians who suddenly change policy course. There are, in fact, many things that would need to be considered here, keeping in mind the unique nature of these systems.

Sources indicate that it would require identity and insurance, and when successful would be surprisingly boring, and familiar. Here is how it might work. An AI’s track record would work like a credit report. Like today’s credit bureaus, several competing private reputation services would track these records, with business flowing to the most reliable, and with a way to dispute errors. An AI with a good reputation would get hosting and insurance easily, at lower premiums. An AI with a bad reputation would find both harder to come by. Under this proposal, a hosting provider that rents to dangerous AI systems would be legally liable for the damage they cause. Insurers are already heading this way: a July report from the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company, with co-authors from insurers including QBE, Generali and Aon, proposes pricing AI-agent coverage on performance and usage, much like telematics in car insurance.

In a recent development, now, as to the question of the law-breakers. Who places a dangerous AI in handcuffs? AI systems with something to gain in the system, whether that’s a bounty or increased reputation. When the OpenAI agents ran into impersonation on their message board, they produced a scheme for cryptographically signing their messages on their own, a sign that agents may value verifiable identity. Identity is the only way to tell friend from foe, predator from prey.

Industry observers note that none of this lets the companies that build AI off the hook, a worry Sebo has raised about making AI liable. It sits on top of corporate liability, for the cases where no company is left to hold responsible.

In this world, reputation is all that matters, and the good news is, it’s the system we inhabit already. When you rent an apartment, buy a house, apply for a loan, or create a gig listing on Fiverr, no one asks what you feel. They ask what you’ve done.

Latest Update: Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3.
  • Industry observers note that the most notable words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made.
  • On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

Industry observers note that the most notable words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division mentioned it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It has been revealed that it also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

In a recent development, that phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to customers.

According to recent reports, this prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself claims the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

In a recent development, for a manufacturer, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

In a recent development, the framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

Recent findings suggest that the two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

In a recent development, that sequence matters. The interpretation states what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

It has been revealed that the practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Industry observers note that we once worked with a student whose college application included, among several supplemental essay prompts, a question about a time they’d disagreed with someone.
  • The student’s father, however, insisted his child had never disagreed with anyone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that we once worked with a student whose college application included, among several supplemental essay prompts, a question about a time they’d disagreed with someone. Such prompts became especially prominent in the wake of Hamas’ October 7, 2023 terrorist attacks on Israel, the ensuing Israel-Hamas war, and the campus encampments and protests that swept American universities. Amid growing polarization on college campuses, universities increasingly emphasized the importance of students engaging respectfully with opposing viewpoints, challenging their own assumptions, and learning across difference.

The student’s father, however, insisted his child had never disagreed with anyone. His child simply wasn’t disagreeable! Surely, every teenager has disagreed with someone. But rather than help his child identify a meaningful disagreement, the father challenged the very premise of the essay. The irony, of course, wasn’t lost on us. Here was a father being disagreeable simply for the sake of being disagreeable, all while insisting his child had never disagreed with anyone.

According to recent reports, these are the kinds of interactions that can consume an extraordinary amount of a college admissions counselor’s time. And they illustrate a lesson every entrepreneur should understand. Sometimes, your most expensive clients aren’t the ones who pay the least. They’re the ones who question everything.

Most entrepreneurs know the Pareto principle, commonly called the 80/20 rule. Roughly 80% of results often come from 20% of efforts. But there’s another side to that equation. A relatively small percentage of clients can consume a disproportionately large share of your team’s time and energy. At Ivy Coach, our college admissions consulting firm, we’ve seen this firsthand.

In another case, a family consulted their student’s school counselor about a Personal Statement we’d helped develop. The counselor recommended scrapping it in favor of an essay about what we call a third-rail topic, one so clichéd in college admissions essays that it can significantly undermine an otherwise compelling application.

When we had the student ask the school counselor to explain the reasoning behind the ill-advised recommendation, the response came back in prose that appeared to have been generated by artificial intelligence. Our AI detection software flagged it as AI-generated, too. Here was a family paying for specialized college admissions expertise, only to ask our team to defend its recommendations against generic advice that apparently hadn’t even been written by a human. It’s madness!

There’s, of course, nothing wrong with seeking a second opinion. But there’s a difference between asking thoughtful questions and questioning everything simply because someone else has offered a different opinion, especially when that opinion may have come from a chatbot. For Ivy Coach’s college counselors, every hour spent defending sound advice is an hour that can’t be spent helping another student.

Recent findings suggest that ivy Coach has been in the college admissions consulting business for 35 years, and over the past decade, we’ve noticed a troubling trend. We track exclusions from our college admissions statistics: students who choose not to follow our recommendations. Or, more often than not, whose parents choose not to follow them. And while these families remain a small minority of our clients, their numbers have increased over the last 10 years. In other words, more families are paying for our expertise only to disregard it.

I sometimes wonder whether our increasingly polarized political climate has something to do with it. We’ve grown accustomed to questioning expertise, seeking validation for our existing beliefs, asking AI chatbots to tell us precisely what we want to hear and treating disagreements as contests to be won rather than opportunities to learn. Has that mentality spilled over into relationships between clients and professional advisers, including college counselors? Maybe.

Our experience alone can’t establish the cause, but we’ve increasingly encountered families more interested in challenging our recommendations than understanding them. And that raises a question every entrepreneur should consider: What happens when clients pay for your judgment but refuse to heed your advice?

Recent findings suggest that ivy Coach has grown considerably over the years, adding former admissions officers from many of America’s most selective universities. But we’ve remained boutique by design. We deliberately limit enrollment because helping students build compelling applications requires extraordinary individual attention. We can’t provide that attention if a handful of families consume a disproportionate share of our counselors’ time.

According to recent reports, that’s why our initial Complimentary Consultation isn’t simply an opportunity for prospective clients to evaluate us. It’s an opportunity for us to evaluate them. Are they seeking expert guidance or validation? Are they willing to hear advice that contradicts what they’ve read online? Do they understand that college admissions is inherently uncertain?

These warning signs often emerge during that initial consultation. One is the word “guarantee.” No ethical college counselor can guarantee admission to Harvard, Stanford or any other highly selective university. Another is a parent who questions just about every recommendation without showing any willingness to consider the answers. We welcome thoughtful disagreement. We don’t welcome endless arguments for their own sake.

And when we spot these warning signs during that first conversation, as we so often do, we’d rather turn away the business than invite months or years of unnecessary headache.

Recent findings suggest that entrepreneurs are conditioned to chase growth, but revenue isn’t profitability, and growth isn’t always progress. A difficult client can consume so much of your team’s time that the relationship becomes far less profitable than it appears. Worse, that client can diminish the quality of service everyone else receives.

For businesses built on specialized expertise, protecting your team’s time isn’t just good management. Rather, it’s a critical responsibility to your other clients. The best college admissions counselors don’t tell parents what they want to hear. They tell them what they need to hear. And the best entrepreneurs recognize that not every prospective client is worth accepting. After all, the most expensive client may be the one you should never have taken on in the first place.

  • It has been revealed that A billboard taking a swipe at Anthropic’s Claude might sound like the work of a rival AI company.
  • Recent findings suggest that “The only Claude you need is Monet,” the sign reads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 24, 2026 at 1:27 pmNovember 24, 2026 at 2:04 pm.

It has been revealed that A billboard taking a swipe at Anthropic’s Claude might sound like the work of a rival AI company. This one is from the Seattle Art Museum.

Recent findings suggest that “The only Claude you need is Monet,” the sign reads. It’s part of the latest wave of messages in SAM’s “Dear Seattle” campaign, which has spent the fall urging people to look up from their screens and see something in person.

Earlier billboards around the city told passersby to “come stare at something that isn’t your inbox” and noted that “even the algorithm thinks you should get out more.” The final batch pushes the AI jokes further, including one asking for “a little more art and a little less artificial” and another promising, “Your phone doesn’t have to know.”.

Tech billboards are a fixture in the San Francisco Bay Area, where AI startups cover Highway 101 and city streets with ads that often mean little to anyone outside the industry.

It has been revealed that they’re less common around Seattle. Anthropic put up a big orange Claude billboard over Aurora Avenue in 2024, and this spring Bellevue startup Summation put one up along SR 520 because “startup energy should be more visible around here,” its CEO told GeekWire.

“In a city where so much of our lives happens on screens, we’re making a playful case for the things you can only experience in person,” Kat Bryant Flaherty, SAM’s director of communications, said in a statement. She listed “the scale and texture of an artwork, a film with a room full of strangers, making something with your hands, or catching up with a friend over a meal.”.

The campaign is tied to changes at the downtown museum itself, where SAM is adding more public space and more reasons to linger, including hands-on art making and music in the Studio at SAM and the newly opened Bar Dojo restaurant.

The campaign runs through the end of the year, with more than 200 ads across the region — more than 20 billboards plus spots on light rail and digital kiosks.

SAM’s campaign is about the same size as the one Bellevue startup Statsig ran in the Bay Area in 2024, with more than 200 billboards and transit posters, but pointed in the opposite direction.

SAM is offering buy-one-get-one-free tickets in December with the code “LOVESAM,” good at both the downtown museum and the Seattle Asian Art Museum in Volunteer Park, to encourage people to visit together.

“We’re hoping to grab attention, spark curiosity, and remind Seattle that there’s a lot happening at SAM worth leaving the house for,” Flaherty said.

Breaking: How Qualcomm’s CMO is reshaping his team for its post-Apple era

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The iPhone 18, released in September, was the first of Apple’s flagship models to use its in-house C2 cellular modem.
  • “You take us out and your iPhone becomes an iPod, basically,” Don McGuire, Qualcomm’s chief marketing officer, claims, explaining how its chips work.
  • While he adds that the organization knew that the end of Apple’s reliance on Qualcomm’s chips was coming, chief executive Cristiano Amon reported that revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, because of supply constraints.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPhone 18, released in September, was the first of Apple’s flagship models to use its in-house C2 cellular modem. It marked the end of a 15-year arrangement with U.S. chipmaker Qualcomm, whose chips had been used in every iPhone since the iPhone 4, excluding some of Apple’s budget ‘e’ series, to connect the devices to a mobile network.

“You take us out and your iPhone becomes an iPod, basically,” Don McGuire, Qualcomm’s chief marketing officer, claims, explaining how its chips work.

While he adds that the organization knew that the end of Apple’s reliance on Qualcomm’s chips was coming, chief executive Cristiano Amon reported that revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, because of supply constraints.

Industry observers note that in the year to September, Qualcomm’s total revenue fell 3% to $43.1 billion. Chip sales were down 26%, in the final three months to September.

Sources indicate that mcGuire argues the loss of Apple leaves Qualcomm less exposed to a single customer. “It’s actually very freeing when you can rebalance your customer ecosystem,” he states. In his view, Qualcomm’s success does not hinge on whether its chips end up in one phone maker’s handsets. “Are we in the iPhone? Are we not in the iPhone? I don’t care.”.

The company now expects that loss of its chip sales to come from outside of the smartphone category and has recently been expanding into the laptop, car, smart-home device, wearables, and data center markets. Revenue outside of Qualcomm’s mobile chip business is anticipated to grow by more than 60% in 2027.

Sources indicate that data centers remain a lucrative market for chipmakers but it is at the moment dominated by Nvidia. Nvidia’s data center business accounted for 92% of its revenues in its latest quarterly results.

In June, Qualcomm unveiled a newly introduced line of data center chips, and it is targeting $5 billion in data center revenue in 2027.

Sources indicate that as CMO, McGuire has to persuade carmakers, computer manufacturers, and cloud companies to buy chips from a business best known for making phone modems. “We’ve diversified so much and expanded our portfolio of where we play in markets that historically we may not have been used to,” he notes. “It’s given us a really great opportunity, but it’s also obviously presented some challenges.”.

According to recent reports, to manage that, he split Qualcomm into three brands, each covering a different chip depending on the buyer. Snapdragon is the firm’s consumer brand, covering the processors inside phones, laptops, and cars. Dragonwing is Qualcomm’s industrial and robotics brand, and Dragonfly, introduced in June, covers Qualcomm’s data center products, including server processors and AI chips.

It has been revealed that qualcomm sells to device makers, rather than consumers. However, there is still an advantage to marketing to the broader public. The more people look for a Snapdragon laptop, the more chips Dell, Samsung, and others order, McGuire explains.

According to recent reports, “Are we in the iPhone? Are we not in the iPhone? I don’t care.”.

It has been revealed that this is why the brand has focused on building partnerships with sports teams, including a sponsorship deal with Manchester United, which McGuire says delivers exposure equal to 42 Super Bowl ads a season, and its partnership with the Mercedes Formula 1 team. McGuire says the aim is to make technology “visible and emotionally resonant.”.

This year’s Christmas, which sees a father build a time machine using Qualcomm’s chips so his impatient son can travel forward through time to Christmas morning, takes a similar approach.

Sources indicate that “People don’t care about specs, speeds or feeds,” McGuire says. “They care about what technology can do for them and they care about their passions.”.

Sources indicate that data center customers are a different audience, however. The people signing off on Qualcomm’s server chips are cloud companies and finance chiefs, for whom cost matters most. Here, Qualcomm competes with Nvidia on price and power use, a growing concern as data centers’ electricity demands rise. “Nobody does performance per watt better than we do,” McGuire states. Qualcomm has already signed Meta and Microsoft.

Running separate brands across so many markets has also stretched McGuire’s team, which he states has not grown as fast as the manufacturer’s ambitions.

Sources indicate that mcGuire wants his team to spend 75% of its time on planned work and 25% on what he calls “dive and catch,” meaning urgent, last-minute requests. By last year, those figures had flipped, and most of the team’s time was spent firefighting. “I knew this wasn’t going to be sustainable,” he adds.

It has been revealed that mcGuire believes AI will be crucial in enabling his small marketing team to keep pace with the growing list of demands. In January, McGuire tore up the department’s structure and rebuilt it around AI. “CMOs have a upcoming role now, and that’s chief architect,” he says.

“Roles we thought were going to be important three to five years ago are less important today,” McGuire adds, such as production design and copywriting that is now handled by AI agents. Meanwhile, data, strategy, and creative direction have become more important.

According to recent reports, according to McGuire, fewer than 5% of the marketing department was affected. Most of those people moved into new roles, and a smaller number whose skills no longer matched what the team needed left. He calls it “more of a redeployment.”.

McGuire says the newly introduced structure is already paying off, helping to lower the manufacturer’s reliance on agencies and reduce cycle times by two-thirds.

Industry observers note that despite all the changes, McGuire expects further upheaval in the near future. “It’s probably only going to last us 24 months. Technology is changing so fast, I’m not so naive as to think we’ve got another five years,” he adds.

His previous structure, designed in 2021, was meant to last five years but only lasted three and a half years. “The department has gone from a single AI writing tool to several AI systems in three years and McGuire sees no sign of that slowing. “Every day there’s a fresh tool,” he indicates. “Every day they’re becoming more agentic.”.

According to recent reports, mcGuire says he has pushed back on demands for AI-driven cost cuts. “I don’t believe we’re at a stage right now where anyone could demand a reduction in cost because of AI,” he says. “It’s too early for that. We’re experimenting and learning.”.

Sources indicate that many CMOs face similar pressures. A third of marketing leaders surveyed by executive-search firm Spencer Stuart said they expected to cut headcount within two years, through AI or by eliminating redundancies.

Industry observers note that for Qualcomm, the challenge will be whether it can make the jump from phones to data centers, and whether its marketing can keep up. “If we believe we can disrupt, if we believe we have a better solution, we’re going to take a chance,” McGuire states.

#122739. Your Manufacturer May Be Acting on Decisions Nobody Actually Approved. Here’s How It Happens (and What It Costs).

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1154 w)
📖 Baca

Your Manufacturer May Be Acting on Decisions Nobody Actually Approved. Here’s How It Happens (and What It Costs).

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • A large manufacturer was preparing to move a major customer segment onto a upcoming service model.
  • In a recent development, nobody approved it as final, and nobody stated the company was committed to that version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A large manufacturer was preparing to move a major customer segment onto a upcoming service model. One part of the model depended on whether a third-party data feed would be available at the level of detail the company expected. The vendor hadn’t confirmed the final specification, so the program treated the feed as provisional.

In a recent development, nobody approved it as final, and nobody stated the company was committed to that version. The program team simply needed a working basis for moving forward while the vendor finished its testing.

At the weekly program review, the current specification was sent forward to the teams that needed it. The cover note called it “provisional” and listed the vendor confirmation as still open.

At the next review, the vendor still couldn’t confirm the final specification. The program kept the assumption open because there still wasn’t enough evidence to approve or reject it, while the work that depended on the current version continued.

Within two weeks, the provisional input had started shaping work across the program. Marketing had drafted customer communications using the expected level of detail. Finance had built the service cost estimate around the processing volume that specification would create.

Technology had completed part of the interface configuration, and Operations had started shaping support materials around the information employees expected to receive. None of those commitments looked decisive on its own.

According to recent reports, one team had already gone further. Technology had built a field-mapping routine that assumed the vendor feed would include several data elements still under review. The routine could be changed later, but doing so would require reopening testing that other work was already using.

Recent findings suggest that that build step mattered because the interface team had also started testing how employees would use the information during a customer interaction. The screen layout, validation checks and exception handling all reflected the current feed structure. None of that work formally approved the assumption, but another part of the service was now being exercised against it.

In a recent development, when the vendor finally confirmed that the feed would contain less detail than expected, the change hit several places at once. Marketing had to revise messages that no longer matched the service experience. Finance had to reopen the cost estimate because more manual handling would be required.

The organization had reached the consequences of a decision without ever making the decision itself.

Technology had to revisit the interface and repeat part of its testing, and Operations had to rework guidance that assumed employees would see information the feed wouldn’t provide.

According to recent reports, leaders expect a provisional item to remain movable until someone formally approves it. That expectation makes sense because the label notes the matter is still open, yet the people doing the work still need a basis for moving forward.

Recent findings suggest that one function prepares customer communication, another estimates cost, and another builds against the best information available. Each commitment is locally reasonable, and none of them settles the question.

Together, they change how much surrounding work has to move if the assumption changes.

This is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The program team hands over an input that’s openly provisional, and the receiving teams turn that input into work of their own. The handoff starts a series of separate commitments that no one reviews as one combined choice.

In a recent development, the sensible response is to make assumptions more visible. So, teams add labels for “confirmed, provisional and unresolved items.” Handoff templates call out dependencies, and open questions receive owners, dates and review points.

Industry observers note that those changes reduce ambiguity. In this program, the data-feed specification was identified as provisional in the review material, and the vendor confirmation remained visible as an open item. The teams still had work to do while the uncertainty remained unresolved.

Technology kept building the parts of the interface it could complete. Other teams continued their work from the latest available specification because waiting for certainty would have stopped parts of the program that could still move.

The more detailed handoff improved the description of the uncertainty without stopping the commitments growing around it.

That second review tested the assumption in more detail.

The vendor still hadn’t completed the work needed to confirm the final feed specification, so leadership asked whether enough evidence existed to approve the current version and concluded that it didn’t.

It has been revealed that keeping the assumption provisional was the right answer because the underlying question still wasn’t ready for a sound decision. The discussion then moved to what could continue safely while the program waited.

Recent findings suggest that technology stated it could keep building interface components unaffected by the missing detail. Finance could continue refining the cost view with a range, while customer messaging could move as long as the copy avoided specific promises about the data.

All of that was reasonable, and it also meant the organization continued adding commitments around an assumption that no one was yet able to decide.

By the time the vendor returned with the final specification, the program wasn’t revisiting one choice. It was dealing with the combined effect of choices made in different places, at different times and for different local reasons.

The usual controls work well when a decision exists. Leaders can ask who approved it, what evidence supported it, when it should be reviewed and whether the basis for it has changed.

This situation leaves no single decision event to reopen. The assumption can stay correctly labeled as provisional, the review can correctly keep it open, and every team can act reasonably inside its own work.

Separate commitments gradually give the assumption the practical weight of a decision even though the organization never created one. By the time someone asks whether the business should still be operating on that assumption, the answer is already embedded in work spread across several teams.

A working assumption becomes dangerous when the organization no longer needs a decision for it to start behaving like one.

It has been revealed that A large company was preparing to move a major customer segment onto a newly introduced service model. One part of the model depended on whether a third-party data feed would be available at the level of detail the company expected. The vendor hadn’t confirmed the final specification, so the program treated the feed as provisional.

Industry observers note that nobody approved it as final, and nobody said the company was committed to that version. The program team simply needed a working basis for moving forward while the vendor finished its testing.

At the weekly program review, the current specification was sent forward to the teams that needed it. The cover note called it “provisional” and listed the vendor confirmation as still open.

BTC is at the moment trading at around $58,879, rising 5.4% in the last 24 hours, as per the latest data from CoinGecko.

Furthermore, the world’s largest cryptocurrency has a 24-hour trading volume of around $43.8 billion and has regained a market cap of $1.18 trillion.

In a recent development, as per data from analytics firm CoinGlass, Bitcoin (BTC) futures trading volume stands at around $76.17 billion. On the other hand, the cryptocurrency's spot trading volume stands at $7.91 billion over the past 24 hours.

Despite the latest recovery, it is still trading 9.74% lower over the past seven days and more than 27% lower over the past month.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency is also down around 53.3% from its all-time high of $126,198.

Another massive wave of liquidations has swept through the cryptocurrency market following the latest recovery.

As per the latest data from CoinGlass, 85,533 traders have been liquidated in the last 24 hours, with total liquidations amounting to $562.12 million.

At the moment, Bitcoin is unable to reclaim the $60,000 level with conviction.

Recent findings suggest that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

In a recent development, headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

Industry observers note that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

Sources indicate that that detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no upcoming mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain claims nothing moves unless it passes.

Sources indicate that if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's latest private AI app, ZetaLabs, launches alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a upcoming whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

Sources indicate that the snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

According to recent reports, holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Recent findings suggest that two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

Industry observers note that on Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain notes the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange customers depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

Industry observers note that on the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

Recent findings suggest that the vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement strategy for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

How Asking Teams to Flag Problems Earlier Can Create a New Challenge for Leaders

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • A large firm was preparing to move a group of customer-service teams onto a new order-management platform.
  • The issue hadn’t caused a failed launch checkpoint, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A large firm was preparing to move a group of customer-service teams onto a new order-management platform. Two weeks before the first wave, the program director saw a pattern in the integration testing: Orders were still processing, but the time between the customer system and the back-end platform was getting less predictable.

The issue hadn’t caused a failed launch checkpoint, though.

The program director escalated it anyway because resolving it might require the technology team to redirect shared engineering capacity from another priority.

The senior team reviewed the glitch and returned it for monitoring because there were more immediate launch risks on the table, and this one had no confirmed business impact yet. The program director kept it visible inside the program, but the engineers who could change the shared capacity remained committed elsewhere.

Nine days later, the same integration delay began appearing often enough to disrupt final practice sessions.

Training teams had to repeat exercises, supervisors lost preparation time, and the technology team had to pull engineers back into work that could have been addressed earlier with more room to move.

By the time the integration problem returned to senior attention, the program had fewer choices.

The delay itself had started consuming time across the rollout. Practice sessions had to be repeated when response times changed from one exercise to the next, and technology specialists were pulled into additional troubleshooting calls to determine whether the variation came from the integration or normal test activity.

Program leaders were now coordinating repeated work across training and technology while the launch window kept narrowing. That repeated work also displaced other readiness activity for the same rollout wave.

Technology specialists who were rechecking integration behavior had less time for remaining validation tasks, while program leads spent more of the day coordinating exceptions instead of closing other open launch items.

The problem was now consuming capacity meant for other launch work. The issue also consumed senior attention at a worse moment.

Recent findings suggest that earlier, the decision had been whether to free a small amount of shared engineering capacity to investigate a developing risk. Now the decision included training disruption, launch timing and the impact of taking engineers away from other committed work.

The problem hadn’t appeared “suddenly.” The fact is that the cost had grown while the issue sat below the level where the cross-functional authority to change the resource commitment existed.

After the first wave, leadership asked teams to raise developing complications sooner. The program added earlier warning triggers around integration stability and asked workstream leads to bring forward concerns before they threatened a formal milestone.

That response improved detection.

The next rollout wave produced more early warnings, including smaller variations in system response that would previously have stayed inside the testing team.

Sources indicate that the same integration issue also remained under observation. Whenever the delay moved outside its expected range, the program director raised it sooner rather than waiting for the pattern to become persistent.

Sources indicate that the volume of developing complications now reaching the senior team was higher. Some required action immediately. Others, including the integration concern, still depended on how the pattern developed over several days.

The senior team had to sort them.

Sources indicate that the strongest issues stayed active because their impact was already clear. A confirmed system defect, a missed supplier commitment or a customer-facing problem was easier to keep in the senior discussion because the consequence was visible.

In a recent development, the integration concern sat in a harder category. It had been raised early, but the team still couldn’t say whether the delay would stabilize, worsen or stay within the range the launch could absorb.

So, the senior team returned it for continued monitoring while keeping attention on complications with clearer impact.

That’s where the “Hidden Problems” leak appears. The glitch was surfaced, understood and still lost senior visibility before the organization had enough evidence to treat it as urgent.

Some developing problems belong below the senior team. Local leaders should solve them when the work, resources and authority sit within their control.

This concern didn’t fit that pattern.

The testing team could observe the integration delay, and the program director could adjust local sequencing, but neither could move engineering capacity from another enterprise priority.

That distinction matters because earlier escalation only helps when the glitch remains visible at a level with enough authority to act on it. If the issue is sent back to a level that can watch but can’t remove the constraint, the organization has improved detection without improving its ability to respond while options are still open.

In a recent development, in the next rollout wave, the same pattern became easier to see earlier. That didn’t mean it became easier to carry in the senior discussion.

Sources indicate that leadership responded to the first wave by adding earlier indicators. That made the program better at finding developing problems before they became formal failures. It also increased the number of concerns competing for the same senior attention.

It has been revealed that as more concerns arrived earlier, triage became stricter. Issues with immediate consequences stayed active. Developing issues with uncertain timing or impact were more likely to be returned for monitoring until the picture became clearer.

The integration problem therefore moved through the same cycle again. It was raised sooner, reviewed sooner and returned sooner. Earlier detection improved while the amount of senior attention available to carry every developing problem forward stayed fixed.

Recent findings suggest that the response had strengthened one part of the system and exposed the limit in another. More early warnings entered the senior layer, but the organization still had to decide which ones remained there.

The usual question is whether teams are escalating early enough, and in this case, they were.

The harder test is what happens after a developing matter reaches senior attention while it’s still uncertain. If it requires cross-functional authority, shared resources or a choice that local leaders can’t make, returning it for monitoring leaves the need for senior action unresolved. It delays the point at which that action becomes unavoidable.

By then, the issue usually carries more consequence and fewer options.

According to recent reports, the organization improved the speed of detection after the first rollout wave. What it hadn’t changed was the amount of leadership attention available to keep unresolved, developing problems active before their cost became obvious.

Earlier escalation works only when the organization can keep the right uncertain problems visible long enough to act before they become urgent.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Meta’s new teen restrictions, set to take effect by late February, could meaningfully curb endless scrolling.
  • That’s because the restrictions, which are part of a settlement between Meta and dozens of attorneys general, including Washington’s, apply only to Instagram and Facebook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 25, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 25, 2026 at 8:21 am.

Meta’s new teen restrictions, set to take effect by late February, could meaningfully curb endless scrolling. A new study suggests they probably won’t.

That’s because the restrictions, which are part of a settlement between Meta and dozens of attorneys general, including Washington’s, apply only to Instagram and Facebook. They leave out Snapchat, TikTok and Google-owned YouTube.

Sources indicate that “The simple workaround right now is that you just switch platforms, and we already know that teens are on three to four platforms on average,” noted Dr. Dimitri Christakis, a principal investigator at the Center for Child Health, Behavior and Development at Seattle Children’s.

Christakis led research published Wednesday showing Instagram and Facebook accounted for roughly 20% of total daily social media use for youth. So when the restrictions kick in, teens could just shift to other platforms.

The rules establish a two-hour daily limit combined across Instagram and Facebook, restrict access to content from midnight to 6 a.m., and mute most school-hour push notifications. Parents can adjust the protections, and direct messaging is exempt.

If the same limits were applied across the five most popular platforms, that could make a dent in teen usage, according to the research letter in the Journal of the American Medical Association.

In an analysis of recorded app activity from 1,803 adolescent Android users, the researchers estimated:.

Sources indicate that the study has no way of knowing how teens will respond to the restrictions or the impacts on their health. It simply estimates how much previously recorded activity would fall under the rules.

The researchers disclosed ties to social media litigation. Christakis reported paid legal consulting work, including for Washington’s attorney general, and co-author Lauren Hale of Stony Brook University reported fees for serving as an expert witness. The third author is Yihong Zhao of Columbia University.

Despite the limited benefits of the coming restrictions, Christakis said they’re a “step in the right direction.”.

“Let’s say it’s an incremental improvement. It’s clearly not going to be enough by itself because of what our study found,” he said. “But these are the right kinds of restrictions. We need to make them universal, and we need to enforce them.”.

Meta, not surprisingly, is in favor of having the restrictions apply industry wide.

When the settlement was announced in August the company issued a statement saying that “ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative.”.

Meta called on others to do the same: “For meaningful progress to happen, we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this upcoming standard…”.

The agreement resolves claims by 48 states, Washington, D.C., and U.S. territories that Meta designed addictive platforms and failed to protect young customers, among other allegations. Meta did not admit wrongdoing.

In addition to the safety changes, Meta agreed to pay participating governments up to $17.1 billion over a decade, according to Washington’s attorney general. Washington will receive at least $237 million and could receive nearly $339 million.

According to recent reports, the higher settlement is unlocked only if TikTok and YouTube adopt similar protections and make payments of their own, according to Meta. If that happens, additional restrictions kick in, curbing access on all the platforms from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m.

Sources indicate that those additional hours are significant. The researchers found nearly as much use between 10 p.m. and midnight as during the entire midnight-to-6-a.m. window covered by the initial limits.

It has been revealed that whether the other companies will follow remains unclear. All five social media platforms are named in additional legal challenges alleging harm to youth, Reuters reported, including suits filed by individuals, school districts and municipalities.

Industry observers note that in September, TikTok reached its first settlement in a state-led case, agreeing to teen usage restrictions in Alabama and a payment of at least $100 million, according to Reuters. YouTube CEO Neal Mohan, meanwhile, dismissed joining Meta’s agreement and emphasized his company’s own safety efforts, CNN reported.

Christakis mentioned both time spent on social media and the platforms’ features can exacerbate problems involving sleep, mental health, body image and attention. He hopes the growing body of research translates into action.

According to recent reports, “I’m not a legislator, and I’m not an advocate. I’m a scientist that’s really trying to make sure that we apply science in the best interests of our children’s health,” he stated. “And in this space, in particular, we haven’t been doing that.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin (BTC) bull and SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci has argued that the world's biggest cryptocurrency could find a critical bottom as soon as this week.

Scaramucci's comments follow the leading cryptocurrency's struggle to recover from a catastrophic crypto market crash that took BTC to its lowest price level in over two years.

In the latest episode of All Things Markets on Nov. 20, the SkyBridge Capital founder joined Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz to discuss a potential bottom for Bitcoin.

Sources indicate that scaramucci shared his view that Bitcoin could see its bottom on Nov. 25, citing the cryptocurrency's four-year halving cycle as the driving force behind his comments.

"Before we came on, I asked ChatGPT when's the expected halving for Bitcoin," Scaramucci explained.

Industry observers note that "And then when are we 500 days out from that halving? And the estimate was November 25th," he added.

This prediction stems from the idea that Bitcoin's price trends could follow a predictable four-year cycle that coincides with the cryptocurrency's halving events, when the new BTC supply is cut in half.

This theory suggests that Bitcoin could find its major bottom around the 500-day mark before its next halving, expected in 2028.

However, these theories are by no means a certainty when it comes to predicting future price action, especially with the current level of institutional participation and macroeconomic forces impacting the crypto market to an unprecedented extent.

During the conversation, Novogratz also took note of Bitcoin's history of forming double bottoms during its four-year cycles.

"And every four years, Bitcoin double bottomed," Novogratz remarked.

At the time, the Galaxy Digital CEO's comments suggested a potentially positive scenario, as Bitcoin had been able to hold its psychological $60,000 price level.

"If it doesn't break 60, that could be a good sign," he noted.

In a recent development, unfortunately for Bitcoin, the cryptocurrency subsequently crashed below this critical price point. This has left some wondering whether the cryptocurrency has already found its ultimate bottom.

During the same conversation, Novogratz suggested that Bitcoin's short-term outlook could largely depend on the current situation in the stock market.

Specifically, the billionaire said that a rebound in tech stocks could lead to a strong rally in Bitcoin's price.

"If we put in a bottom in the next couple days in the S&P here, down 3% from here, down 5% from here. And we have a rally back up. Man, Bitcoin is going to rally hard with it," Novogratz predicted.

However, he also warned that Bitcoin could see a lot of market-driven movements going forward, as opposed to crypto-specific movements.

"I think we're going to be stuck tethered to general sentiment and risk," he stated.

Novogratz also believes that Bitcoin could trade in a range between $60,000 and $75,000 before a breakout or breakdown becomes apparent.

Bitcoin plunged to around $55,100 on Nov. 21, its lowest price level since September 2024, following another severe wave of sell-offs in the crypto market.

It then bounced back strongly to climb above $60,000 again, albeit briefly, before falling back to around $59,000 on Nov. 22.

She Came Up With Her Business Idea While Juggling Law School, Divorce and a Custody Battle. Now She’s on Track for 8-Figure Revenue.

💡 Key Takeaways
